# Eclipse Atesor

> Eclipse Atesor is an open-source agentic framework that ports software to RISC-V. It builds each package natively on riscv64, repairs what breaks, checks that every binary is real riscv64 code, and writes a recipe that a person or a CI job can replay.

---

# What is Atesor

Section: Introduction
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/what-is-atesor/

Eclipse Atesor™ is an open-source agentic framework that ports software to RISC-V. It builds each package natively on riscv64, repairs what breaks, checks that every binary is real riscv64 code, and writes a recipe that a person or a CI job can replay.

You give Atesor the URL of a source repository. Atesor clones the repository into a riscv64 sandbox and builds it. It repairs the build when it fails, and gives back the result, the evidence and the steps.

## Who is Atesor for?

- **Porters.** Porting work repeats the same steps: clone, find the build system, install packages, hit a known issue, patch, try again. Typical issues are a stale `config.guess`, x86-only SIMD code, the Go `-buildvcs` check, and differences between musl and glibc headers. Atesor runs this loop and records each change that it makes.
- **Distribution and package maintainers.** Atesor builds in an Alpine sandbox (musl) and in a Debian/Ubuntu sandbox (glibc). It keeps a separate recipe for each sandbox, because the `apk` and `apt` commands are different.
- **RISC-V hardware vendors.** The native target runs the same pipeline on a riscv64 machine that Atesor reaches over SSH. Native results stay separate from QEMU results. On the native target, performance mode can also find a faster build of a package for the board.
- **CI owners.** Each run ends with an exit code that a CI job can test. The codes are 0 (verified port), 1 (failure), 2 (packaging failure), 3 (not verified) and 130 (interrupt). The repository also has a batch runner and GitHub Actions workflows that port lists of packages.

## What does a run give back?

Each run that completes the agent pipeline writes a build report and a JSON snapshot of its state. It also writes a debug log and a log of every LLM call. A successful run also gives these items:

- **riscv64 binaries.** The build outputs stay in the build tree. Atesor reads the ELF header of each output to prove that it is riscv64 code. With `--package`, Atesor also writes a zip file with the source tree, the recipe and a `manifest.json`. The manifest lists each riscv64 output, with a SHA-256 for each output inside the zip.
- **A replayable recipe.** The file `<repo>_recipe.md` gives the prerequisites, the build commands, the architecture notes and the commands to check the binaries. Atesor keeps the recipe of each verified port in its recipe cache, so a second request for the same package does not build again. Only `--force` and `--optimize` make Atesor build it again.
- **Patches.** Each patch that the fixer applied, in its own `.patch` file.
- **A faster build (optional).** With `--optimize` on the native target, Atesor can find a faster tune: the same build with other compiler or toolchain settings. With `--package`, the zip holds the artifacts of that tune in `optimized/`.

[Read the output](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/read-the-output/) describes each file.

## What does Atesor support today?

| Area | Current scope |
|---|---|
| Languages | C, C++ and Go. Rust and Node.js have partial support only. |
| Build systems | Make, CMake, Meson, autotools and Go modules. Cargo and npm at a lower level. |
| Sandboxes | Alpine Linux riscv64 (musl) and Debian/Ubuntu riscv64 (glibc) |
| Targets | `qemu` (default): QEMU emulation on an x86 or ARM Linux host. `native`: a riscv64 machine over SSH. |
| LLM providers | Gemini (default), OpenAI, OpenRouter and Anthropic |
| Performance mode | Optional, with `--optimize`: faster builds of a verified port for the machine. Only the `native` target measures speed. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/). |
| Install | A `.deb` package for Ubuntu 22.04, or a source checkout |

[Limitations](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/limitations/) lists what is out of scope today.

## What is Atesor not?

- **It is not a cross-compiler.** Atesor does not build riscv64 code with an x86 or ARM toolchain. Each build runs in a riscv64 container, with the riscv64 compilers and tools of the sandbox image. If one build output is x86-64, aarch64 or riscv32 code, verification fails the port.
- **It is not binary translation.** Atesor does not convert an existing x86 or ARM binary. It builds the package from its source code. On an x86 or ARM host, QEMU runs the riscv64 tools of the sandbox, and the result is riscv64 machine code. [About the name](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/name/) compares Atesor with Rosetta, a binary translator.
- **It is not a hardware test.** Verification proves the architecture of each output. The package's own tests run one time after the build, but they do not decide the result of the port.

## Licence and governance

Atesor uses the MIT licence. It is an Eclipse Foundation project in incubation, under the OpenHW Group. See [Governance](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/governance/) and the [Eclipse project page](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/openhw.atesor). The source code is at [github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor).

## Next steps

- [How it works](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/how-it-works/): the flow from a repository URL to a recipe.
- [Requirements](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/requirements/): what your host needs.
- [Your first port](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/first-port/): port zlib to riscv64.

# How it works

Section: Introduction
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/how-it-works/

Eclipse Atesor™ takes a repository URL and runs a fixed sequence: a cache check, a sandbox start, a graph of agents, and the output files. Scripts do each step that a script can do. Atesor makes an LLM call only where a step needs judgment. Two examples are a build plan for an unusual project and a fix for a new error.

This page gives the concept. [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/) gives the detail.

## What happens when you start a port?

You start a port with a command such as `python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib`. Then `main.py` does these steps:

1. **Check the input.** Atesor accepts only a plain `http` or `https` URL without shell metacharacters. It takes the package name from the URL, for example `zlib`.
2. **Look in the recipe cache.** If the cache has a recipe for this package, this sandbox and this URL, Atesor writes the recipe file and stops. This step needs no API key and no Docker. The `--force` flag skips the cache. The `--optimize` flag also skips this step, because performance mode needs a real build tree.
3. **Check the API key.** Atesor reads `LLM_PROVIDER` and stops if the key for that provider is not set.
4. **Start the sandbox.** Atesor checks that the host can run riscv64 code through binfmt_misc. It builds the sandbox image if the image does not exist, starts the container, and checks that the container reports `riscv64`.
5. **Run the agent graph.** A LangGraph state machine runs the nodes in the next section. One `AgentState` object carries all data of the run from node to node.
6. **Write the outputs.** Atesor writes the state snapshot, the build report, the recipe and the patches. With `--package`, it also writes a zip file.

## How does the graph go from source code to recipe?

The graph is in `src/graph.py`. The arrows show the usual path.

```text
init_node             clone + scripted analysis                (no LLM)
   |
   +--> cached_recipe_node   cached build plan, --optimize only    (no LLM)
   |                         then to supervisor_node
   |
analyst_node          read the build files, write an analysis  (LLM)
   |
heuristic_plan_node   default build plan                       (no LLM)
   |        \
   |         scout_node   LLM build plan, only when needed
   |        /
supervisor_node       route by rules                           (no LLM)
   |
   +--> build_fix_subgraph:  build_node -> verify_node -> fix_node -> build_node
   +--> scout_node           new plan after some failures
   +--> finish_node          package tests, recipe, learning
   |       |
   |       +--> optimize_node   performance mode, --optimize only
   +--> escalate_node        report for a person
```

1. `init_node` clones the repository inside the sandbox. It then runs a scripted analysis: build system detection, dependency extraction, and a scan for architecture-specific code.
   - With `--optimize`, if the recipe cache has a verified recipe of the package, `init_node` sends the run to `cached_recipe_node`. This node makes the cached build plan the plan of the run and applies the cached patches. The analyst and the scout make no LLM call. If the cached recipe has no command, the run goes to `analyst_node`. `--force` makes Atesor plan again.
2. `analyst_node` reads excerpts of the real build files and docs. It writes a package analysis: the purpose, the build system, the dependencies, the RISC-V risks and the expected artifacts. It also sets `needs_custom_plan` when a standard recipe will not work.
3. `heuristic_plan_node` writes a default build plan for CMake, Make, autotools and Go. It sends the work to `scout_node` in these cases:
   - The analyst set `needs_custom_plan`.
   - The confidence in the build system is less than 0.5.
   - The scan found one critical, or three or more high, architecture-specific findings.
   - The build system has no default plan, for example Meson or Cargo.
4. `scout_node` asks the LLM for a build plan, based on the analysis and the build files. When it plans again after a failure, it also sees the error.
5. `supervisor_node` chooses the next node with rules only. A `SUCCESS` status always goes to `finish_node`. A failure with a `DEPENDENCY` or `MISSING_TOOLS` error goes back to the scout for a new plan. A known plan error, such as a missing `./configure` script, also goes back to the scout, one time for each error type. Other failures go back into the build-fix loop.
6. Inside `build_fix_subgraph`, `build_node` runs the phases of the plan. When a command fails, it first tries its recovery heuristics. `verify_node` reads the ELF header of each build output. `fix_node` asks the LLM for a fix, applies it, and sends the run back to `build_node`.
7. `finish_node` runs the package's own tests one time. It then asks the LLM to write the recipe. When the port is verified, it saves the recipe in the recipe cache and adds few-shot examples.
8. `optimize_node` runs after `finish_node` only with `--optimize`. The next section describes it.
9. `escalate_node` writes a report for a person when the run cannot finish.

## What happens after a verified port with `--optimize`?

Performance mode is an optional stage after the port. It tries faster builds of a verified port for the machine that runs Atesor. Each build that it tries is a tune: the same build with other compiler or toolchain settings. The verified build always stays the result of the port. A faster tune is an extra output.

1. **Probe the machine.** Atesor reads the ISA extensions, the core, the CPUs and the compilers of the machine.
2. **Build a baseline.** Atesor builds the verified build again in a copy. It compares each tune with this copy.
3. **Select a workload.** The workload is a run that does the same fixed work each time, for example the benchmarks of a Go module. For programs and libraries, the optimizer agent (an LLM) proposes a program run or writes a small harness.
4. **Build the tunes.** Examples are `-march` with the probed extensions, `-O3`, LTO, clang and PGO (profile-guided optimization).
5. **Check each tune.** Each tune must make riscv64 artifacts with its settings. The package tests must still pass, and the workload output must be the same as the baseline output.
6. **Measure each tune.** Only on the native target, Atesor times each tune against the baseline. A faster tune must win again in a second check. Under QEMU, Atesor checks the tunes but makes no speed claim.

For a port that is not verified, performance mode stops with the status `skipped`. It never changes the exit code of the port. [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) tells how to use it. [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/) gives the design.

## What does "deterministic first" mean?

Deterministic first is the first design rule of Atesor: do not spend an LLM call on work that a script can do. A deterministic step gives the same result for the same input. The rule shows in each part of the pipeline:

- **Analysis.** The clone, the build system detection, the dependency extraction and the architecture scan are scripts in `src/scripted_ops.py`.
- **Planning.** For a known build system, the default plan comes from code. The LLM scout runs only when the default plan cannot work.
- **Routing.** The supervisor uses rules. It makes no LLM call.
- **Repair.** The builder tries its recovery heuristics before the fixer gets the error. For example, it installs the distro package for a missing header, or it builds again on one thread after a suspected out-of-memory kill under QEMU.
- **Verification.** A script reads the ELF headers. No LLM decides if a binary is riscv64 code.
- **Performance mode.** Scripts probe the machine, build the tunes, check them and time them. The LLM only proposes a workload. Statistics, not an LLM, decide if a tune is faster.
- **LLM answers.** Each answer must pass a schema check. When an answer is not valid after the retries, a deterministic fallback takes its place where one exists.

## Where does Atesor use an LLM?

An LLM call happens only at these points:

| Step | When | Fallback if the LLM fails |
|---|---|---|
| Analyst | Once at the start of the run, but not in a run from a cached recipe | An analysis from the scripted detection |
| Scout | No default plan, or a new plan after a dependency, tool or plan error | A fallback build plan |
| Fixer | After a build or verification failure | None. The run fails or escalates. |
| Summarizer | Once at the end of a successful run | A short recipe from the build steps |
| Artifact curator | Once at the end, to rank the build outputs | Rule-based ranking |
| Optimizer | Only with `--optimize`, after a verified port: a program run or a harness for the workload | The next workload source. The package tests are the last source. |

Before the fixer proposes a fix, it can ask for one round of read-only commands, such as `cat` or `readelf`. The round has a limit of 4 commands.

Atesor writes each call to the LLM call log, with its tokens and its cost. The cost cap stops a port at $1.00 of LLM cost. The supervisor applies the cap, so the cap does not stop the optimizer, which runs after the port. See [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).

## How does a run end?

A run stops at the first of these conditions:

- The build succeeds. Atesor goes to `finish_node`, also when the success comes on the last attempt.
- The run reaches the attempt limit, 5 by default (`--max-attempts`).
- The last three errors have the same signature (an error loop).
- The last error is a permission error or a disk space error.
- The LLM cost is more than $1.00.

Every stop except a success goes to `escalate_node`, and the command exits with code 1. A success exits with code 0 when verification proves riscv64 output, or with code 3 when it does not. With `--optimize`, performance mode runs after a success and does not change the exit code.

## Next steps

- [Concepts](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/concepts/): the terms on this page.
- [Your first port](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/first-port/): see the flow on a real package.
- [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/): the nodes, the routing functions and the state.

# Concepts

Section: Introduction
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/concepts/

This glossary defines the terms that the Eclipse Atesor™ docs use. Most terms are also names in the code, so you can search for them in the source and in the logs.

## Where builds run

### Sandbox

A sandbox is the riscv64 Linux container where Atesor clones and builds a package. On the QEMU target, it is a Docker container (`atesor-ai-sandbox` or `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian`) with the host workspace mounted at `/workspace`. On the native target, it is a rootless podman container on the riscv64 machine.

### Platform

A platform is the Linux distribution inside the sandbox. You select it with `--platform` or `ATESOR_PLATFORM`. The `alpine` platform uses musl, and the `debian` and `ubuntu` platforms share one profile with glibc. Each profile is a `PlatformProfile` in `src/platforms.py`, with its package manager and its map of package names.

### Target

A target is the place where builds run. You select it with `--target` or `ATESOR_TARGET`. The `qemu` target (the default) runs the sandbox on your computer under QEMU emulation. The `native` target runs it on a riscv64 machine over SSH and keeps its state in `workspace-native/`.

## How a port runs

### Scripted operations

Scripted operations are the deterministic steps in `src/scripted_ops.py`: the clone, the build system detection, the dependency extraction and the scan for architecture-specific code. They make no LLM call. The build report shows their number as "Scripted Operations".

### Agent and node

A node is one step of the LangGraph state graph in `src/graph.py`, for example `analyst_node` or `fix_node`. Each node has an agent role (`AgentRole`: planner, supervisor, scout, builder, fixer or summarizer). The `@agent_node` decorator gives each node the same error capture, rate-limit retry and audit log.

### AgentState

`AgentState` is the one dataclass in `src/state.py` that carries all data of a run from node to node. It holds the plan, the build status, the errors, the fixes, the cost and the verification verdict. Nodes change it in place. Atesor saves it as `<repo>_state_<timestamp>.json` when the graph finishes.

### Package analysis

The package analysis (`PackageAnalysis`) is the result of `analyst_node`, which reads the real build files and docs of the package. It gives the purpose, the build system, the dependencies, the RISC-V risks, the expected artifacts and the `needs_custom_plan` flag. The heuristic planner, the scout, the fixer and the verification step all use it.

### Recovery heuristic

A recovery heuristic is a repair in the builder that needs no LLM, for a known failure pattern. For example, the builder installs the distro package for a missing header. It builds again on one thread after a suspected out-of-memory kill (exit 137). It adds `-mcmodel=medany` after a RISC-V relocation error. The builder tries a heuristic before the fixer gets the error.

### Escalation

Escalation is the end of a run that cannot finish. The supervisor escalates in these cases:

- The run reaches the attempt limit.
- The last three errors have the same signature (an error loop).
- The last error is a permission error or a disk space error.
- The LLM cost goes above the cost cap.
- A node crashes.

`escalate_node` writes a report for a person, and Atesor exits with code 1.

### Cost cap

The cost cap stops a port when its LLM cost is more than $1.00. Atesor prices each call from the token usage that the provider reports (`cost_for_usage` in `src/models.py`). Free OpenRouter models count as $0. The supervisor applies the cap, so the cap does not stop the optimizer agent of performance mode, which runs after the port.

## What a port produces

### Verification

Verification is the ELF check in `verify_node`. A program in the sandbox reads the ELF header of every build output and of every member of every static archive. The verdict is one of these:

- `verified`: riscv64 ELF64 outputs, and no output for another architecture. Exit code 0.
- `wrong_arch`: one output or more for another architecture, such as x86-64, aarch64 or riscv32. The port fails, and the fixer gets an `ARCHITECTURE` error.
- `unverified`: Atesor cannot prove a riscv64 output, for example for a header-only library. Exit code 3.

### Artifact

An artifact is a file that the build produced: an executable, a shared library or a static archive. Atesor records the riscv64 artifacts in the state, and the artifact curator ranks them as primary or secondary for the recipe. With `--package`, the zip manifest lists each one, with a SHA-256 for each file inside the zip.

### Recipe

The recipe is the Markdown file `<repo>_recipe.md` that the summarizer writes at the end of a successful run. The prompt asks for six sections, from the prerequisites to the commands that check the binaries. A person or a CI job can use it to do the build again.

### Recipe cache

The recipe cache is the file `recipe_cache.json` in the data folder. It holds one entry for each package and sandbox key, for example `alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64-native`. On a cache hit, Atesor writes the recipe file from the entry and does not build. Atesor adds an entry only for a verified port. A measured performance mode result from the native target goes into the entry, under `optimizations`.

### Few-shot memory

Few-shot memory is the set of example files in `data/examples/`, one file for each agent role. A verified port adds examples with `source: "auto"`, up to 100 for each agent. The scout and fixer prompts show the examples that match the build system and the sandbox, found by keywords and regular expressions.

## How performance mode runs

### Performance mode

Performance mode is the optional stage that `--optimize` adds after a verified port, in `optimize_node`. It builds tunes of the port for the machine, checks them, and measures them on the native target. The verified build always stays the result of the port.

### Machine probe

The machine probe is a sandbox program that reads the ISA extensions, the core, the misaligned access speed, the CPUs and the compilers. Test instructions decide which extensions are present (`src/machine.py`). `--probe` runs only the probe and saves the result as `machine_profile_<native|qemu>.json`.

### Tune

A tune is one optimized build of the package: the same build commands with other compiler or toolchain settings (`Variant` in `src/optimize.py`). Examples are core tuning (`-mtune`), machine ISA (`-march`), `-O3`, link-time optimization, clang, `GORISCV64` for Go, and PGO. Each tune builds in its own copy of the patched tree, `<repo>.opt/<id>`.

### Baseline

The baseline is a copy of the verified build that Atesor builds again in `<repo>.opt/base`, in the same way as each tune. Atesor compares each tune with this copy, so only the change of the tune counts.

### Workload

The workload is the run that Atesor times. It must do the same fixed work in each run (`src/workload.py`). Atesor tries the sources that fit the package type, in this order:

1. The Go benchmarks of a Go module.
2. A run of a program of the package.
3. A harness for a library.
4. A test or example program of the package that calls its library.
5. The package tests.

### Optimizer agent

The optimizer agent is the LLM step of performance mode. It proposes a program run, or writes a harness: a small driver program against the public API of a library. It uses the model of the `builder` role for a harness and the model of the `planner` role for a program run.

### PGO

PGO (profile-guided optimization) is the last tune, for C/C++ and Go only. For C/C++, Atesor builds the best tune with profile instrumentation, runs the workload to record a profile, and builds again with that profile. For Go, Atesor records a CPU profile from the Go benchmarks of the workload.

### Gates

The gates are the correctness checks of each tune:

- The artifacts must be riscv64 code that the settings of the tune built.
- The package tests must still pass.
- The workload output must be the same as the baseline output.

### Measurement

On the native target only, the measurement times the baseline and a tune in rounds, pinned to one CPU (`src/bench.py`). Each round runs the two builds in random order. A tune is faster when the upper bound of the 95% interval of its time ratio is below 0.98 and p < 0.05.

### Accepted tune

An accepted tune is a tune that the measurement found faster and that won again in a second check. Atesor copies its riscv64 artifacts to `<repo>.opt/accepted`. Under QEMU, Atesor never accepts a tune.

## Related pages

- [How it works](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/how-it-works/): these terms in the order of a run.
- [Agent state](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/): every field of `AgentState`.
- [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/): the full rules of the ELF check.
- [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/): how to use `--optimize` and `--probe`.

# Limitations

Section: Introduction
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/limitations/

This page lists the current limits of Eclipse Atesor™ in the code on the `main` branch. Read it before you depend on a result, so that you know what a verified port proves and what it does not prove.

## Which ecosystems does Atesor not fully support?

- **Default build plans exist for four build systems only:** CMake, Make, autotools and Go. For Meson, Cargo, Python and every other build system, the LLM scout must write the plan.
- **Rust, Python and Node.js are not first-class targets.** Atesor has only partial heuristics for them. It detects an npm project only when the project has a `package-lock.json` file or a build script.
- **Gradle, Maven and Bazel have no special support.** Atesor detects their build files, but it has no default plan and no recovery heuristic for them.
- **Atesor cannot verify header-only and script-only packages.** They produce no riscv64 binary, so the result is `unverified` and the exit code is 3.

## What can a verified port not tell you?

A `verified` verdict means that the ELF header of each build output shows a 64-bit RISC-V file, and that no output is for another architecture. It does not prove these points:

- The program runs correctly. The package's own test suite runs one time after the build (`ctest`, `meson test`, `go test`, `cargo test`, `make check` or `make test`). The result goes into the report, but it never fails the port.
- The program runs well on a specific board. On the QEMU target, the build and the tests run under QEMU user-mode emulation on an x86 or ARM host. A port makes no performance measurement. Only performance mode (`--optimize`) on the native target measures speed.
- The build is complete. Atesor checks the outputs that the build produced. If the build makes some riscv64 outputs but skips a target, the port still counts as verified. Atesor looks for the expected artifacts from the analysis only when the build tree has no output.

For results from real hardware, use the [native target](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## Why does Atesor not cross-compile?

Atesor builds only inside a riscv64 container, with the riscv64 compilers of the sandbox image. It never uses an x86 or ARM cross toolchain. This choice has two results:

- On the QEMU target, every compiler and build tool runs under emulation.
- An output for another architecture is a failure. One x86-64, aarch64 or riscv32 output fails the verification, also when the other outputs are riscv64.

## What are the hard limits?

| Limit | Value | Where to change it |
|---|---|---|
| Fix attempts for each port | 5 | `--max-attempts` |
| Error loop | 3 errors in a row with the same signature | Not configurable |
| LLM cost for each port | $1.00 | Not configurable (`should_escalate` in `src/state.py`) |
| Graph steps for each run | 120 | Not configurable (`recursion_limit` in `main.py`) |
| Time for one build command | 1800 s | Not configurable (default of `execute_command`) |
| Time for the package tests | 600 s | `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT` |
| Candidate files that the artifact scan reads | 20000 | Not configurable. A scan that stops at this limit gives `unverified`. |
| Time for one LLM request | 120 s | `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` |
| LLM output tokens | 8192 | `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` |
| Fixer investigation | 1 round of up to 4 read-only commands | Not configurable |
| Few-shot examples for each agent | 100 | Not configurable |
| Memory of the QEMU container | 8 GB | Not configurable (`mem_limit` in `main.py`) |
| Time for performance mode | 3600 s | `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` |

## What limits apply to the input?

- **Repository URLs.** Atesor accepts only a plain `http` or `https` URL without shell metacharacters. It refuses an SSH URL such as `git@github.com:owner/repo.git`.
- **Private repositories.** Atesor sends `GIT_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` only to URLs that start with `https://github.com/`. It has no token support for other hosts.

## What limits apply to the recipe cache?

- **Old entries are not verified.** Cache entries from before the verification step have no verdict. A cache hit on such an entry prints `NOT VERIFIED` and exits with code 3. The bundled cache has such entries, for example for zlib. Use `--force` to build and verify again.
- **A cache hit does not package.** With `--package`, a cache hit writes no zip file, because no fresh source tree exists. Use `--force`.
- **Only verified ports are learned.** An `unverified` or failed run adds nothing to the recipe cache or to the few-shot examples.
- **Example retrieval uses keywords.** Atesor matches few-shot examples by keywords and regular expressions, not by vector search.

## What limits apply to the LLM layer?

- **Repository content goes to the provider.** The prompts contain excerpts of the build files, the docs and the source code around each error. Use a provider that you trust with that code.
- **Free tiers have caps.** OpenRouter limits free models to a daily request count. When the account reaches the cap, Atesor stops the model rotation and uses its deterministic fallbacks. Easy packages can still build, but the fixer has no fallback.
- **Cost depends on usage reports.** Atesor prices each call from the token usage that the provider reports. A call without usage data counts as 0 tokens. Atesor prices an unknown paid model at a conservative default rate.

## What are the security limits?

- **Untrusted code runs as root in the sandbox.** The cloned code, the commands from the LLM and the harness code of the optimizer agent run as root inside the container. The container is the security boundary.
- **The command whitelist is a guard, not a jail.** `CommandValidator` in `src/tools.py` blocks commands that do not match its patterns. It does not isolate the build.
- **The workspace is shared with the host.** Atesor mounts the host workspace into the container at `/workspace` with read and write access.

## What limits apply to the native target?

- **No CI.** The native target is for local builds and tests only. The CI workflows use the QEMU target.
- **The platform must be explicit.** Set `--platform` or `ATESOR_PLATFORM`. Atesor does not read the distribution from a native container.
- **Clock skew can hide outputs.** The artifact scan counts a file outside the repository, such as `/usr/local/bin/<name>`, only if the file is new. Its time stamp must be later than the run start minus 10 minutes. A large clock difference between your computer and the machine can hide such a file.

## What limits apply to performance mode?

- **It needs a verified port.** For a port that is not verified, performance mode stops with the status `skipped`.
- **Only the native target measures speed.** Under QEMU, each tune gets the correctness gates but no time measurement, and Atesor never accepts a tune.
- **Under QEMU, ISA tunes need a CPU model.** Without `--emulate-cpu` or `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`, Atesor builds no ISA tune: no `-march`, vector, `GORISCV64` or Rust target tune.
- **It needs a workload.** Without a workload, a native run builds no tune. Atesor does not use benchmark suites that run for a fixed time, such as Google Benchmark or criterion.
- **One workload run must be short.** On native hardware, one run must take 5 seconds or less.
- **The cost cap does not stop the optimizer agent.** Round limits and the time budget limit its LLM calls.
- **A batch run never optimizes.** `batch_test.py` has no option for performance mode.

See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

## What limits apply to the packages?

- **The `.deb` targets Ubuntu 22.04 and Python 3.10.** For another distribution or Python version, build the package again with a matching base image.
- **The `.deb` has no batch runner.** `batch_test.py` needs a source checkout. See [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

## Related pages

- [What is Atesor](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/what-is-atesor/): the current scope.
- [Troubleshooting](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/troubleshooting/): known failures and what to do.
- [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/): the cost cap and the price table.

---

# Requirements

Section: Getting Started
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/requirements/

Eclipse Atesor™ runs on a Linux host and builds each package in a riscv64 Docker container under QEMU emulation. Make sure that your host has the items on this page before you [install Atesor](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/).

## What does the host need?

| Item | Requirement | Needed for |
|---|---|---|
| Operating system | Linux on an x86-64 or ARM computer | Every run |
| Docker | A running Docker daemon that your user can reach | Sandbox setup, and each port that is not a cache hit |
| riscv64 emulation | `qemu-riscv64` registered in binfmt_misc | Every sandbox start |
| Python | 3.10 or newer | Every run |
| LLM API key | One key for Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter or Anthropic | Each port that is not a cache hit |
| git | Installed on the host | A source install. The `.deb` recommends it. |

## Which operating system do I need?

Use a Linux host. Before Atesor starts a container, it reads `/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/qemu-riscv64` on the host. If the riscv64 handler is not there and Atesor cannot register it, Atesor stops.

The host can be x86-64 or ARM. The release workflow builds the `.deb` package on Ubuntu 22.04 for `amd64`. On an ARM host, build the package yourself: `build_deb.sh` takes the architecture from its build container, so an `arm64` host gives an `arm64` package.

## How do I prepare Docker?

1. Install a Docker engine and start the daemon.
2. Add your user to the `docker` group:

   ```bash
   sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER"
   ```

3. Log out and log in again, so that the new group applies.

Atesor connects to Docker through the Docker SDK for Python. If it cannot connect, it prints `ERROR: Docker is not running or not accessible` and stops.

## How do I register riscv64 emulation?

On an x86 or ARM host, register the QEMU handlers one time:

```bash
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all
```

Atesor also checks the riscv64 handler before each sandbox start. If the handler is not registered, Atesor runs this command one time:

```bash
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64
```

If that command fails, Atesor prints it as the fix and stops. Without the handler, every riscv64 container exits with `exec format error`.

The `.deb` package installs `qemu-user-static` and `binfmt-support` as dependencies. To check the registration, run:

```bash
ls /proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/ | grep -i riscv
```

## Which Python version do I need?

- **Source install.** Use Python 3.10 or newer, as `requirements.txt` states.
- **`.deb` package.** The package brings its own virtual environment, built in an `ubuntu:22.04` container for `python3.10`. The package depends on `python3 (>= 3.10)`. For another distribution or another Python version, build the package again with a matching base image, for example `packaging/deb/build_deb.sh debian:12`.

## Which API key do I need?

You need one key, for the provider that `LLM_PROVIDER` selects:

| `LLM_PROVIDER` | Key variable |
|---|---|
| `gemini` (default) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |

Atesor checks the key only before a port. `--setup-only`, `--probe` and a recipe cache hit need no key. [Configure the LLM provider](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/) tells where to put the key.

## What network access does Atesor need?

- **Image build.** Docker pulls the base image, and the image build downloads distribution packages and the Go and Rust toolchains.
- **Ports.** Atesor clones each repository inside the container, and the build installs distribution packages. The container uses the DNS servers `8.8.8.8` and `8.8.4.4`.
- **LLM calls.** Each call goes to the provider over HTTPS.

## How much disk space and memory do I need?

The code and the project docs state no minimum disk space for a QEMU host. The workspace holds the cloned repositories, the outputs, the logs and the zip files. `--clean-workspace` shows the size of each workspace folder and asks which ones to empty. It does not offer the `packages/` folder, which holds the zip files.

Atesor starts the QEMU container with a memory limit of 8 GB.

The only stated disk figure is for a native machine. It needs 10 GB free for podman storage and 10 GB free in the work directory, or 20 GB when one filesystem holds both.

## What does the native target need?

The native target needs a riscv64 Linux machine on real hardware, with SSH key login, podman 4.0 or newer, rootless user IDs and `rsync`. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

Performance mode (`--optimize`) measures speed only on the native target. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

## Next step

[Install Atesor](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/).

---

# Install Atesor

Section: Getting Started
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/

You can install Eclipse Atesor™ in two ways: from the `.deb` package on the release page, or from a source checkout. After the install, you build a riscv64 sandbox image one time. Check the [requirements](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/requirements/) first.

## Which install method should I use?

| Method | Use it when | Command name |
|---|---|---|
| `.deb` package | You port packages on an Ubuntu 22.04 `amd64` host | `atesor-ai` |
| Source checkout | You use another distribution or Python version, you run batch ports, or you change the code | `python3 main.py` |

In these docs, `python3 main.py` and `atesor-ai` are the same command. The two methods take the same flags, with the exception in the next note.

:::note
Performance mode (`--optimize`, `--probe` and `--emulate-cpu`) and the Anthropic provider are in the `main` branch from 2026-10-15. The v0.2.0 `.deb` package (2026-10-01) does not include them. To use them, install from source until the next release.
:::

## Install the .deb package

1. Open the [release page](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/releases).
2. Download `atesor-ai_<version>_amd64.deb` and `atesor-ai_<version>_amd64.deb.sha256` from the assets of a release.
3. Calculate the checksum of the package:

   ```bash
   sha256sum atesor-ai_<version>_amd64.deb
   ```

4. Compare the result with the first field of the `.sha256` file, or with the `SHA256` line in the release notes. Do not continue if they are different.
5. Install the package:

   ```bash
   sudo apt-get install ./atesor-ai_<version>_amd64.deb
   ```

   `apt` also installs the dependencies: `python3`, a Docker engine (`docker.io`, `docker-ce` or `docker-engine`), `qemu-user-static`, `binfmt-support` and `ca-certificates`. It recommends `git`.

6. Add your user to the `docker` group, then log out and log in again:

   ```bash
   sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER"
   ```

7. Check the install:

   ```bash
   atesor-ai --version
   atesor-ai --help
   ```

### What does the package install?

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| `/opt/atesor-ai/app/` | The application code, the Dockerfiles and the seed data |
| `/opt/atesor-ai/app/.env-example` | The reference list of supported environment variables |
| `/opt/atesor-ai/app/BUILD_INFO` | The build date and the versions of the bundled Python packages |
| `/opt/atesor-ai/venv/` | The bundled Python virtual environment |
| `/usr/bin/atesor-ai` | The launcher |

Atesor never writes to `/opt`. It writes its runtime state to `$ATESOR_HOME` if you set it, or else to `~/.local/share/atesor-ai`. On the first run, it copies the bundled recipe cache and few-shot examples into that folder.

To remove the package, run `sudo dpkg -r atesor-ai`. The package scripts then remove `/opt/atesor-ai`. Your state folder stays.

### Build the .deb yourself

To make a package for another base image or another architecture, build it from a source checkout. The build needs Docker on the host.

```bash
packaging/deb/build_deb.sh                # ubuntu:22.04 base
packaging/deb/build_deb.sh debian:12      # another base image
```

The script writes `dist/atesor-ai_<version>_<arch>.deb` and a build log, `dist/atesor-ai_<version>_build.log`. To check the package in a clean container, run `packaging/deb/validate_deb.sh [image]`.

## Install from source

1. Clone the repository:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor
   cd atesor
   ```

2. Install the Python dependencies:

   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

   The list includes `langchain-anthropic`, which the Anthropic provider needs.

3. Make your `.env` file from the template:

   ```bash
   cp .env-example .env
   ```

4. Add your API key to `.env`. See [Configure the LLM provider](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

:::tip
You can install the dependencies into a Python virtual environment. Create it with `python3 -m venv .venv`, then activate it with `. .venv/bin/activate` before step 2.
:::

Unless you set `ATESOR_HOME`, a source checkout keeps its runtime state inside the checkout. The workspace is in `workspace/`, and the recipe cache and the examples are in `data/`. If you plan to contribute, also read [Development setup](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/development-setup/).

## Build the sandbox image

A sandbox is the riscv64 container where Atesor builds packages. Build the image one time before your first port:

```bash
python3 main.py --setup-only                     # Alpine (musl), the default
python3 main.py --setup-only --platform debian   # Debian/Ubuntu (glibc)
```

With the `.deb`, use `atesor-ai --setup-only` and `atesor-ai --setup-only --platform debian`.

`--setup-only` needs no API key. It does these steps:

1. It checks that `qemu-riscv64` is registered in binfmt_misc, and tries to register it if not.
2. It looks for the image. If the image does not exist, it builds it for `linux/riscv64` from the Dockerfile of the platform.
3. It starts the container and mounts the workspace at `/workspace`.
4. It checks that the distribution in the container matches the platform and that `uname -m` reports `riscv64`.
5. It prints `Setup complete!`.

| Platform | Dockerfile | Image | Container |
|---|---|---|---|
| `alpine` | `Dockerfile` | `atesor-ai-sandbox:latest` | `atesor-ai-sandbox` |
| `debian` or `ubuntu` | `Dockerfile.debian` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian:latest` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian` |

The image builds under QEMU emulation. The setup message of Atesor tells you to expect 15 to 45 minutes for the first build. Later runs use the cached image.

:::note
Without `--platform`, Atesor looks at the default container `atesor-ai-sandbox` and uses Alpine when it cannot tell. To use the Debian sandbox, pass `--platform debian` on each run, or set `ATESOR_PLATFORM=debian` in your `.env` file.
:::

### Rebuild or remove the sandbox

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--rebuild` | Builds the image again before the run. Without `--repo`, `--platform` and `--container`, it rebuilds both the Alpine and the Debian sandbox. |
| `--cleanup` | Stops and removes the sandbox container |
| `--clean-image` | Also removes the sandbox image |
| `--clean-workspace` | Shows the size of the workspace folders and asks which ones to empty: `repos/`, `output/`, `logs/`, `.cache/`, or all |

## Next step

[Configure the LLM provider](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

---

# Configure the LLM provider

Section: Getting Started
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/

Eclipse Atesor™ uses one LLM provider for a run. You select the provider with `LLM_PROVIDER` and give its API key in the environment or in a `.env` file. This page lists the providers, tells where the `.env` file goes, and shows the model of each agent role.

## Which providers can I use?

| `LLM_PROVIDER` | Key variable | Models |
|---|---|---|
| `gemini` (default) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` for every role |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `gpt-4o` and `gpt-4o-mini` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Free models (ids that end in `:free`), with a fallback chain |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `claude-haiku-5-5` and `claude-sonnet-5-5` |

:::note
The Anthropic provider is in the `main` branch from 2026-10-15. The v0.2.0 `.deb` package (2026-10-01) does not include it. To use it, run Atesor from a source checkout until the next release.
:::

The Anthropic provider needs the `langchain-anthropic` package. `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs it. If the package is not installed, the key check stops the port with `ERROR: langchain-anthropic is not installed (pip install -r requirements.txt)`.

## How do I select the provider?

Set the provider and its key, in your `.env` file or in the environment:

```bash
LLM_PROVIDER=openrouter
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<your key>
```

Atesor applies these rules:

- If `LLM_PROVIDER` is not set, Atesor uses `gemini`.
- Atesor changes the value to lower case before it uses it.
- An unknown value stops the port with `ERROR: Unknown provider: <value>`.
- A key that is not set, or that has the placeholder value `your_key_here`, stops the port with `ERROR: <KEY_NAME> not found in environment`.

Atesor checks the key only before a port. `--setup-only`, `--probe` and a recipe cache hit do not need a key. After a good check, Atesor prints the provider and the models of the supervisor (S), planner (P) and builder (B) roles.

## Where does the .env file go?

| Install | Put the file here |
|---|---|
| Source checkout | `.env` in the root of the checkout |
| `.deb` package | `~/.config/atesor-ai/.env` |

For a source checkout, make the file from the template in the checkout root:

```bash
cp .env-example .env
```

For the `.deb` package, copy the template that the package installs:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/atesor-ai
cp /opt/atesor-ai/app/.env-example ~/.config/atesor-ai/.env
```

Then open the file and set `LLM_PROVIDER` and the key. The template lists the provider keys and the main optional settings. [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/) lists every variable.

You can also export the variables in your shell:

```bash
export LLM_PROVIDER=gemini
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=<your key>
```

### In which order does Atesor read the files?

A variable that is already in the environment wins over every file. Between the files, the first file that sets a variable wins. Atesor reads them in this order:

1. A `.env` file in the folder of `main.py`, or in a parent folder of it.
2. `$ATESOR_HOME/.env`, when `ATESOR_HOME` is set.
3. `~/.config/atesor-ai/.env`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atesor-ai/.env` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set.
4. `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/.env`, or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai/.env` when `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set.

:::caution
With the `.deb` package, a `.env` file in your current folder has no effect. `main.py` calls `load_dotenv()` without a path, so python-dotenv searches from the folder of `main.py` (`/opt/atesor-ai/app`) and its parents. It does not search the current folder. Use `~/.config/atesor-ai/.env`, or export the variables.
:::

## Which model does each agent use?

The model table is `MODEL_CONFIG` in `src/models.py`.

| Role | `gemini` | `openai` | `openrouter` | `anthropic` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| supervisor | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| planner | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| scout | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| builder | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| fixer | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| summarizer | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |

The `gemini`, `openai` and `openrouter` entries set a temperature. It is 0.0 for the supervisor and the builder, 0.1 for the planner, the scout and the summarizer, and 0.2 for the fixer.

The two Anthropic models do not accept a temperature, so Atesor sends none. In its place, each `anthropic` entry sets an `effort` value for the adaptive thinking of the model. The value is `low` for the supervisor and the summarizer, and `medium` for the other roles.

These roles make the LLM calls:

- The analyst uses the `planner` entry.
- The scout uses the `scout` entry.
- The fixer uses the `fixer` entry.
- The summarizer writes the recipe, and the artifact curator ranks the build outputs. Both use the `summarizer` entry.
- In performance mode, the optimizer agent uses the `builder` entry to write a harness, and the `planner` entry to propose a program run. If no model of that role answers in time, Atesor asks the models of the other role one time.

The supervisor routes by rules, so its entry makes no calls. The `builder` entry makes calls only in performance mode.

## How do I change a model?

1. Use a source checkout. The `.deb` package keeps its install tree identical to the package contents.
2. Edit the `model` value of the role in `MODEL_CONFIG` in `src/models.py`.
3. If the new model is a paid model, add its price to `MODEL_PRICES_PER_MTOK` in the same file.

Without a price entry, Atesor prices a paid model at $3.00 for each million input tokens and $12.00 for each million output tokens. This rate counts toward the cost cap of $1.00 for each port. See [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).

## How does the OpenRouter fallback chain work?

OpenRouter is the only provider with fallback models. Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic use the primary model only.

- **The chain.** `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS` sets the chain as a comma-separated list of model ids. Atesor always adds `openrouter/free`, the OpenRouter router for free models, at the end. Without the variable, the chain is `qwen/qwen3-coder:free`, `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free`, `openai/gpt-oss-20b:free`, `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free`, `qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct:free` and `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free`.
- **Server-side fallback.** Each request names three models for OpenRouter to try: the first two models of the chain that are not the primary model, and `openrouter/free`. OpenRouter refuses a request with more than three.
- **Client-side rotation.** When a call fails with a provider error, Atesor tries the next model of the chain. For a short `Retry-After` of 65 seconds or less, it waits one time for each model before it rotates.
- **Daily cap.** When the account reaches the OpenRouter daily cap for free models, Atesor stops the rotation and uses its deterministic fallback.

The default chain does not contain `openrouter/auto`, because that router selects paid models only.

## Which other LLM settings exist?

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` | `8192` | The output token limit of each LLM request |
| `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` | `120` | The request timeout in seconds. Atesor also stops a call after this value plus 15 seconds (60 seconds for the artifact curator, 240 seconds for a harness of the optimizer agent). |
| `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS` | The default chain | The OpenRouter fallback chain |

[Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/) lists every variable.

## Next step

[Port your first package](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/first-port/).

---

# Your first port

Section: Getting Started
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/first-port/

This page shows a full port of zlib, a small C compression library, with Eclipse Atesor™. You run one command, follow the stages of the run, and then find the output files.

## Before you start

1. [Install Atesor](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/).
2. [Set the LLM provider and its API key](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).
3. Build the Alpine sandbox one time:

   ```bash
   python3 main.py --setup-only
   ```

The commands on this page use a source checkout. With the `.deb` package, write `atesor-ai` in place of `python3 main.py`.

## Why does the first port need `--force`?

The recipe cache that comes with Atesor (`data/recipe_cache.json`) already has zlib entries for the `alpine-riscv64` and `debian-riscv64` sandboxes. These entries are older than the verification step, so they have no verdict.

Without `--force`, Atesor finds the entry, writes the recipe file, prints `CACHED (not rebuilt), NOT VERIFIED` and exits with code 3. It builds nothing. To see the full pipeline and get a verified result, add `--force`.

## How do I run the port?

Run this command from the root of your checkout:

```bash
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --force --verbose
```

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--repo` | The repository to port |
| `--force` | Skip the recipe cache and run the full pipeline |
| `--verbose` | Show the agent activity and the debug log on the console |

You can add these flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--package` | On success, also write a zip file with the recipe, the source tree and a manifest |
| `--platform debian` | Use the Debian/Ubuntu sandbox. Build it first with `--setup-only --platform debian`. |
| `--max-attempts N` | Allow `N` fix attempts before escalation. The default is 5. |
| `--optimize` | After a verified port, try faster builds for this machine. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/). |

## What does Atesor do at each stage?

1. **Input check.** Atesor checks the URL and takes the package name `zlib` from it. It sets the debug log to `agent_zlib.log` and the LLM call log to `agent-call_zlib.log`.
2. **Cache.** `--force` makes Atesor skip the recipe cache.
3. **Key check.** Atesor checks the key of your provider. Then it prints the provider and the models.
4. **Sandbox.** Atesor checks the riscv64 handler, starts the Alpine container, and checks that it reports `riscv64`.
5. **Agent graph.** Atesor prints `Starting RISC-V Porting Agent`, the repository, the attempt limit and the platform. For each node of the graph, it prints a `[Step N]` line with the node name and a `Status:` line.
6. **`init_node`.** Atesor clones zlib into `/workspace/repos/zlib` inside the container. On the host, this is `repos/zlib` in your workspace folder. Then the scripted analysis detects the build system, the dependencies and any architecture-specific code.
7. **`analyst_node`.** The LLM reads excerpts of the zlib build files and docs and writes the package analysis. The status is `PLANNING`.
8. **`heuristic_plan_node` or `scout_node`.** For a known build system, Atesor writes a default build plan without an LLM. If no default plan fits, for example because the analysis asks for a custom plan, the scout asks the LLM for a plan. The status of the scout is `SCOUTING`.
9. **Build-fix loop.** The builder runs the phases of the plan, with the status `BUILDING`. When a command fails, the builder tries its recovery heuristics, and then the fixer asks the LLM for a fix (`FIXING`). After the build commands pass, `verify_node` reads the ELF header of each output.
10. **`finish_node`.** Atesor runs the zlib test suite one time, if it finds one. It then asks the LLM to write the recipe. When the port is verified, it saves the recipe in the recipe cache and adds few-shot examples. With `--optimize`, an `optimize_node` step with the status `OPTIMIZING` comes next.
11. **Outputs.** Atesor saves the output files and prints the path of each one. Then it prints the result line. With `--optimize`, the summary after a success also has an `Optimized:` line.

| Result line | Exit code |
|---|---|
| `PORTING SUCCESSFUL! (riscv64 output verified)` | 0 |
| `PORTING FINISHED, NOT VERIFIED` | 3 |
| `PORTING STOPPED / FAILED` | 1 |
| `Packaging FAILED: <error>` (only with `--package`) | 2 |

After a failure, Atesor also prints `Last Error Capture:`, with the category and severity of the last error. It then prints `Agent Decision Audit:`, with the last 10 events of the run.

## Where do the outputs go?

| Install | Workspace folder |
|---|---|
| Source checkout | `workspace/` in the checkout |
| `.deb` package | `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/workspace/` |
| `ATESOR_HOME` set | `$ATESOR_HOME/workspace/` |

For this port, Atesor writes these files in the workspace folder:

```text
output/zlib_recipe.md
output/zlib_report_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.md
output/zlib_state_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.json
output/zlib_patches_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/patch_<N>.patch     (only if the run applied a patch)
logs/agent_zlib.log
logs/agent-call_zlib.log
packages/madler-zlib-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-alpine.zip         (only with --package)
repos/zlib/                                               (the build tree)
```

[Read the output](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/read-the-output/) explains each file and what to look at first.

## What happens when I run it again?

After a verified port, run the command without `--force`:

```bash
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib
```

Atesor finds the new cache entry and prints `CACHED (not rebuilt): recipe for 'zlib' from an earlier verified run`. It writes `zlib_recipe.md` again and exits with code 0. A cache hit needs no API key and no Docker. It also writes no zip file, even with `--package`.

:::note
In a source checkout, a verified port writes to `data/recipe_cache.json` and to the files in `data/examples/` of your clone. `git status` shows these changes.
:::

## Next step

[Read the output](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/read-the-output/).

---

# Read the output

Section: Getting Started
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/read-the-output/

Each Eclipse Atesor™ run writes a set of files: a recipe, a build report, a state snapshot, patches, logs and, on request, a zip package. This page tells where each file is, what it contains, and which file to open first for each result.

## Where are the output files?

Atesor writes to a workspace folder and a data folder:

| Install | Workspace folder | Data folder |
|---|---|---|
| Source checkout | `workspace/` in the checkout | `data/` in the checkout |
| `.deb` package | `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/workspace/` | `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/data/` |
| `ATESOR_HOME` set | `$ATESOR_HOME/workspace/` | `$ATESOR_HOME/data/` |

When `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set, the `.deb` package uses `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai/` in place of `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/`. On the native target, the workspace folder is `workspace-native/` in place of `workspace/`.

| File | Folder | Written when |
|---|---|---|
| `<repo>_recipe.md` | `workspace/output/` | A run ends with `SUCCESS`, or a cache hit |
| `<repo>_report_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.md` | `workspace/output/` | The agent graph finishes, with any result |
| `<repo>_state_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.json` | `workspace/output/` | The agent graph finishes, with any result |
| `<repo>_patches_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/` | `workspace/output/` | The run applied one patch or more |
| `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip` | `workspace/packages/` | `--package` and a `SUCCESS` result |
| `<repo>.opt/accepted/` | `repos/` in the work directory of the native machine | `--optimize` and an accepted tune |
| `machine_profile_<target>.json` | `workspace/output/` | A `--probe` run |
| `agent_<repo>.log` | `workspace/logs/` | Each run with `--repo` |
| `agent-call_<repo>.log` | `workspace/logs/` | Each LLM call |
| `recipe_cache.json` | data folder | A verified port |
| `examples/*.json` | data folder | A verified port |

`<repo>` is the package name that Atesor takes from the URL, for example `zlib`. `<target>` is `native` or `qemu`.

Atesor accepts a tune only on the native target. There, the `<repo>.opt` folder is on the machine, and Atesor removes it at the end of the run. With `--package`, Atesor first copies the accepted artifacts into the zip, under `optimized/`.

## Which file should I open first?

| Result | Exit code | Open first | Then |
|---|---|---|---|
| Verified port | 0 | The recipe | The "Artifact Verification" section of the report |
| Not verified | 3 | The "Artifact Verification" section of the report, and its reason | The "Recommendations" section |
| Failure or escalation | 1 | The "Error Resolution History" section of the report | `context_cache.escalation_report` in the state snapshot, then `agent_<repo>.log`, then `agent-call_<repo>.log` |
| Packaging failure | 2 | `agent_<repo>.log`, at the `Packaging failed` line | The build succeeded. Only the zip step failed. |
| Performance mode result | The same as the port | The `Performance Mode (--optimize)` section of the report | `optimized/` in the zip, with `--package` |

## What is in the recipe?

The recipe, `<repo>_recipe.md`, is the guide to build the package again on riscv64. The summarizer LLM writes it at the end of a successful run, from the build steps, the fixes and the verification verdict. The prompt asks the LLM for these sections, in this order:

1. `## Executive Summary`: the status and a short verdict on portability.
2. `## Prerequisites`: the package install commands for the sandbox distribution.
3. `## Build Instructions`: the build commands, one code block for each step.
4. `## Architecture Notes`: the architecture-specific changes that the package needed.
5. `## Verification`: how to check that the binaries are riscv64, with `file` or `readelf -h`.
6. `## Known Issues & Recommendations`: remaining problems and ideas to send upstream.

If the summarizer call fails, Atesor writes a short recipe with the build steps and the verification verdict.

The file name has no time stamp. A new successful run or a cache hit writes a new recipe file in its place. On a cache hit, Atesor writes the stored recipe text. For an old cache entry without stored text, it writes a recipe from the cache fields, with a note to run again with `--force`.

## What is in the report?

The report, `<repo>_report_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.md`, has these sections. Atesor leaves out the architecture, patch and error sections when they have no data. The two performance mode sections appear only with `--optimize`.

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| Executive Summary | The status, the target (`qemu` or `native`), the repository and the time |
| Metrics | The duration, the attempts, the API calls, the scripted operations, the LLM tokens and the cost |
| Artifact Verification | The verdict, its reason, the source commit, the counts, and up to 20 files of each kind |
| Package Tests (not gating) | The result, the command, the exit code, the duration and the output tail |
| Machine Profile | The result of the machine probe |
| `Performance Mode (--optimize)` | The `Optimized` answer (`YES`, `NO`, or `NOT TIMED` under QEMU), the reason, the machine, the package, the baseline, the workload, one row for each tune, and the workload source code |
| Build System Analysis | The build system, the build phases with their commands, and the dependencies |
| Architecture-Specific Code | The first 5 findings of the architecture scan |
| Patches Applied | Each patch, cut at 500 characters |
| Error Resolution History | Each error, with its category |
| Recommendations | The next steps for this result |

The status of a successful run is `SUCCESS (riscv64 output verified)` or `SUCCESS, NOT VERIFIED (no riscv64 output proven)`. The counts table of the verification has three columns: riscv64 outputs, outputs for another architecture, and committed files for another architecture. Committed files never decide the verdict.

## What is in the state snapshot?

The state snapshot, `<repo>_state_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.json`, is the full `AgentState` of the run. Start with these fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `build_status` | `SUCCESS`, `FAILED` or `ESCALATED` at the end of a run |
| `artifact_verification` | The verdict (`verified`, `wrong_arch` or `unverified`), the reason and the evidence |
| `package_tests` | The result of the package's own tests |
| `error_history` | Each error, with its category, severity, command and message |
| `fixes_attempted` | Each fix, with its strategy, its changes and its success |
| `build_plan` | The build plan with its phases and commands |
| `package_analysis` | The analysis from `analyst_node` |
| `context_cache.escalation_report` | The escalation report, after an escalation |
| `api_cost_usd`, `api_tokens_in`, `api_tokens_out` | The LLM cost and the tokens |
| `audit_trail` | The events of each agent, in order |
| `optimization` | The performance mode result, with one record for each tune. Only with `--optimize`. |
| `machine_profile` | The machine probe. Only with `--optimize`. |

## What is in the patches folder?

The folder `<repo>_patches_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/` holds one file for each patch that the fixer applied: `patch_1.patch`, `patch_2.patch` and so on. In a run from a cached recipe (`--optimize`), it also holds each cached patch that applied. It holds only patch actions. Commands that the fixer ran and files that it created are in `fixes_attempted` in the state snapshot, as `Executed: <command>` and `Created file: <path>` lines.

## What is in the zip package?

With `--package`, a successful run writes a zip file to `workspace/packages/`. The name is `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip` in lower case, for example `madler-zlib-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-alpine.zip`. The platform is `alpine` or `debian`, also for `--platform ubuntu`. On the native target, the name ends in `-native.zip`.

| Entry | Content |
|---|---|
| `build_recipe.md` | The recipe |
| `manifest.json` | The metadata of the package: schema version 2, or 3 with `--optimize` |
| `agent_<repo>.log` | The debug log, if present |
| `<repo>.log` | The batch log, only in a batch run |
| `optimized/` | The riscv64 artifacts of the accepted tune, only with `--optimize` and an accepted tune |
| `<repo>/` | The source tree with the build outputs, without `.git` and without symbolic links |

The main keys of the manifest are:

- `verification`: the status, the reason, the source commit, the counts and the ABI warnings.
- `artifacts`: each verified riscv64 output, with its type, architecture and size. An output inside the zipped tree also has its SHA-256 and `in_zip: true`. An output installed outside the tree, such as in `/usr/local/bin`, has `in_zip: false`.
- `package_tests`: the status, the framework, the command, the exit code and the duration.
- `repo_url`, `platform`, `created_at` and the names of the files in the zip.
- `machine` and `optimization`, only in schema version 3: the machine probe, the performance mode result, each tune with its verdict, and a SHA-256 for each file in `optimized/`.

## What is in the debug log?

`agent_<repo>.log` has every log line of the run at the `DEBUG` level, with the time, the level and the module name. It shows each command, each routing decision and each recovery heuristic. After an escalation, it also contains the escalation report. Without `--verbose`, the console shows only errors from this log.

## What is in the LLM call log?

`agent-call_<repo>.log` has one entry for each LLM response, also for each retry after an answer that was not valid. A call that fails with an error has no entry in this log. The debug log records it. Each entry has these lines:

```text
CALL: call_<id>
TIMESTAMP: <time>
AGENT: <role>
MODEL: <model>
COST: $<cost>
TOKENS: in=<input tokens> out=<output tokens>
METADATA: <JSON>
--- PROMPT ---
<the first 10000 characters of the prompt>
--- RESPONSE ---
<the first 10000 characters of the response>
```

Use this log to see what an agent received and what it answered. A call with `TOKENS: in=0 out=0` means that the provider reported no usage, so the cost of that call is unknown.

## Related pages

- [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/): the full reference of every file and field.
- [Exit codes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/exit-codes/): each code and its meaning.
- [Troubleshooting](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/troubleshooting/): what to do after a failure.

---

# Sandboxes

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/

A sandbox is the riscv64 Linux container in which Eclipse Atesor™ clones, builds and checks a package. Atesor has two sandboxes: Alpine Linux with musl libc, and a Debian/Ubuntu image with glibc. You select one with `--platform`, and Atesor keeps the results of each sandbox apart.

## What are the two sandboxes?

| | Alpine | Debian/Ubuntu |
|---|---|---|
| `--platform` value | `alpine` | `debian` or `ubuntu` |
| libc | musl | glibc |
| Dockerfile (QEMU target) | `Dockerfile` | `Dockerfile.debian` |
| Base image | `docker.io/library/alpine:latest` | `ubuntu:jammy` |
| Image name | `atesor-ai-sandbox:latest` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian:latest` |
| Container name | `atesor-ai-sandbox` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian` |
| Install command | `apk add` | `apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends` |
| Target triplet | `riscv64-alpine-linux-musl` | `riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu` |

The `ubuntu` platform is an alias. It uses the same profile, image and container as `debian`. On the QEMU target, the Debian/Ubuntu image starts from `ubuntu:jammy`, not from a Debian image.

### What do both images contain?

- Go 1.26.5, from the official riscv64 tarball on go.dev, with a SHA-256 check. It is in `/usr/local/go`.
- Rust 1.99.0, installed with rustup into `/root/.cargo`.
- `CC=gcc` and `CXX=g++`.
- `GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`, `GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct` and `GONOSUMCHECK=*`.
- `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`. Go does not download a different toolchain in the middle of a build.
- The directories `/workspace/repos`, `/workspace/output`, `/workspace/logs` and `/workspace/patches`.
- A container health check that runs `gcc --version`.

The images do not use the Go and Rust packages of the distro, because those versions are older. Before an `apk add`, `apt-get install` or `apt install` command runs, Atesor removes these package names from it: `golang`, `golang-*`, `go-1.*`, `gccgo`, `gccgo-*`, `rust`, `rust-*`, `rustc`, `rustc-*`, `cargo` and `cargo-*`.

### What does the Alpine image add?

The Alpine image installs these packages with `apk`: `build-base`, `cmake`, `git`, `curl`, `bash`, `python3`, `ca-certificates`, `file`, `tar`, `xz`, `pkgconfig`, `meson`, `ninja`, `autoconf`, `automake`, `libtool`, `gettext-dev`, `nasm`, `perl`, `linux-headers`, `zlib-dev`, `samurai`, `py3-pip`, `py3-jinja2`, `py3-jsonschema`, `gfortran`, `texinfo`, `patch`, `diffutils`, `protobuf-dev`, `protoc`, `abseil-cpp-dev`, `openssl-dev`, `libpng-dev`, `util-linux` and `coreutils`.

### What does the Debian/Ubuntu image add?

- These packages, installed with `apt-get`: `build-essential`, `cmake`, `git`, `curl`, `ca-certificates`, `file`, `tar`, `xz-utils`, `pkg-config`, `meson`, `ninja-build`, `autoconf`, `automake`, `libtool`, `patch`, `diffutils`, `ccache`, `zlib1g-dev`, `libssl-dev`, `python3`, `python3-pip` and `bash`.
- Autoconf 2.72, built from source. The `Dockerfile.debian` comment says that jammy ships autoconf 2.71, and some projects require 2.72.
- The apt pin file `/etc/apt/preferences.d/99-no-distro-go`. It makes an `apt install` of the distro Go packages fail.
- ccache through `PATH` (`/usr/lib/ccache`), with `CCACHE_DIR=/workspace/.ccache`. `CC` stays `gcc`, because Go's CGO also uses `CC` as its assembler driver.

The image installs only the core build tools. The agents install the libraries that each project needs, for example `libpng-dev`, when the build needs them.

## How do I select a sandbox?

Use `--platform` on any command. Alpine is the default.

```bash
atesor-ai --setup-only                       # Alpine
atesor-ai --setup-only --platform debian     # Debian/Ubuntu
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --platform debian
```

In a source checkout, run `python3 main.py` instead of `atesor-ai`.

Atesor selects the profile in this order:

1. The `--platform` flag (`alpine`, `debian` or `ubuntu`). The flag sets `ATESOR_PLATFORM` for the run.
2. `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, from the environment or from `.env`.
3. With `--platform auto` (the default) and no `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, Atesor reads `/etc/os-release` from the sandbox container. It uses the container in `ATESOR_CONTAINER`, else `atesor-ai-sandbox`.
4. When that read fails, or the distro is unknown, Atesor uses Alpine.

The native target does not detect the platform. Set `ATESOR_PLATFORM` or pass `--platform`. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

After the container starts, Atesor makes two checks:

- The `ID` in `/etc/os-release` must match the profile. If it does not, the run stops with `ERROR: Platform mismatch` and gives the command `docker rm -f <container>`.
- `uname -m` in the container must report `riscv64`.

## Why does Atesor verify on both libc families?

musl and glibc do not supply the same GNU extensions. Thus a package that builds with glibc can fail with musl. The knowledge block that Atesor gives to the agents on Alpine lists musl symptoms, for example a missing `execinfo.h`, an undefined `backtrace` or `mallinfo`, and an undeclared `REG_RIP`. The Debian/Ubuntu prompt does not include this musl guidance.

Package names are also different. For example, the zlib headers are `zlib-dev` on Alpine and `zlib1g-dev` on Debian. Each profile holds a list of names from the other distro, and Atesor replaces them in install commands before they run.

Atesor does not port to both sandboxes in one command. Run the port one time for each platform. Each result has its own recipe cache entry (`alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64`) and its own few-shot examples. The CI batch workflows run each package list on both platforms. See [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

## How do platform profiles work?

`src/platforms.py` defines one `PlatformProfile` for each distro. The `PROFILES` dictionary maps `alpine` to the Alpine profile, and `debian` and `ubuntu` to the Debian profile. The rest of the code reads the active profile through `get_active_profile()` and contains no distro names.

| Field | What Atesor does with it |
|---|---|
| `name`, `display_name`, `libc`, `target_triplet` | Identify the sandbox in prompts, reports and cache keys. |
| `dockerfile`, `native_dockerfile` | Select the Dockerfile for the QEMU target and the native target. |
| `image_name`, `container_name` | Name the image and the default container. |
| `pkg_install`, `pkg_update` | Make install commands, for example `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends <packages>`. |
| `pkg_lock_file` | Serialize package installs: Atesor wraps each package command in `flock -w 120 <lock file>`. |
| `package_map` | Map a canonical name to a distro package, for example `zlib` to `zlib-dev` or `zlib1g-dev`. |
| `name_corrections` | Replace package names that belong to the other distro. |
| `extra_notes` | Add distro notes to the knowledge block of the scout and fixer prompts. |

To add a distro, see [Add a platform](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-platform/).

## How does Atesor build or pull the images?

On the QEMU target, Atesor does these steps for `--setup-only` and for every run that needs the sandbox:

1. Atesor checks that `/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/qemu-riscv64` is enabled. If it is not, Atesor runs `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64` one time.
2. If the local Docker has the image name of the profile, Atesor uses that image. Else it builds the image from the Dockerfile of the profile, for `linux/riscv64`, and pulls the newest base image for the build.
3. Atesor creates the container if it does not exist. The container uses `--platform linux/riscv64`, the bridge network, the DNS servers `8.8.8.8` and `8.8.4.4`, an 8 GB memory limit (`mem_limit="8g"`), and a bind mount of the local workspace at `/workspace`.
4. If the container mounts a different workspace directory, Atesor removes it and creates it again.

The build runs under QEMU emulation, so the first image build is slow. Later runs use the same image. A lock file, `.container_setup.lock` in the logs directory, lets only one process build the image and create the container. Other batch workers wait for it.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--setup-only` | Build the image if it is missing, start the container, then stop. |
| `--rebuild` | Build the image again before the run. You can also set `REBUILD_IMAGE=true`. |
| `--rebuild` with no `--repo`, `--platform` and `--container` | On the QEMU target, build the Alpine image and the Debian image again. |
| `--cleanup` | Stop and remove the container. |
| `--clean-image` | Also remove the image. It includes `--cleanup`. |
| `--container NAME` | Use another container name. Batch workers use this. |

### Prebuilt images in CI

The CI smoke jobs, in the main batch workflow and in the retry workflow, do not build the image. They pull a prebuilt image from Docker Hub and give it the local image name. Then `--setup-only` finds the image and skips the build:

```bash
docker pull --platform linux/riscv64 cloudv10x/atesor-sandbox:debian-latest
docker tag cloudv10x/atesor-sandbox:debian-latest atesor-ai-sandbox-debian:latest
python3 main.py --setup-only --platform debian
```

The Alpine jobs use `cloudv10x/atesor-sandbox:alpine-latest` and the local name `atesor-ai-sandbox:latest`. The full-list CI jobs, and the full-list retry jobs, build the image in the job. The maintainers publish the images with `.github/scripts/release-sandbox.sh`. It builds `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.debian` and pushes the tags `<variant>-v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>` and `<variant>-latest`.

### Images on the native target

On the native target, podman builds the image on your riscv64 machine. The `alpine` platform builds `Dockerfile`.
