The `debian` and `ubuntu` platforms build `Dockerfile.native`, which uses Debian trixie. Only `Dockerfile.native` installs clang: `clang-19`, `lld-19`, `llvm-19` and `libclang-rt-19-dev`. [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) uses them for its compiler tune and for profile-guided optimization with clang. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

---

# Native RISC-V machine

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/

The native target makes Eclipse Atesor™ build on a real riscv64 machine instead of under QEMU emulation. Atesor reaches the machine over SSH and runs each build in a rootless podman container there. QEMU stays the default target. Use the native target for local builds and tests. CI does not use native machines.

## How does Atesor reach the machine?

Select the target with `--target native` or with `ATESOR_TARGET=native` in `.env`. The flag overrides `.env`. Write the flag in full: Atesor stops with `ERROR: write --target in full, for example --target native.` when you write a short form such as `--targ`.

On the native target, Atesor uses these tools:

- **SSH.** Each native command is one `ssh` call. Every call uses the options `BatchMode=yes`, `ConnectTimeout=10`, `ServerAliveInterval=15`, `ServerAliveCountMax=4`, `ControlMaster=auto` and `ControlPersist=10m`. Each Atesor process opens its own SSH connection and closes it when the command ends.
- **Rootless podman.** Atesor builds the sandbox image on the machine and runs one container there. The container mounts only the work directory, at `/workspace`.
- **rsync.** Atesor reads repository files on your computer too, for example for analysis and packaging. It copies each repository from the machine into a local mirror with `rsync -a --delete --modify-window=-1 --exclude=.git`. The copy goes in one direction only: from the machine to your computer.

Atesor does not use the local Docker daemon or `binfmt_misc` on the native target.

## What does the machine need?

Atesor installs nothing on the machine and never runs `sudo`. The owner of the machine installs these items:

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| riscv64 Linux on real hardware, not a QEMU virtual machine | Native results are the purpose of this target. |
| SSH key login, and a POSIX login shell: bash, dash, zsh or ksh | Atesor runs with no prompts and sends POSIX shell scripts. |
| podman 4.0 or newer, `uidmap`, and subordinate UID and GID ranges for the login user | The builds run in a rootless container. |
| `rsync` on the machine, and `ssh` and `rsync` on your computer | Atesor drives the machine with `ssh` and copies the build tree back with `rsync`. |
| A work directory that is not `$HOME`, not a parent of `$HOME`, and not in `~/.ssh` | Atesor mounts the work directory into the container with SELinux relabeling (`:Z`). |
| 10 GB free for podman storage and 10 GB free in the work directory, or 20 GB when one filesystem holds both | Images, build trees and build caches use this space. |
| Outbound HTTPS | Image builds and package builds download toolchains and sources. |

On a Debian or Ubuntu machine, the owner can install the packages and the ID ranges with these commands:

```bash
sudo apt install podman uidmap rsync
sudo usermod --add-subuids 100000-165535 --add-subgids 100000-165535 "$USER"
```

Do not run the `usermod` line when `/etc/subuid` already lists the user. Then install your SSH key from your computer one time:

```bash
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/<key>.pub -p <port> <user>@<address>
```

## How do I configure the native target?

Put these keys in `.env`. Set the target, the platform, and one of the two SSH modes.

| Key | Mode | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_TARGET` | both | `native`. The default is `qemu`. `--target` overrides it. |
| `ATESOR_PLATFORM` | both | `alpine`, `debian` or `ubuntu`. Required on native. `--platform` overrides it. |
| `ATESOR_REMOTE_WORKDIR` | both | The work directory on the machine. The default is `~/atesor-ai`. Use only letters, digits and `. _ / ~ -`. |
| `ATESOR_SSH_HOST` | alias | What you type after `ssh`: a `Host` alias from `~/.ssh/config`, a host name, or `user@host`. |
| `ATESOR_SSH_HOSTNAME` | field | The address of the machine. |
| `ATESOR_SSH_PORT` | field | The SSH port, from 1 to 65535. The default is 22. |
| `ATESOR_SSH_USER` | field | The login user. |
| `ATESOR_SSH_IDENTITY_FILE` | field | The path to your private key, never the key itself. No spaces, quotes or `%`. |

- **Alias mode.** Use it when a plain `ssh <machine>` already logs in. Atesor gives the value to `ssh` with no change.
- **Field mode.** Use it when the provider gives you an address, a port, a user and a key. Atesor writes these values to `~/.cache/atesor-ai/ssh_config` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/atesor-ai/ssh_config`) with mode 0600. The file has one `Host atesor-native` block with `StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new`. Thus the address does not appear in the process list.

Set one mode, not both. Login uses a key only. Any other `ATESOR_SSH_*` key, for example a password key, stops the run. A key with a passphrase needs an active `ssh-agent`.

The platform selects the Dockerfile that podman builds on the machine:

| `ATESOR_PLATFORM` | Dockerfile | Base |
|---|---|---|
| `alpine` | `Dockerfile` | `docker.io/library/alpine:latest` |
| `debian`, `ubuntu` | `Dockerfile.native` | `docker.io/library/debian:trixie` |

`Dockerfile.native` follows `Dockerfile.debian`, with Go 1.26.5 and Rust 1.99.0. It also installs `clang-19`, `lld-19`, `llvm-19` and `libclang-rt-19-dev` for [performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/). It has no `HEALTHCHECK` and no `VOLUME`, and it sets `PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1`.

## What does the preflight check?

The preflight is a ladder of 11 rungs in `src/preflight.py`. Run it before your first native build:

```bash
atesor-ai --target native --preflight
```

| Rung | Name | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Configuration | `--target` and the `.env` keys are valid: one SSH mode, a known platform, safe values. |
| 2 | Local tools | `ssh` and `rsync` are on your computer. |
| 3 | SSH config | The SSH control socket path fits the Unix limit. In field mode, the key file exists with mode 0600 or stricter, and Atesor writes the SSH config. |
| 4 | Login and shell | Key login works, and the login shell keeps quoted text unchanged. |
| 5 | Architecture | `uname -m` on the machine reports `riscv64`. |
| 6 | Real hardware | The machine is not a QEMU `virt` board. This check is a heuristic: it reads `/proc/device-tree/compatible` and `mvendorid`. |
| 7 | Podman | The machine has podman 4.0 or newer. |
| 8 | Rootless IDs | `newuidmap` is present, the login user has subordinate UID and GID ranges, and podman runs rootless. |
| 9 | Remote rsync | `rsync` is on the machine. |
| 10 | Work directory | The work directory is safe and writable. Atesor creates it when it does not exist. |
| 11 | Disk | Free space for podman storage and the work directory. |

Rungs 1 to 4 stop at the first failure, because Atesor cannot inspect the machine without them. Rungs 5 to 11 all run. When a rung fails, the report lists every item that the machine still needs, with the command that provides it. Atesor never runs these commands. The owner of the machine runs them, then you run `--preflight` again.

`--preflight` exits with 0 when every rung passes, and with 1 when a rung fails. Without the native target, `--preflight` prints a note and exits with 1.

Every native command also runs the preflight:

- Rung 1 runs first on every command, also on the QEMU target.
- Rungs 2 to 11 run after the recipe cache check, and before `--probe` and the API key check.
- `--cleanup` and `--clean-image` run rungs 2 to 8 only, so they also work on a full disk.
- `--clean-workspace` runs rungs 2 to 10 before it removes the cloned repositories from the machine.

Rung 8 runs `podman info`. On the first run, rootless podman creates its storage directory and starts its pause process (`catatonit -P`). Podman keeps both after the run. Rung 10 creates the work directory with `mkdir -p`.

## How do I build on the machine?

```bash
atesor-ai --target native --setup-only       # build the image one time
atesor-ai --target native --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --package
```

1. When the image is missing, Atesor builds it on the machine with `podman build --pull=always`. Run `--setup-only` one time to do this before your first port. Atesor sends the Dockerfile over SSH into an empty temporary build context. The build stops at a time limit of 5400 seconds.
2. Later commands find the image and start the container. Atesor creates the container with `podman run -d --init` and one bind mount, `<work directory>:/workspace:Z`. It sets no memory, CPU, DNS or network option.
3. After a port, Atesor removes the repository tree `/workspace/repos/<name>` from the machine. The local mirror keeps its copy. With `--optimize`, Atesor also removes `/workspace/repos/<name>.opt`. Use `--package` to keep the accepted artifacts of performance mode in the zip.
4. The container stops when each command ends.

| Command | What it does on native |
|---|---|
| `--rebuild` | Build the image on the machine again. |
| `--cleanup` | Remove the container with `podman rm -f --volumes`. |
| `--clean-image` | Also remove the image. |
| `--clean-workspace` | Clean the local workspace. When you select the `repos/` option (1 or 5), also remove `<work directory>/repos` on the machine with `podman unshare rm -rf`. |

To find and measure faster builds of a verified port on the machine, use `--optimize`. `--probe` shows what the machine supports. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

A batch run on native gets its default worker count from the machine: the core count or the memory in GiB divided by 4, whichever is smaller, and at least 1. `--workers` overrides it, up to the core count.

```bash
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py --target native --platform debian --list smoke
```

## Do native and QEMU results mix?

No. Native results and QEMU results never share a file or a cache entry:

| Result | QEMU | Native |
|---|---|---|
| State directory | `workspace/` | `workspace-native/` |
| Recipe cache key | `<platform>-riscv64` | `<platform>-riscv64-native` |
| Zip name | `<owner>-<repo>-<time>-<platform>.zip` | `<owner>-<repo>-<time>-<platform>-native.zip` |
| Report line | `**Target**: qemu` | `**Target**: native` |

## What are the safety rules?

- Atesor never runs `sudo` and never installs anything on the machine. The preflight prints the fix commands for the owner.
- Login uses an SSH key only, with `BatchMode=yes`. Atesor never answers a password prompt.
- Secret values, for example the GitHub token for a private clone, go to the machine on the SSH standard input. They never go in an argv on either computer.
- Before Atesor prints or logs SSH error text, it replaces every IPv4 address with a placeholder. In field mode, it also replaces the host name and the user.
- The work directory must not be `$HOME`, a parent of `$HOME`, or a directory in `~/.ssh`. The `:Z` mount relabels the directory for SELinux, so these locations are not safe.
- The physical path of the work directory must have no spaces or shell metacharacters.
- The container mounts only the work directory.
- When the SSH connection never opened, Atesor checks the login (rung 4) and tries the command one more time. When the connection dropped during a command, the command can be half done, so Atesor does not try again. The run escalates instead.
- When the host key of the machine changes, rung 4 stops. Before you run `ssh-keygen -R <host>`, make sure that the owner reinstalled the machine.

See [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/) for the image contents, and [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/) for the full list of keys.

---

# Recipe cache

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/

The recipe cache is a JSON file in which Eclipse Atesor™ keeps the recipe of each verified port. When you port the same repository again on the same sandbox, Atesor writes the recipe from the cache and skips the full pipeline. A cache hit needs no API key, no LLM call and no running sandbox.

## What does the cache store?

The file is `data/recipe_cache.json` in the state home of Atesor. It has this shape:

```json
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "packages": {
    "zlib": {
      "alpine-riscv64": { "repo_url": "...", "build_plan": { "phases": [] } },
      "debian-riscv64": { "repo_url": "...", "build_plan": { "phases": [] } }
    }
  }
}
```

Each entry holds these fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `repo_url` | The repository URL of the port. |
| `build_system` | The detected build system. |
| `architecture` | `riscv64`. |
| `sandbox` | The sandbox key, for example `debian-riscv64`. |
| `last_built` | The time of the build. |
| `build_plan` | The phases of the build, each with its name and commands. |
| `dependencies` | The system packages of the build. |
| `patches` | The applied diffs, at most 10. |
| `artifacts` | The build outputs, at most 20, each with its type, path and role. |
| `build_duration_seconds` | The duration of the run. |
| `recipe_file` | `output/<repo>_recipe.md`. |
| `recipe_markdown` | The full text of the recipe. |
| `verification` | The verdict of the artifact scan: `status`, `reason` and `source_commit`. |
| `optimizations` | Only after `--optimize` on the native target: the results of performance mode, one for each machine. |

## What is the cache key?

The key has two parts: the package name and the sandbox.

- **Package name.** Atesor derives it from the URL with `derive_repo_name()`. It is the last segment of the URL, without `.git`. Each character that is not a letter, a digit, `.`, `_` or `-` becomes `-`. When that segment is a generic name (`cli`, `core`, `src`, `app`, `main`, `client`, `server` or `lib`), Atesor adds the owner. For example, `github.com/smallstep/cli` gives `smallstep-cli`.
- **Sandbox.** The key is `<profile>-riscv64`, for example `alpine-riscv64`. The native target adds `-native`, for example `debian-riscv64-native`. The `ubuntu` platform uses the Debian profile, so its key is `debian-riscv64`.

An entry for one sandbox never answers for another sandbox, because `apk` and `apt` commands are not interchangeable. An entry also counts only when its stored URL matches the URL of the run. Atesor compares the URLs without case, without a trailing slash and without `.git`. Thus a different repository with the same name does not get the recipe.

## When does Atesor write an entry?

Atesor writes an entry only after a verified port. The build must end with the status `SUCCESS`, and the artifact scan must give the verdict `verified`. Atesor does not cache a build whose commands pass but that proves no riscv64 output (exit code 3). It also does not cache a failed or escalated run.

A new entry for the same package and sandbox replaces the old one, also its `optimizations`. Atesor takes a file lock (`recipe_cache.json.lock`, next to the file) and writes the file atomically, so parallel batch workers do not damage it.

See [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/) for the scan that decides the verdict.

### What does performance mode add?

After a native run with `--optimize`, Atesor adds the result of [performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) to the entry of the verified build, under `optimizations`. The key is the core name of the machine, else its ISA label, so results from different boards stay apart. Each result has the date, the machine, the status, the accepted tune, its time ratio and the workload. An accepted tune also has its settings: the compiler, the flags and the environment.

- Atesor stores only a native result with a workload and the status `accepted` or `no gain`. It never stores a QEMU result.
- Atesor adds a result only to an entry that exists. A result never makes a new entry.

## How does a cache hit work?

A run with `--repo`, and without `--force` or `--optimize`, checks the cache before the API key check and before sandbox setup:

1. Atesor looks up the package name and the sandbox key of the run, and compares the URL.
2. It writes `<repo>_recipe.md` to the output directory. When the entry holds `recipe_markdown`, the file is that text. Else Atesor makes a recipe from the stored fields, with a note to run again with `--force`.
3. It prints the build system, the last build time, the source commit and the path of the recipe file.
4. It exits. The run clones nothing, builds nothing and calls no LLM.

The exit code depends on the verdict that the entry holds:

| Entry | Console | Exit code |
|---|---|---|
| Verified verdict | `CACHED (not rebuilt): recipe for '<repo>' from an earlier verified run` | 0 |
| No verified verdict | `CACHED (not rebuilt), NOT VERIFIED: recipe for '<repo>'; ...` | 3 |

An entry without a verified verdict comes from an older version of Atesor, for example from a time before verification existed. Run again with `--force` to build and verify the package. `--package` does nothing on a cache hit, because no fresh source tree exists to package.

### How does `--optimize` use the cache?

Performance mode needs a real build tree, so `--optimize` skips the cache hit. When the cache has an entry with a verified verdict, Atesor builds the package again with the cached build plan and patches, and makes no planning LLM call. `--force` makes Atesor plan again. Atesor does not use an entry without a verified verdict.

## How do I bypass or clear the cache?

Pass `--force` to ignore the cache for one run. Atesor then runs the full pipeline. If the new port is verified, its entry replaces the old one.

```bash
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --force
```

`batch_test.py` always passes `--force` to each run, so batch runs never use the cache.

No flag clears the cache. `--clean-workspace` does not touch it, because the cache is in `data/` and not in the workspace. To remove one package, delete its key from `packages` in the JSON file. When the file is missing at start, Atesor copies the cache file that ships with Atesor. If no such file exists, Atesor writes an empty cache.

## Where does the cache live?

The cache is in `<state home>/data/recipe_cache.json`. Atesor selects the state home in this order:

1. `ATESOR_HOME`, when you set it.
2. `/workspace`, when Atesor itself runs inside a container.
3. The source checkout, when you run from a writable clone.
4. `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai`, by default `~/.local/share/atesor-ai`.

The source repository also ships a `data/recipe_cache.json`. The `.gitattributes` file of the repository stops git from a line-by-line merge of this file. To merge two versions by meaning, run `sh .github/scripts/setup_git_merge_driver.sh` one time in your clone, or use `.github/scripts/merge_data_artifacts.py --merge-caches`. In both cases, the newest recipe of each package and sandbox wins.

## What is the few-shot store?

The few-shot store is a second learned data set in `data/examples/`. It has one JSON file for each of three agent roles: `scout_examples.json`, `fixer_examples.json` and `builder_examples.json`. The file `supervisor_examples.json` is a legacy file that no code reads. Atesor writes new examples at the same time as the cache entry, only after a verified port:

- a scout example with the build plan,
- a fixer example for each fix that worked,
- a builder example with the build phases.

Atesor puts the examples that match best into the scout and fixer prompts. It first removes examples from another sandbox. Then it scores the rest, for example by build system, error pattern and tags. Each file keeps at most 100 examples. When a file is full, Atesor removes the oldest auto-learned examples first and keeps the manual examples. The few-shot sandbox key has no `-native` suffix, so native and QEMU runs share examples. They do not share recipe cache entries.

See [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/) for how the prompts use the examples, and [Few-shot examples](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/few-shot-examples/) to add your own.

---

# Batch runs

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/

A batch run ports a list of packages in parallel. Eclipse Atesor™ uses the script `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` for this. Each worker runs `main.py` for one package at a time, in its own sandbox container. The CI workflows use the same script for the weekly and monthly sweeps.

## How do I run a batch?

Run the script from the root of a source checkout. It starts `python3 main.py` for each package and reads `.env` from the root of the repository.

```bash
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py                          # the smoke list
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py --list full              # the full catalog
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py --list full anew gron    # two packages of the full list
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py --list path/to/custom.json
python3 .github/scripts/batch_test.py --target native --platform debian --list smoke
```

## What are the flags?

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--list NAME` | `smoke` | The package list. A bare name means `.github/packages/<name>.json`. A value that has a `/` or ends in `.json` is a path. |
| `--workers N` | The CPU count of the host | The number of parallel workers. It must be from 1 to the CPU count. On native, see below. |
| `--platform NAME` | `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, else `debian` | `alpine`, `debian` or `ubuntu`. It selects the image and the worker container names. |
| `--target NAME` | `ATESOR_TARGET`, else `qemu` | `qemu` or `native`. It overrides `ATESOR_TARGET` for every run. |
| `--package` | off | Pass `--package` to each run. Each build with the status `SUCCESS` then writes a zip under `workspace/packages/`. |
| `--shard-index I` | none | Run only shard `I` (counted from 0). It needs `--shard-total`. |
| `--shard-total N` | none | Cut the list into `N` contiguous shards of `ceil(packages / N)` packages. `1` turns sharding off. |
| `names` | all | Positional package names. The script runs only these packages from the list. |

You cannot use positional names together with `--shard-index` and `--shard-total`. An unknown name, a bad worker count or a bad shard value stops the script with exit code 2.

The CI full jobs do not use `--shard-index` and `--shard-total`. They compute their own shards and pass the package names.

The default platform of `batch_test.py` is `debian`. The default platform of `main.py` is Alpine. Set `--platform` or `ATESOR_PLATFORM` to make them agree.

`batch_test.py` has no option for [performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/), so a batch run never optimizes.

## What do the package lists contain?

The lists are JSON files in `.github/packages/`. Each list has `$schema_version` 1, a `packages` array with a `name` and a `url` for each package, and optional `defaults`:

| List | Packages | `max_attempts` | `timeout_seconds` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `smoke.json` | 8 | 5 | 1800 |
| `full.json` | 698 | 5 | 2400 |

The script passes `max_attempts` to `main.py --max-attempts`. It stops a run when `timeout_seconds` ends. Without `defaults`, the values are 5 attempts and 3600 seconds.

## How do the workers share the sandboxes?

Each worker gets its own container, so `apk` and `apt` locks of one package never block another package:

1. The script makes a pool of container names: `<base>-w1` to `<base>-wN`. The base is `atesor-ai-sandbox` for Alpine and `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian` for Debian/Ubuntu.
2. A worker takes a name from the pool and runs `main.py --repo <url> --max-attempts <N> --force --container <name> --platform <platform>`. On native, it also passes `--target native`.
3. `main.py` creates the container on first use from the shared image. The setup lock lets one worker build the image while the others wait.
4. When the run ends, the worker puts the name back. The next package reuses the container and its package cache.

Two list entries with the same derived package name never run at the same time. Each run passes `--force`, so a batch never uses the recipe cache. See [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

Before the first package, the script runs `main.py --setup-only` for the `w1` container. Then it reads the Go and Cargo versions in the image. If Go is older than 1.26.5 or Cargo is older than 1.90.0, it builds the image again and creates each worker container again.

On the native target, the default worker count is the core count of the machine or its memory in GiB divided by 4, whichever is smaller, and at least 1. `--workers` can go up to the core count. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## How does the script report results?

Each package gets one status from the exit code of `main.py`:

| Status | Cause |
|---|---|
| `PASS` | Exit code 0: riscv64 output verified. |
| `UNVERIFIED` | Exit code 3: the commands passed, but no riscv64 output was proven. |
| `FAIL` | Any other exit code, or an exception in the worker. |
| `TIMEOUT` | The run passed `timeout_seconds`. The script sends `SIGTERM` to its process group, then `SIGKILL` after 10 seconds. |
| `SKIPPED` | The run did not start, or you stopped the batch. |

The script writes the full output of each run to `output/batch_logs/<package>.log`. At the end, it prints a table of all packages, the counts for each status, and the pass rate. The pass rate is the `PASS` count divided by the packages that ran. It counts verified passes only.

Each child run gets `ATESOR_RUN_DEADLINE`, its kill time in epoch seconds. `main.py` then shortens its package test phase, so the report and the zip still fit before the kill. Set `ATESOR_SETUP_STREAM=1` to see the setup output live.

The first Ctrl-C cancels the queued packages, sends `SIGTERM` to the packages that run, and prints the summary. A second Ctrl-C sends `SIGKILL` and exits with 130.

| Exit code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | No `FAIL`, `TIMEOUT` or `UNVERIFIED` result. |
| 1 | At least one `FAIL`, `TIMEOUT` or `UNVERIFIED` result. Also a missing or invalid list file, a failed setup check, or a native machine whose cores and memory Atesor cannot read. |
| 2 | A bad flag, worker count, shard value or package name, or an unknown `ATESOR_PLATFORM`. |
| 130 | You stopped the batch with Ctrl-C. |

## Which CI workflows run batches?

### `batch-port.yml`

The workflow `ATESOR AI Batch Porting Tests` runs the batches on GitHub Actions under QEMU.

- **Schedule.** Every Saturday at 01:17 UTC, and on the first day of each month at 01:07 UTC. A scheduled run does the full list on both platforms.
- **Manual inputs.** `target` (`smoke`, `full` or `both`), `platform` (`debian`, `alpine` or `both`), `workers` (default 2), `group_size` (default 25), `force_all`, and `llm_provider` (`openrouter`, `gemini`, `openai` or `anthropic`; default `openrouter`).
- **Preflight.** The job first calls `llm-health.yml`, which sends a small real completion to the LLM providers. A manual run gates on the provider that you selected. A scheduled run uses the first working provider of the chain in the repository variable `LLM_PROVIDER_CHAIN`, by default `openrouter,anthropic`. Each batch job then uses that provider. When the provider does not work, the batch jobs do not run.
- **Smoke jobs.** They pull the prebuilt sandbox image, run `--setup-only`, then run `batch_test.py --list smoke --workers <N> --package`.
- **Full jobs.** The `plan-full` job reads the releases of the current month and lists the packages of `full.json` that have no zip for that platform yet. It cuts that list into shards of `group_size` packages. Each shard job runs `batch_test.py --list full --workers <N> --package <names>` and has a limit of 350 minutes.
- **After the full jobs.** One job collects the logs of all shards. Another job merges the new recipe cache entries and few-shot examples of all shards and opens a draft pull request with them. A maintainer reviews and merges it by hand.

### `batch-port-retry.yml`

This workflow starts when `ATESOR AI Batch Porting Tests` completes. It does not start when someone cancelled that run, or when a pull request started it. You can also start it by hand with the ID of a main run. It finds the packages that have no zip from the main run and runs only those again, with `--workers 2 --package`.

- The retries are the hard cases, so the default provider is `anthropic`. A manual run can select `openrouter`, `gemini`, `openai` or `anthropic`.
- An automatic retry uses the first working provider of the chain in the repository variable `RETRY_LLM_PROVIDER_CHAIN`, by default `anthropic,openrouter`.
- The default `group_size` is 25. It must match the main run, so that the retry shards match the main shards.

### Other workflows

- `regression-tests.yml` runs the test suite on each push and pull request to `main` and `dev`, in groups. The `performance-mode` group runs the tests of performance mode. The workflow runs no ports.
- `llm-health.yml` checks the LLM providers `openrouter`, `gemini`, `openai` and `anthropic` every day at 01:00 UTC, and when a batch workflow calls it.
- `package-deb.yml` builds the Debian package of Atesor on a `vX.Y.Z` tag, or when you start it by hand. It runs no ports.

## What are the monthly builds releases?

The batch and retry jobs publish each zip as an asset of a monthly GitHub release in the [releases](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/releases) of the repository.

- The tag is `builds-YYYY-MM`, with the title `<Month YYYY> builds`.
- GitHub allows at most 1000 assets in one release. When a release is full, the jobs continue in `builds-YYYY-MM-01`, `builds-YYYY-MM-02` and so on.
- The asset name is `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip`, with `alpine` or `debian` as the platform.
- Each repository keeps one asset for each platform in a month. Before an upload, the job deletes the older asset of the same repository and platform from all releases of that month.
- A later full run in the same month does not build a package again when it has an asset for that platform. The manual input `force_all` builds all packages again.

`main.py --package` writes a zip when the build ends with the status `SUCCESS`. This includes a build that is not verified (exit code 3). The `manifest.json` in the zip records the verdict. See [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) for the content of the zip.

---

# Cost control

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/

Eclipse Atesor™ counts the real tokens and the cost of every LLM call in a run. A run escalates when its cost passes $1.00. Many steps make no LLM call at all, and when the LLM fails, most steps fall back to rules.

## What is the cost cap?

The cap is $1.00 for each package run. It is the local variable `cost_limit = 1.0` in `should_escalate()` in `src/state.py`. No flag or environment variable changes it.

```python
# Hard per-package spend cap, in USD.
cost_limit = 1.0
if state.api_cost_usd > cost_limit:
    return True, f"API cost limit (${cost_limit}) exceeded"
```

- The supervisor checks the cap each time that it routes the run. When the total cost is above $1.00, it sends the run to escalation with the reason `API cost limit ($1.0) exceeded`. The run exits with code 1.
- The build-fix loop does not check the cap between its steps. Thus the total can pass $1.00 by the cost of the calls after the last check.
- A build with the status `SUCCESS` always goes to the finish step, also above the cap. Atesor does not discard a build that worked.
- The cap is for one run. In a batch, each package run has its own total.
- The cap does not stop [performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) (`--optimize`). Performance mode runs after the finish step, so the supervisor does not check the cap again. Its LLM calls still add to the run total.

`--max-attempts` (default 5) also limits the cost, because each fix attempt can call the LLM. See [Troubleshooting](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/troubleshooting/) for all escalation rules.

## How does Atesor count tokens and cost?

After each LLM call, Atesor reads the token counts that the provider returns. It reads `usage_metadata` first, then the OpenAI-style `token_usage`. Then `cost_for_usage()` in `src/models.py` calculates the cost:

- A free-tier model costs $0. A model is free when its ID ends in `:free`, or when it is `openrouter/free`.
- A paid model costs its input tokens and output tokens at the prices in `MODEL_PRICES_PER_MTOK`.
- A paid model that is not in the table uses a high default price, $3.00 for each million input tokens and $12.00 for each million output tokens. Thus an unknown model reaches the cap early. It never counts as free.
- When the provider reports no token usage, the call counts as 0 tokens and $0.
- Every attempt that returns a response counts. This includes a response that Atesor rejects before it tries again.

`MODEL_PRICES_PER_MTOK`, in USD for each million tokens:

| Model | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `gpt-4o` | 2.50 | 10.00 |
| `gpt-4o-mini` | 0.15 | 0.60 |
| `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | 0.10 | 0.40 |
| `gemini-flash-latest` | 0.30 | 2.50 |
| `claude-haiku-5-5` | 0.10 | 0.50 |
| `claude-sonnet-5-5` | 2.00 | 10.00 |

The table holds one base price for each model. Atesor does not apply a higher price for a long prompt.

Two other settings limit each call: `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` (default 8192 output tokens) and `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` (default 120 seconds).

## Which models does each provider use?

`MODEL_CONFIG` in `src/models.py` gives one model to each agent role. When `LLM_PROVIDER` is not set, Atesor uses `gemini`.

| Role | `openrouter` | `gemini` | `openai` | `anthropic` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| planner (the analyst) | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| scout | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| fixer | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| summarizer | `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| supervisor | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| builder | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |

- The supervisor makes no LLM call. Its entry exists only in the table.
- The builder makes an LLM call only in performance mode: its models write the harness of the optimizer agent. In performance mode, the planner models also select a program run.
- With `anthropic`, Atesor sends no temperature. It sends an `effort` level instead: `low` for the supervisor and the summarizer, and `medium` for the other roles.

With the `openrouter` provider, every default model is a free-tier model, so the run cost is $0. With the `anthropic` provider, every model is a paid model in `MODEL_PRICES_PER_MTOK`. If you add a paid model to `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS`, Atesor counts its cost. See [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/) to set the provider.

### What happens when a free model is not available?

- `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS` is a comma-separated list of fallback model IDs. Without it, Atesor uses a built-in list of free models. Atesor always adds `openrouter/free`, the OpenRouter router that selects an available free model, as the last entry.
- Each OpenRouter request names the main model, two fallback models and `openrouter/free`. OpenRouter tries them in the same request.
- When a call still fails with a provider error, Atesor tries the next model in the list.
- When the provider sends a short `Retry-After` value (65 seconds or less), Atesor waits one time on the same model.
- When the provider returns HTTP 402 with the number of tokens that the account can pay for, Atesor lowers the output token limit and tries again.
- When OpenRouter reports that the account has no daily free-model requests left, Atesor stops the retries and uses the deterministic fallback of that step.

## What runs when the LLM is not available?

Many steps make no LLM call. The rest fall back to rules when all attempts fail:

| Step | LLM call | Fallback when the LLM fails |
|---|---|---|
| Recipe cache hit | None | Not needed. A cache hit needs no API key. |
| Clone and scripted analysis | None | Not needed. |
| Analyst | Yes | `_fallback_analysis()` makes the analysis from the scripted detection. When detection confidence is below 0.5, the plan goes to the LLM scout. |
| Heuristic plan | None | Not needed. It makes a default build plan for a known build system. |
| Scout | Yes | `create_fallback_build_plan()` makes a basic plan for the detected build system. The failure counts as an attempt. |
| Supervisor | None | Not needed. The routing uses rules. |
| Builder and its recovery steps | None | Not needed. For example, it installs a missing header package or runs a build again with one job. |
| Verification | None | Not needed. |
| Fixer | Yes | No fallback. The fixer records the failure as an attempt, and the run goes back to the supervisor. |
| Summarizer (the recipe) | Yes | A short recipe with the build steps and the verification verdict. |
| Artifact curator | Yes | Rule-based curation of the build outputs. |
| Cached recipe (`--optimize`) | None | Not needed. A verified cached recipe replaces the analyst and the scout. |
| Performance mode (`--optimize`) | Yes, for a program run or a harness | No fallback. Atesor tries the next workload source. The result of the port does not change. |

See [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/) for the prompts and the retry rules.

## How do I see the cost of a run?

- **The report.** The Metrics table of `<repo>_report_<time>.md` in the output directory has the rows `API Calls`, `LLM Tokens (in/out)` and `Cost (from token usage)`.
- **The state file.** `<repo>_state_<time>.json` has the fields `api_calls_made`, `api_tokens_in`, `api_tokens_out` and `api_cost_usd`.
- **The call log.** `logs/agent-call_<repo>.log` has one block for each LLM call, with the agent, the model, `COST: $...`, `TOKENS: in=... out=...`, the prompt and the response.
- **The agent log.** Each supervisor step writes `Supervisor summary: ...` with `cost=$...` to `logs/agent_<repo>.log`.
- **The escalation report.** An escalated run records its cost in the escalation report in the state file.

The artifact curator call appears in the call log, but Atesor does not add it to the run total. `batch_test.py` does not add up the cost of a batch. See [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) for the location of each file.

---

# Troubleshooting

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/troubleshooting/

This page lists the common failures of Eclipse Atesor™ by symptom. For each failure, it tells you what you see, what Atesor does by itself, and what you can do. Atesor puts each build error into a category, and the category decides the next step of the run.

## Where do I find the cause of a failure?

When a run does not succeed, the console shows `PORTING STOPPED / FAILED` and the final status. Then it shows these items:

- `Last Error Capture`: the category, the severity and the first 500 characters of the last error.
- `Agent Decision Audit`: the last 10 events of the run.

The output directory and the logs directory hold more data:

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `<repo>_report_<time>.md` | The status, the metrics, the error history and recommendations. |
| `<repo>_state_<time>.json` | The full run state, with the escalation report in `context_cache.escalation_report`. |
| `<repo>_patches_<time>/` | The patches that the fixer applied. |
| `logs/agent_<repo>.log` | The full debug log of the run. |
| `logs/agent-call_<repo>.log` | Each LLM call, with its prompt and response. |

Add `--verbose` to see the agent messages in the console. See [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) for the locations.

## What do the error categories mean?

`classify_error()` in `src/state.py` compares the error text with ordered patterns. The first rule that matches gives the category. The category decides the next step:

| Category | Typical error text | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| `DEPENDENCY` | `unable to locate package`, `No package 'x' found`, CMake `Could not find`, `not found`, `No such file` | The scout makes a new plan. |
| `MISSING_TOOLS` | `command not found`, `go.mod requires go >=`, `requires rustc` | The scout makes a new plan. |
| `COMPILATION` | `syntax error`, `undeclared`, `implicit declaration`, `error[E0...]` | The build-fix loop. |
| `LINKING` | `undefined reference`, `relocation truncated to fit`, `cannot find -l`, `__atomic_load_` | The build-fix loop. |
| `ARCHITECTURE` | `immintrin.h`, `unsupported architecture`, `-msse`, `-mavx`, `-march=native` options, `invalid instruction mnemonic` | The build-fix loop. |
| `CONFIGURATION` | `config.guess: unable to guess system type`, `configure: error`, `CMake Error`, `no rule to make target` | The build-fix loop. |
| `NETWORK` | `timed out`, `connection`, `could not read Username`, `unreachable` | The build-fix loop. |
| `RATE_LIMIT` | `rate limit`, `429`, `too many requests`, `quota exceeded` | The build-fix loop. |
| `UNKNOWN` | Any other text | The build-fix loop. |
| `PERMISSION` | `permission denied`, `access denied`, `forbidden` | Escalation. |
| `DISK_SPACE` | `no space left`, `virtual memory exhausted`, `exit 137`, a bare `Killed` | Escalation. |
| `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE`, `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE` | `classify_error()` does not give these categories. | Escalation. |

In the build-fix loop, the builder runs the plan again, and the fixer (an LLM agent) proposes a fix after each failure. Some error texts make the scout plan again, one time for each text. Examples are `./configure: No such file or directory`, `unable to locate package` and `inconsistent vendoring`.

The severity is `low`, `medium` or `high`. A failed `which` probe is `low`. `PERMISSION`, `DISK_SPACE` and the three other blocker categories are `high`. A failed command such as `git clone`, `apt-get update` or `apk add` is also `high`.

## What does "escalated" mean?

An escalation stops the run and asks a person to continue. The final status is `ESCALATED`, and the exit code is 1. The run escalates in these cases:

1. The run used all its attempts. The limit is `--max-attempts`, by default 5. Each recorded error counts as one attempt.
2. The last three errors have the same category and the same first error line. Atesor removes paths and numbers before it compares the lines.
3. The last error is in a blocker category: `PERMISSION`, `DISK_SPACE`, `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE` or `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE`.
4. The cost of the run passed $1.00. See [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).
5. A step of the run raised an error, for example a lost SSH connection on the native target.
6. The clone failed, or the analyst step gave no result.

**What you get:**

- The report, with `Manual intervention required`, the reason and the error history.
- The escalation report in the state file. It holds the attempts, the cost, the duration, the last error, the last 5 fixes, the architecture issues of high severity, the escalation reason and the last 5 failures with their commands.
- The patches that the fixer applied.
- No recipe, no recipe cache entry, no few-shot example and no zip.

**What you can do:**

- Read the last error and its category first. They show the step that stopped the run.
- If the run used all its attempts, and each attempt failed with a different error, run again with a higher `--max-attempts`.
- Run the package on the other platform. A failure on one libc family only points to a libc difference.
- Use the report, the patches and the logs to finish the port by hand.

## What does "not verified" (exit code 3) mean?

The build commands succeeded, but the artifact scan found no proof of riscv64 output. The console shows `PORTING FINISHED, NOT VERIFIED` and the reason. The report status is `SUCCESS, NOT VERIFIED (no riscv64 output proven)`.

The scan gives one of these reasons:

- `the build produced no ELF executable or library`: for example a header-only library or a package of scripts.
- `the scan stopped after <N> candidate files, before it read every build output`.
- `artifact scan failed: ...`.

**What Atesor does:** It writes the recipe and the report, and with `--package` the zip. It does not write a recipe cache entry or few-shot examples. `batch_test.py` counts the result as `UNVERIFIED`, not as a pass.

**What you can do:** For a header-only or script package, check the install tree yourself. Otherwise, check that the build plan builds the main targets of the package.

A recipe cache hit also exits with 3 when the cache entry has no verified verdict. The console then shows `CACHED (not rebuilt), NOT VERIFIED`. Run again with `--force` to build and verify the package. See [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/).

## Setup problems

### No binfmt handler for riscv64

**What you see:** `qemu-riscv64 binfmt handler not detected; attempting to register`. When the registration fails: `ERROR: qemu-riscv64 is not registered in /proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc.` Without the handler, every riscv64 container exits with `exec format error`.

**What Atesor does:** On the QEMU target, Atesor reads `/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/qemu-riscv64`. When the handler is missing, Atesor runs `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64` one time.

**What you can do:** Run the command yourself, then run Atesor again:

```bash
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64
```

The native target does not use binfmt.

### Docker does not respond

**What you see:** `ERROR: Docker is not running or not accessible`.

**What you can do:** Start the Docker daemon, and make sure that your user can use it. Then run the command again.

### The platform does not match the container

**What you see:** `ERROR: Platform mismatch` with the distro of the container and the selected platform.

**What Atesor does:** It stops before the build, because the package commands of one distro do not work on the other.

**What you can do:** Remove the old container with the command that the error gives, for example `docker rm -f atesor-ai-sandbox`. Then run again. See [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/).

### The API key is missing

**What you see:** For example `ERROR: GOOGLE_API_KEY not found in environment`, `ERROR: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not found in environment`, or `ERROR: Unknown provider: <name>`. With `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic`, a missing Python package gives `ERROR: langchain-anthropic is not installed (pip install -r requirements.txt)`.

**What Atesor does:** It checks the key of `LLM_PROVIDER` before a run with `--repo`. A missing key, and the placeholder `your_key_here`, stop the run with exit code 1. When `LLM_PROVIDER` is not set, Atesor expects `GOOGLE_API_KEY` for `gemini`. A recipe cache hit, `--setup-only` and `--probe` need no key. `--optimize` always needs a key, also when the cache has a verified recipe.

**What you can do:** Put the key in a `.env` file. Atesor reads these files in this order, and the first value of a key wins:

1. A `.env` in the directory of `main.py` or in a parent directory. In a source checkout, this is the `.env` in the root of the checkout. The search starts at `main.py`, not at the current directory.
2. `$ATESOR_HOME/.env`, when you set `ATESOR_HOME`.
3. `~/.config/atesor-ai/.env` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atesor-ai/.env`).
4. `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/.env` (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai/.env`).

A variable that is already in the environment wins over all files. A key that is present can still fail, for example when its quota is empty. In a source checkout, this script sends one small real request to the provider that you name:

```bash
python3 .github/scripts/check_llm_providers.py -p openrouter
```

See [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

### The native preflight fails

**What you see:** `Native preflight stopped at rung <N>` or `Native preflight failed. Still required on the machine:`, with a list of items and fix commands.

**What you can do:** Give the list to the owner of the machine. Then run `atesor-ai --target native --preflight` again. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## Build failures

### A stale config.guess

**What you see:** `config.guess: unable to guess system type`, `machine 'riscv64' not recognized`, or `invalid configuration`. The `config.guess` and `config.sub` scripts of the project are older than riscv64 support.

**What Atesor does:**

- The scripted analysis flags each `config.guess` and `config.sub` whose timestamp is before 2018-02-22, with high severity.
- The error goes to the fixer as `CONFIGURATION`. The fixer prompt tells it to copy new scripts from automake (`cp /usr/share/automake-*/config.* .`) or to run `autoreconf -fi`, and to use `--build`, never `--host`.
- When a project has no committed `configure` script, the builder first runs `autogen.sh`, `buildconf`, `bootstrap` or `autoreconf -fi`.

**What you can do:** Copy the scripts from the automake of the sandbox into the project, or run `autoreconf -fi`. Then run the build again.

### x86 SIMD intrinsics

**What you see:** `'immintrin.h' file not found`, `unknown type name '__m128'`, `undefined reference to '_mm_*'`, or an unknown option such as `-msse2`, `-mavx` or `-march=native`.

**What Atesor does:**

- The scripted analysis flags includes of x86 and ARM intrinsic headers, and hard `-m` flags in build files, as architecture issues.
- With a critical issue, or 3 or more issues of high severity, Atesor does not use a default plan. The LLM scout makes the plan, and its prompt tells it to turn off optional SIMD features.
- A build error of this type goes to the fixer as `ARCHITECTURE`. The prompt lists the fixes: SIMDe, a scalar C fallback, RVV intrinsics when the V extension is present, or a build option that turns SIMD off.
- When the artifact scan finds a build output for another architecture, the run also goes to the fixer as `ARCHITECTURE`.

**What you can do:** Look for a build option of the project that turns off SIMD or assembly. If none exists, add a portable fallback in the code.

### Go -buildvcs errors

**What you see:** `error obtaining VCS status`, `Use -buildvcs=false`, or `dubious ownership`. The sandbox runs as root, which trips the VCS ownership check of Go.

**What Atesor does:**

- Both images set `GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`.
- The default Go plans use `go build -buildvcs=false`.
- When a `go build` or `go install` still fails with one of these texts, the builder adds `-buildvcs=false` and runs it one more time.
- The builder removes `-buildvcs=false` from other Go commands, for example `go mod tidy`, because they do not accept it.

**What you can do:** Normally nothing. If you replay a recipe outside the sandbox, keep `-buildvcs=false` on `go build`.

### musl and glibc header differences

**What you see:** On Alpine, for example `execinfo.h: No such file or directory`, `undefined reference to 'backtrace'`, `undefined reference to 'mallinfo'`, `'REG_RIP' undeclared` or `'sys/cdefs.h' file not found`.

**What Atesor does:**

- On Alpine, the scout and fixer prompts state that musl lacks some GNU extensions. They give the fixes: guard the code with `#ifdef __GLIBC__`, or use libunwind for backtraces. `libexecinfo` is no longer in Alpine, so the prompt says not to install it.
- Atesor replaces package names of the other distro in install commands, for example `libssl-dev` with `openssl-dev` on Alpine.

**What you can do:** Run the same package with `--platform debian`. If it builds there, the problem is a musl difference.

### Relocation truncated to fit

**What you see:** `relocation truncated to fit: R_RISCV_...`. The default RISC-V code model cannot reach the address in large code.

**What Atesor does:** When the error text has `relocation truncated` and `R_RISCV`, the builder runs the command one more time with `CFLAGS='-mcmodel=medany' CXXFLAGS='-mcmodel=medany'` in front. If that works, the new command goes into the plan and the recipe. Otherwise the error goes to the fixer as `LINKING`.

**What you can do:** The retry has no effect when the build system ignores `CFLAGS` and `CXXFLAGS` from the environment. In that case, add `-mcmodel=medany` to the compiler flags of the project, for example in its CMake or Makefile flags.

### QEMU out of memory (exit 137)

**What you see:** A build command that ends with exit code 137, or a parallel build that stops with no output. An error with exit code 137 gets the category `DISK_SPACE`.

**What Atesor does:**

1. The builder treats exit 137 as a probable QEMU out-of-memory kill. It runs the command one more time with one job: `make -j1`, `ninja -j1`, `go build -p 1` with `GOMAXPROCS=1`, `cargo build -j 1`, or `MAKEFLAGS=-j1` for `pip install`.
2. If the command still fails with exit 137, the run escalates, because `DISK_SPACE` is a blocker category.

Both images set `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, so Go does not download a new toolchain in the middle of a build. Such downloads can also end with exit 137 under QEMU.

**What you can do:**

- On the QEMU target, the sandbox container has an 8 GB memory limit. Free memory on the host, or use the [native target](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/), which sets no memory limit.
- Exit 137 can also come from the time limit of a command. The default limit of a build command is 1800 seconds. Atesor stops the command inside the sandbox with `timeout --signal=KILL`, 30 seconds before that limit. Check the duration of the command in `agent_<repo>.log`.

### Missing -dev packages

**What you see:** `fatal error: <header>.h: No such file or directory`, `No package '<name>' found`, CMake `Could not find <name>`, or `Unable to locate package`.

**What Atesor does:**

- For a missing header, the builder maps the header to a distro package through the `package_map` of the platform profile. It installs the package and runs the command one more time. This step needs no LLM.
- When an install command names a package that does not exist on riscv64, the builder installs the packages one by one and skips the missing ones.
- The error goes to the scout as `DEPENDENCY`, and the scout makes a new plan with the missing packages.

**What you can do:** Find the package name for the distro of the sandbox, and check that it exists for riscv64. A header that is not in the `package_map` needs a person or the scout to find the package.

### Command blocked by safety validation

**What you see:** `Command blocked by safety validation: <reason>` in the log.

**What Atesor does:** Atesor compares each command with a whitelist of allowed command patterns before the command runs. Each part of a chained command must match. Atesor blocks a command that does not match, and the command counts as failed.

**What you can do:** Read the blocked command in `agent_<repo>.log`. A blocked command usually comes from an LLM proposal, and the next fix attempt uses another command.

## Performance mode problems

These problems apply to runs with `--optimize`. Performance mode never changes the exit code of the port. The console shows its answer in the `Optimized:` line, and the report has the full record. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

### Atesor skipped performance mode

**What you see:** `Optimized: NO: performance mode was skipped`, with one of these reasons after `Why:`:

- `the port is not verified, so there is no baseline`
- `no tune applies to this machine and build system`
- `the verified build has no repeatable command or no artifact in the tree`

**What you can do:** For the first reason, make the port verified first. See [What does "not verified" (exit code 3) mean?](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/troubleshooting/#what-does-not-verified-exit-code-3-mean). For the second reason, run `--probe`. It shows the extensions, the core and the compilers that the tunes need.

### The machine gives wrong data

**What you see:** A `Health` line such as `3 of 40 zlib round trips gave wrong data (CPU 0: 1, CPU 1: 2)`, then `Fix: make the machine stable first (a lower CPU frequency, a memory test), then run again`.

**What Atesor does:** It stops before it builds anything, because no time measurement on that machine is reliable. The status is `not measured`.

**What you can do:** Ask the owner of the machine to lower the CPU frequency or to test the memory. Then run again.

### No tune could be timed

**What you see:** `Optimized: NO: no tune could be timed`. On native hardware, the reason often starts with `no workload, so no tune was built or measured`.

**What Atesor does:** It tries each workload source in order and records why each one failed. Without a workload, a native run builds no tune.

**What you can do:** Read the `Notes` list in the `Performance Mode (--optimize)` section of the report. It has one note for each workload source. A console line that starts with `port problem:` means that the verified build itself crashed on the machine. The report lists that crash under `Warnings`.

### A gain is not confirmed

**What you see:** `Optimized: NO: no faster tune was confirmed`, with `Fix: run again with a larger ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET`.

**What Atesor does:** A tune was faster in its first measurement, but the time limit ended before its second check. Atesor does not accept a tune without a second check.

**What you can do:** Set a larger `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET`, in seconds. The default is 3600.

### No compiler tune

**What you see:** The tune list has no `compiler` tune.

**What you can do:** The compiler tune needs clang in the sandbox image. Only `Dockerfile.native` installs it. Build the native image again one time with `python3 main.py --target native --setup-only --rebuild`.

### The CPU model or `--probe` is rejected

**What you see:** `ERROR: --emulate-cpu '<model>' is not a QEMU CPU model`, or `ERROR: --probe runs alone. Remove --repo, or remove --probe to port the repository.` The exit code is 1.

**What you can do:** Give a model that starts with a letter, for example `rva22u64`. Run `--probe` without `--repo`.

---

# Performance mode

Section: Guides
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/

Performance mode (`--optimize`) builds faster variants of a verified port for the machine that runs Eclipse Atesor™. Atesor checks each variant and measures it against the verified build. Use it on a native riscv64 machine to find out if other compiler or toolchain settings make the package faster on that machine.

Each variant is a "tune": the same build with other compiler or toolchain settings. The verified build always stays the result of the port. An accepted tune is an extra output, and only a measurement on real riscv64 hardware can accept it.

## What do I need?

- **A verified port.** Performance mode runs after the finish step of the port. A port that is not verified gets the status `skipped`. A port that fails goes to escalation, and performance mode does not run.
- **A native machine for a time measurement.** Use `--target native`. On the QEMU target, Atesor builds and checks the tunes, but it measures no time and never accepts a tune. See [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/) for the setup of the machine.
- **A quiet machine.** Set the cpufreq governor of the board to `performance`. Atesor never changes a board setting. It warns when the governor is different, when other work uses the CPUs, and when other Atesor containers run on the machine.
- **clang for the compiler tune.** Only `Dockerfile.native` installs a clang (`clang-19`, with `lld-19`, `llvm-19` and `libclang-rt-19-dev`). The Alpine image and the QEMU images have no clang, so they get no compiler tune. A native image that you built from an older checkout has no clang. Build it again one time with `python3 main.py --target native --setup-only --rebuild`.
- **An LLM API key**, as for a port. The optimizer agent (an LLM) proposes a program run or writes a harness, which is a small driver program for a library. A harness comes from the models of the builder role, with a 240-second time limit. A program run comes from the models of the planner role. When no model of the role answers in time, the models of the other role get the question one time.
- **Time.** The default time limit is one hour, after the port.

The LLM calls of performance mode add to the API calls, tokens and cost of the run. Each workload round costs at least one LLM request. The $1.00 cost cap does not stop performance mode: the supervisor checks the cap, and performance mode runs after the finish step. The module's own Go benchmarks and the package tests need no LLM call. See [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).

:::note
Performance mode is on `main` since 2026-10-15. The v0.2.0 `.deb` package (2026-10-01) does not include it. Run it from a source checkout with `python3 main.py` until the next release. See [Install Atesor](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/).
:::

## How do I run it?

```bash
python3 main.py --probe --target native
python3 main.py --target native --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --optimize --package
```

The first command shows what the machine supports and the settings that follow from it. The second command ports the package, then runs performance mode. To build and check the tunes under QEMU, give a QEMU CPU model:

```bash
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --optimize --emulate-cpu rva22u64
```

| Flag or variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--optimize` | off | After a verified port, build, check and measure tunes. |
| `--probe` | off | Probe the machine, print the result, save it to `machine_profile_<native\|qemu>.json` in the output directory, then exit. |
| `--emulate-cpu MODEL` | not set (QEMU `max` CPU) | The `QEMU_CPU` model for `--optimize` and `--probe` on the QEMU target. |
| `--target` | `qemu` | Use `native` for a time measurement. |
| `--force` | off | With `--optimize`, ignore the cached recipe and plan again. |
| `--package` | off | Also put the accepted artifacts in the zip, under `optimized/`. |
| `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` | `3600` | The time limit of performance mode, in seconds. A value that is not a number gives 3600. |
| `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` | not set | The environment form of `--emulate-cpu`. The flag wins. |

### Rules for `--probe`

- `--probe` runs alone. With `--repo`, Atesor stops with an error and exit code 1.
- `--probe` needs the sandbox, but no API key. On the native target, the preflight runs first.
- The output has the lines `Machine:`, `ISA label:`, `Extensions:`, `Vector:`, `Core:`, `Misaligned:`, `CPUs:`, `Kernel/libc:`, `Sources:`, `Governor:` and one `Compiler:` line for each compiler. Then it shows the settings: `Flags:`, `Go:` and `Rust:`.
- On the native target, the last line is `QEMU model:`. It gives an `--emulate-cpu` value that models your board under QEMU. This value needs QEMU 9.0 or later.

### Rules for the CPU model

- A model must start with a letter. It can contain letters, digits and `_ . , = + -`, up to 512 characters. Else Atesor stops with `is not a QEMU CPU model` and exit code 1.
- The model `max`, with or without extra properties, counts as no model. Atesor then builds no ISA tune, because no real board has that extension set.
- On the native target, Atesor ignores `--emulate-cpu` and gives a warning: on the console with `--probe`, and in the report with `--optimize`. It also ignores `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`.
- Without `--optimize` or `--probe`, Atesor ignores the model.

### Performance mode and the recipe cache

`--optimize` needs a real build tree, so it skips the recipe cache fast path. When the cache has a verified recipe of the package, that recipe becomes the build plan. At the start of the run, the console then shows a `Recipe:` line that says `from the cache`.

- `cached_recipe_node` turns the cached build plan into the plan and applies the cached patches first. The analyst and the scout make no LLM call.
- When the build fails anyway, for example because the source changed, the fixer and the normal planning loop take over.
- `--force` makes Atesor plan again.

Performance mode never changes the exit code of the port. An error in performance mode goes into the report. `batch_test.py` has no option for performance mode, so a batch run never optimizes.

## What happens during a run?

The console shows performance mode as its own step, `optimize_node`, with the status `OPTIMIZING`, after `finish_node`. Atesor prints one line for each part of the work. The full internals are in [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/).

1. **Machine probe.** Atesor reads the ISA extensions (test instructions, `riscv_hwprobe` and `/proc/cpuinfo`), the core, the speed of misaligned memory access, the CPUs, the cpufreq governor, and the compilers with the flags that they accept. A probe that fails stops performance mode with the status `error`.
2. **Machine check (native only).** Each CPU that the sandbox may use runs 10 zlib round trips of 8 MiB, all CPUs at the same time. Unchanged code must give the data back. When it does not, Atesor stops before it builds anything, because no time measurement on that machine is reliable.
3. **Package type.** The artifacts of the verified build give the language (C/C++, Go or Rust) and the type: a library, programs, or both. Programs in test, example and benchmark folders do not count as programs of the package.
4. **Baseline.** Atesor builds the verified build again in a copy, `<repo>.opt/base`. It compares each tune with this copy, so only the change of the tune counts. When the code of the copy is different from the verified build, Atesor warns that the build is not reproducible.
5. **Workload.** Atesor selects a workload that does the same fixed work in every run.
6. **Tunes.** Atesor makes the list of tunes from the probe and the language. It skips a tune that the build already has.
7. **Rebuild.** Each tune builds in a fresh copy of the patched tree, `<repo>.opt/<id>`, with the commands of the verified build. A tune build does not repeat package installs, install steps, source control steps, or writes outside the tree.
8. **Gates.** Each tune must pass three correctness checks.
9. **Measurement (native only).** Atesor times each tune against the baseline.
10. **Profile-guided optimization.** After the list, Atesor tries profile-guided optimization (PGO) on top of the best tune.
11. **Second check (native only).** A faster tune must win again in a second check before Atesor accepts it.
12. **Finish.** The verified tree never changes. Atesor copies the riscv64 artifacts of the accepted tune to `<repo>.opt/accepted` and removes the other trees.

## Which tunes does Atesor try?

| Language | Technique | What the tune changes | When Atesor builds it |
|---|---|---|---|
| C/C++ | `core tuning` | `-mtune=<core>` | The probe knows the core, and GCC accepts a tune name for it. |
| C/C++ | `machine ISA` | `-march=rv64gc_<extensions>`, with only the probed extensions | The machine has one or more of Zicond, Zfa, Zfhmin, Zba, Zbb and Zbs, and GCC accepts them. |
| C/C++ | `vector ISA` | `-march=rv64gcv_<extensions>` | The machine has V, and GCC accepts it. |
| C/C++ | `optimization level` | `-O3` | Not every source compile of the build uses `-O3` already. |
| C/C++ | `link-time optimization` | `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects` | GCC accepts both flags, and no source compile uses `-flto` already. |
| C/C++ | `compiler` | The newest probed clang, with its own `-mtune`, `-march` (with V) and `-O3` | The probe finds a clang (`clang`, or `clang-19` to `clang-22`) that emits bitmanip code. |
| Go | `machine ISA` | `GORISCV64=rva22u64` or `GORISCV64=rva23u64` | The probe gives a level above `rva20u64`, the default of Go. |
| Rust | `target CPU` | `RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=<cpu>` | rustc knows the CPU of the core, and every feature that it adds is on the machine. |
| Rust | `machine ISA` | `RUSTFLAGS=-C target-feature=...` with the probed ones of `+zba`, `+zbb` and `+zbs` | Instead of `target CPU`, when that tune does not apply. |
| Rust | `link-time optimization` | `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat` and `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1` | Always. |
| C/C++ and Go | `profile-guided optimization` | A profile from a training run, on top of the best tune | C/C++ with a workload, and Go with a Go benchmark workload. Never Rust. |

- Each GCC tune keeps the flags of the tune before it. The vector tune replaces the scalar `-march`.
- When misaligned access is not `fast`, each C/C++ tune also gets `-mstrict-align`, if the compiler accepts it.
- The core table in `src/machine.py` knows five cores: `sifive-u74`, `sifive-p550`, `spacemit-x60`, `thead-c906` and `thead-c910`. An unknown core gets no core tuning.
- Under QEMU, ISA tunes need a named `--emulate-cpu` model.
- `GORISCV64=rva23u64` needs Go 1.25 or later. `rva22u64` needs Go 1.23 or later. A machine with Zba and Zbb but without Zbs can still get `rva22u64` with Go 1.23 to 1.26, because these releases emit no Zbs instruction for it. Then the package tests decide.
- When the build sets `RUSTFLAGS` itself, Atesor tries only the Rust LTO tune.
- Without GCC in the probe, Atesor tries no C/C++ tune.
- At most 7 tunes run: up to 6 from the list and one PGO tune.

The flags of a C/C++ tune reach each compiler call through wrapper scripts in `<tree>/.atesor/`, which `CC`, `CXX` and `MAKEFLAGS` name. The wrapper adds the tune flags after the flags of the project, so the tune wins for repeated options such as `-O` and `-march`. Go and Rust tunes use environment variables.

Example: `tests/test_optimize.py` uses a test profile of a SiFive P550 core with Zba and Zbb, no Zbs, no V, and slow misaligned access. For that profile, the C/C++ list is:

| Tune | Technique | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Tune-1` | `core tuning` | `-mtune=sifive-p550 -mstrict-align` |
| `Tune-2` | `machine ISA` | `-march=rv64gc_zba_zbb` |
| `Tune-3` | `optimization level` | `-O3` |
| `Tune-4` | `link-time optimization` | `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects` |
| `Tune-5` | `compiler` | `clang-19` |

The same profile gives Go `GORISCV64=rva22u64`, with a note about Zbs. It gives Rust `-C target-cpu=sifive-p550`, then fat LTO.

## How does Atesor judge a tune?

### Which workload does Atesor time?

A workload must do the same fixed work in every run, so its run time shows the speed of the build. Atesor tries these sources in order and uses the first one that passes its checks:

1. **Go benchmarks.** For a Go module, the benchmarks of the package that has the most benchmarks, with a fixed iteration count.
2. **A program run.** When the package builds its own programs, the optimizer agent proposes one command that runs a program on generated input.
3. **A harness.** For a library, or any Go module, the optimizer agent writes a harness against the public API: a C or C++ file, a Go benchmark `BenchmarkAtesor`, or a Cargo example `atesor_bench` for a Rust crate. A C/C++ harness links the library of the tree. With a shared library, `ldd` must show that the harness loads the copy in the tree.
4. **A test or example program** of the package that calls its library. The optimizer agent proposes a run of it.
5. **The package tests.** They are a weak signal, because tests check correctness and do not model real use. Atesor never times Go tests, because `go test` caches results.

Each candidate runs on the baseline tree first. The checks are:

- The candidate must build and exit with 0. A run that exits with 0 and still writes to stderr also fails.
- A harness must print the same `ATESOR-CHECK` line in two runs. A program run compares its whole output. Go benchmarks compare no output.
- On native hardware, one run must take 0.5 to 5 seconds. Atesor sets the iteration count of a harness or of Go benchmarks for about 2 seconds for each run. It scales the input of a program run instead, and a program run can take less than 0.5 seconds.
- The package tests run one time, on native hardware only, and only the 5-second limit applies.
- Under QEMU, one iteration is enough, because QEMU measures no time.

When a check fails, the optimizer agent gets the error and tries again: 3 rounds, and up to 8 rounds while each round gives a new error. The rounds stop when less than 600 seconds of the time limit are left. The input is generated data of the kind `binary`, `text`, `json` or `csv`. The same seed always gives the same bytes. Atesor does not use benchmark suites that run for a fixed time, for example Google Benchmark or criterion, because their run time does not show the speed.

### The gates

1. **Artifacts.** The artifacts must exist and be riscv64. For C/C++, the wrapper log must show compiler calls, so the flags reached the compiler. For Go, a binary must carry the `GORISCV64` value of the tune. Code that is equal to the baseline gives the result `no effect`.
2. **Package tests.** When the tests of the baseline pass, the tests of the tune must pass too. When the baseline tests did not pass, this gate does not decide. When the tests build an artifact again, Atesor puts back the build of the tune.
3. **Workload output.** The output of the workload must be equal to the output of the baseline, and a run must not change its input file.

- Gate 1 fails a tune that does not build a library of the package or the program that the workload times. Another missing artifact gives only a warning.
- Instructions from extensions that the machine lacks give a warning, not a failure, because runtime dispatch can contain them legitimately. Gates 2 and 3 decide.
- A tune with the same code as an earlier tune gets the result of that tune, without a new measurement.

### The measurement (native only)

1. Atesor warms up both builds with 3 runs each. Then it times 10 baseline runs. These runs give the noise and the minimum detectable effect. For a workload with output to compare, the outputs of these runs must match.
2. Atesor runs 20 rounds, or 40 rounds when 20 rounds cannot detect a 2% change. Each round runs the baseline and the tune in random order.
3. Each run is pinned to one CPU, the highest-numbered CPU that the sandbox may use. Each run also gets a random environment padding, so a lucky stack address cannot favor one build.
4. Atesor compares the time ratio of tune to baseline: the median of the ratios of the rounds, a 95% bootstrap interval, and a Mann-Whitney p-value.
5. A tune is `faster` when the upper bound of the interval is below 0.98 and p is below 0.05. It is `slower` when the lower bound is above 1.02 and p is below 0.05. Else the result is `no change`.
6. Atesor discards a session as `unstable` when the CPU frequency changes or the temperature reaches 75 °C.

One measurement needs about 56 runs. A measurement that the remaining time cannot finish does not start. When the unchanged baseline fails 2 timing runs, Atesor times no more tunes, because the machine or the workload gives wrong results.

### The second check and the acceptance

A faster tune must win again in a second check:

- **C/C++.** Atesor builds the tune again with `-falign-functions=64`. It compares it with a baseline that has the same flag, so a gain from a lucky code layout cannot pass.
- **Rust.** The same change through LLVM: `-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=6` in `RUSTFLAGS`.
- **Go.** A second measurement session.

Atesor checks the faster tunes in order, the best time ratio first. The first tune that passes the second check is the accepted tune. A faster tune after it gets `not checked`. A gain that did not hold, or that got no second check, is `not confirmed`. After a tune is faster, Atesor runs a later tune only when the time limit still covers that tune and the second check.

## What do I get back?

### The console

During the step, each line starts with a key: `Machine`, `Health`, `Package`, `Baseline`, `Workload`, `Tune-<n>`, `Check` or `Result`. Indented lines under a key give the details, for example the lines that start with `why:`, `fix:` and `note:`. This example from `tests/test_optimize.py` shows a port that is not verified:

```text
Result   : NO: performance mode was skipped
           why: the port is not verified, so there is no baseline
```

After the port summary, Atesor prints the answer in one line, then one line for each tune:

```text
   Optimized: <answer>
     Why: <reason>
     Fix: <advice>
     Tune-<n>  <technique>  <value>  <result>  <- accepted
   Optimized files: /workspace/repos/<repo>.opt/accepted (with --package also in the zip under optimized/)
```

`Why:` shows when Atesor accepts no tune. `Fix:` shows when Atesor has advice. The answer is one of these:

| Answer | Status |
|---|---|
| `YES: <tune> (<settings>) is <n>% faster than the verified build` | `accepted` |
| `NO: no tune was clearly faster than the verified build` | `no gain` |
| `NO: no faster tune was confirmed` | `not confirmed` |
| `NO: no tune could be timed` | `not measured` |
| `NOT TIMED: QEMU checks the builds and their output; only native hardware measures speed` | `checked` |
| `NO: performance mode was skipped` | `skipped` |
| `NO: performance mode stopped with an error` | `error` |

For the status `no gain` or `not confirmed`, the answer also names the best timed tune in parentheses, after `best:`.

### Files and records

- **The report.** `<repo>_report_<time>.md` has a `Machine Profile` section and a `Performance Mode (--optimize)` section. The second section gives the answer, the status, the machine, the package, the baseline, the workload and the duration. Its table has the columns `Tune`, `Technique`, `Settings`, `Result`, `Time ratio (95% CI)` and `Details`. Then it lists the warnings, the notes and the source of the harness.
- **The state file.** `<repo>_state_<time>.json` has the fields `optimization` and `machine_profile`.
- **The accepted artifacts.** They are in `<repo>.opt/accepted`, next to the repository tree. On the native target, Atesor removes `<repo>.opt` from the machine when the command ends. With `--package`, Atesor first copies it to the local mirror.
- **The zip.** With `--package`, the zip has the accepted artifacts in `optimized/`. The manifest has schema version 3, with the sections `machine` and `optimization`. A run without `--optimize` writes schema version 2.
- **The recipe cache.** A native result with a workload and the status `accepted` or `no gain` goes into the cache entry of the verified build, under `optimizations`. The key is the core name of the machine, else its ISA label, so results from different boards stay apart. Atesor never makes a new cache entry for a result.
- **The machine profile.** `--probe` writes `machine_profile_native.json` or `machine_profile_qemu.json` to the output directory.
