See [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) for the location of each file.

### Native and QEMU

| | Native | QEMU |
|---|---|---|
| Probe | The board | The `--emulate-cpu` model, else the QEMU `max` CPU |
| Machine check | Yes | No |
| ISA tunes | Yes | Only with a named `--emulate-cpu` model |
| Gates | Yes | Yes, on the emulated CPU |
| Time measurement | Yes | No |
| Accepted tune | Yes | Never |

Emulation speed says nothing about the speed of hardware, so a QEMU run only builds and checks the tunes. Under QEMU, a tune without a workload, or with a workload that has no output to compare, gets `built` after gates 1 and 2.

## What are the limits?

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| The port is not verified | `skipped`: `the port is not verified, so there is no baseline` |
| No tune applies to the machine and the build system | `skipped` |
| The verified build has no repeatable command, or no artifact in the tree | `skipped` |
| The machine probe fails | `error` |
| The verified build does not build again in the copy | `error` |
| The machine check gives wrong data | `not measured`, with `Fix: make the machine stable first (a lower CPU frequency, a memory test), then run again` |
| The time limit is below 300 seconds | `not measured`, before any build |
| No workload passes its checks on native hardware | `not measured`, and Atesor builds no tune |
| The verified build crashes while it runs the workload | A `port problem:` line, because the baseline has no tune flags |
| The time limit ends before a second check | `not confirmed`, with `Fix: run again with a larger ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` |

This example from `tests/test_optimize.py` shows a machine check that failed:

```text
Health   : 3 of 40 zlib round trips gave wrong data (CPU 0: 1, CPU 1: 2)
```

Other limits come from the code:

- Before each tune, Atesor checks the time limit. With less than 300 seconds left, it skips the tune. Each build has a limit of 1800 seconds, or the time that is left when that is shorter (at least 60 seconds).
- A harness may not use calls that make runs differ or reach outside the sandbox. Examples are `system`, `fork`, `socket`, `rand`, `time` and `clock_gettime` in C, `os/exec`, `net` and `time.Now` in Go, and `std::process::Command` and `Instant::now` in Rust. A harness source must be 32,000 bytes or less.
- A program run uses a strict grammar. Each pipe stage starts with `{bin}` or a helper such as `cat`, `gzip`, `head`, `sha256sum` or `wc`. `<` reads only `{input}` or `/dev/null`, and `>` writes only `{output}` or `/dev/null`.
- A program run that takes more than 5 seconds with the smallest input (1 MiB) fails. The command must do less work for each byte.
- Instructions that the machine lacks give only a warning. A tune with such instructions can stop with `SIGILL` in the package tests or in the workload run.
- Atesor never accepts a QEMU result, and never stores one in the recipe cache.

---

# Architecture overview

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/

Eclipse Atesor™ runs each port as a LangGraph state graph in `src/graph.py`. The graph has 13 nodes and 9 routing functions, and 5 nodes can call an LLM. Read this page to know which node runs when, and why a run finishes or escalates.

## What is the state graph?

LangGraph is a Python library that runs a graph of functions over one shared state object. Atesor builds a `StateGraph(AgentState)` in `create_workflow()`. Each node is a Python function that receives the `AgentState`, changes it, and returns it. A routing function reads the state after a node and returns the name of the next node.

The build, verify and fix steps form a separate compiled graph, the subgraph, from `create_build_fix_subgraph()`. The parent graph uses the compiled subgraph as one node, `build_fix_subgraph`.

`main.py` runs the graph with `app.stream(initial_state, config={"recursion_limit": 120})`. The real limit on a run is `max_attempts` (default 5, flag `--max-attempts`) and the cost limit. See [Agent state](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/) for both checks.

## How many nodes and routing functions are there?

These counts come from `create_workflow()` and `create_build_fix_subgraph()` on `main`:

- The parent graph registers 10 nodes. One of them is the compiled subgraph.
- The subgraph registers 3 nodes.
- The total is 13 registered nodes, backed by 12 node functions and 1 compiled subgraph.
- There are 9 routing functions: 6 in the parent graph and 3 in the subgraph.
- The parent graph also has 4 fixed edges: `scout_node` to `supervisor_node`, `build_fix_subgraph` to `supervisor_node`, `optimize_node` to `END`, and `escalate_node` to `END`.
- Two nodes run only with `--optimize`: `cached_recipe_node` and `optimize_node`.

| Node | Graph | Calls an LLM | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `init_node` | parent | No | Clones or updates the repository and runs the scripted analysis. |
| `cached_recipe_node` | parent | No | With `--optimize`, turns a verified recipe cache entry into the build plan. |
| `analyst_node` | parent | Yes, planner role | Reads build files and docs, and writes a `PackageAnalysis`. |
| `heuristic_plan_node` | parent | No | Writes a default `BuildPlan` when it is safe. |
| `scout_node` | parent | Yes, scout role | Writes a custom `BuildPlan` from the evidence. |
| `supervisor_node` | parent | No | Logs a summary. Its routing function picks the next node. |
| `build_fix_subgraph` | parent | Through `fix_node` | Runs the build, verify and fix loop. |
| `finish_node` | parent | Yes, summarizer role | Runs package tests, writes the recipe, and saves learning data. |
| `optimize_node` | parent | Yes, planner and builder roles | Runs performance mode after a finished port. |
| `escalate_node` | parent | No | Writes the escalation report. |
| `build_node` (`builder_node`) | subgraph | No | Runs the plan commands and the recovery heuristics. |
| `verify_node` | subgraph | No | Reads the ELF header of every build output. |
| `fix_node` (`fixer_node`) | subgraph | Yes, fixer role | Proposes one fix strategy and applies it. |

`finish_node` can make two LLM calls: one for the recipe and one for the artifact curator. Both use the summarizer role. `optimize_node` calls a model only when the workload of performance mode comes from the optimizer agent. `cached_recipe_node` runs under the `planner` role label, but it makes no LLM call. The model for each role is on the [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/) page.

## What does the flow look like?

The parent graph:

```text
atesor-ai --repo <url>
  |
  |-- recipe cache hit, without --optimize and without --force
  |     (main.py, before the graph runs)
  |     write <repo>_recipe.md, exit 0 (verified) or 3 (not verified)
  |
  |-- --optimize without --force: main.py puts a verified
  |     cache entry into state.cached_recipe
  v
init_node ............................... no LLM
  |  route_init_to_next
  |-- FAILED or ESCALATED ---------------------------> escalate_node --> END
  |-- cached_recipe is set --> cached_recipe_node ... no LLM
  |                              |  route_cached_recipe_to_next
  |                              |-- build_plan is set --> supervisor_node
  |                              |-- no build_plan ------> analyst_node
  v
analyst_node ............................ LLM (planner role)
  |  route_analyst_to_next
  |-- no package_analysis ---------------------------> escalate_node --> END
  v
heuristic_plan_node ..................... no LLM
  |  route_heuristic_plan_to_next
  |-- no build_plan --> scout_node ...... LLM (scout role)
  |                        |
  v                        v
supervisor_node ......................... no LLM  <------------------+
  |  route_supervisor_to_next                                       |
  |-- SUCCESS -----------------------------> finish_node            |
  |-- ESCALATED, or an escalation check ---> escalate_node --> END  |
  |-- no package_analysis -----------------> analyst_node           |
  |-- FAILED and a new plan is needed -----> scout_node             |
  |-- FAILED, or plan PENDING / BUILDING --> build_fix_subgraph ----+
  |-- all other states --------------------> scout_node

finish_node ............................. LLM (summarizer role)
  |  route_finish_to_next
  |-- optimize_requested (--optimize) -----> optimize_node --> END
  |-- all other states --------------------> END

optimize_node ........................... LLM (planner and builder roles),
                                          only for a workload from the agent
```

The subgraph:

```text
build_fix_subgraph (entry point: build_node)

build_node ........ no LLM
  |  route_build_result
  |-- SUCCESS ------------------------------> verify_node
  |-- ESCALATED, or no attempts remain -----> __end__
  |-- all other states ---------------------> fix_node

verify_node ....... no LLM
  |  route_verify_result
  |-- SUCCESS or ESCALATED -----------------> __end__
  |-- no attempts remain -------------------> __end__
  |-- a fix exists and the error category
  |   is not LINKING, COMPILATION or
  |   ARCHITECTURE -------------------------> __end__
  |-- all other states ---------------------> fix_node

fix_node .......... LLM (fixer role)
  |  route_fix_result
  |-- ESCALATED or FAILED ------------------> __end__
  |-- no attempts remain -------------------> __end__
  |-- all other states ---------------------> build_node

__end__ returns control to supervisor_node in the parent graph.
```

## What does each routing function decide?

**`route_init_to_next`** sends the run to `escalate_node` when `build_status` is `FAILED` or `ESCALATED`. A failed clone sets `FAILED`. When `cached_recipe` is set, the run goes to `cached_recipe_node`. Otherwise the run goes to `analyst_node`.

**`route_cached_recipe_to_next`** sends the run to `supervisor_node` when `cached_recipe_node` wrote a `build_plan`. Otherwise the run goes to `analyst_node` and plans as usual.

**`route_analyst_to_next`** sends the run to `escalate_node` when `package_analysis` is `None`. The analyst always writes an analysis, from the LLM or from its deterministic fallback, so `None` means the node crashed. Otherwise the run goes to `heuristic_plan_node`.

**`route_heuristic_plan_to_next`** sends the run to `supervisor_node` when a `build_plan` exists. Otherwise the run goes to `scout_node`.

**`route_supervisor_to_next`** makes no LLM call. It checks these conditions in this order and returns the first match:

1. `build_status` is `SUCCESS`: go to `finish_node`. This is true also at the attempt or cost limit.
2. `build_status` is `ESCALATED`: go to `escalate_node`.
3. `should_escalate(state)` returns true: go to `escalate_node`.
4. `attempt_count` is `max_attempts` or more: go to `escalate_node`.
5. `attempt_count` is 3 or more and the last 3 errors have one signature: go to `escalate_node`.
6. `package_analysis` is `None`: go to `analyst_node`.
7. `build_status` is `FAILED` and a new plan is needed: go to `scout_node`.
8. `build_status` is `FAILED`: go to `build_fix_subgraph`.
9. A `build_plan` exists and `build_status` is `PENDING` or `BUILDING`: go to `build_fix_subgraph`.
10. In all other states: go to `scout_node`.

A new plan is needed when the last error category is `DEPENDENCY` or `MISSING_TOOLS`. A new plan is also needed one time for each of 6 error signatures, for example `unable to locate package` or `./configure: no such file or directory`. The [recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/) page lists all 6.

**`route_finish_to_next`** sends the run to `optimize_node` when `optimize_requested` is true, which only `--optimize` sets. Otherwise the run ends. `optimize_node` itself skips a port that is not verified, so the report always gives the reason.

**`route_build_result`** sends a `SUCCESS` build to `verify_node`. It ends the subgraph on `ESCALATED` or when `attempt_count` reaches `max_attempts`. Otherwise it sends the run to `fix_node`.

**`route_verify_result`** ends the subgraph on `SUCCESS` or `ESCALATED`, or when no attempts remain. It also ends the subgraph when a fix exists and the last error category is not `LINKING`, `COMPILATION` or `ARCHITECTURE`. Otherwise it sends the run to `fix_node`. `verify_node` sets `FAILED` only for a wrong-architecture verdict, with category `ARCHITECTURE`, so that verdict goes to the fixer while attempts remain.

**`route_fix_result`** ends the subgraph on `ESCALATED` or `FAILED`, or when no attempts remain. Otherwise it sends the run to `build_node` again.

## Which plan does the build use?

`heuristic_plan_node` writes a default plan with no LLM call. It does this only for `cmake`, `make`, `autotools` and `go`, and only when all of these conditions are true:

- The analyst did not set `needs_custom_plan` in an LLM-grounded analysis.
- The architecture scan found no `critical` finding and fewer than 3 `high` findings.
- The build-system confidence is 0.5 or more.

The analyst's build system can replace the detected one. This happens when the analysis is LLM-grounded, the analyst type is not `unknown`, and its confidence is the same or higher. The default plan installs the dependencies that the analyst and the scripted detection found, if each name is in the platform package map. In all other cases the LLM scout writes the plan. If the scout fails, `create_fallback_build_plan()` writes a fixed plan for the detected build system.

With `--optimize` and without `--force`, a verified recipe cache entry replaces the planning steps. `cached_recipe_node` does these steps:

1. It builds the `BuildPlan` from the phases and commands of the cached entry.
2. It writes a `PackageAnalysis` with `llm_grounded=False`. The expected artifacts come from the cached artifact names.
3. It applies the cached patches. A patch that does not apply is only a warning, and the build decides.
4. It logs a note when the current commit is not the commit that the entry verified.

The analyst and the scout make no LLM call in this path. A failed build still goes to the fixer and the normal re-plan loop. When the cached entry has no command, the node clears `cached_recipe` and the run plans as usual.

## How do nodes handle exceptions?

Every node function has the `@agent_node(AgentRole.X)` decorator. The decorator does three things:

1. It sets `state.current_agent` to the role.
2. When the exception text looks like a rate limit, for example `429`, `quota exceeded` or `402`, it runs the node again. A node runs 3 times at most. The wait before a new run is `30 * 2**attempt` seconds plus up to 15 seconds of random jitter.
3. For any other exception, or a third rate-limit failure, it adds an error record, sets `build_status` to `ESCALATED`, and returns the state.

The routing functions then send an `ESCALATED` run to `escalate_node`. The run does not return to the scout or the fixer, because an LLM cannot repair an infrastructure fault.

`optimize_node` is the exception to this rule. It catches every exception itself and writes it to `state.optimization` with the status `error`. A performance mode failure therefore never escalates a finished port, and the rate-limit retry never runs the measurements a second time.

## What happens at the finish?

`supervisor_node` routes every `SUCCESS` to `finish_node`, verified or not. `finish_node` does these steps:

1. It sets `build_status` to `SUCCESS`.
2. It runs the package's own tests one time. The result never changes the build status.
3. It asks the summarizer model for the recipe. If that call fails, it writes a short fallback recipe with the build steps and the verification verdict.
4. It ranks the build outputs with the artifact curator.
5. If the build is verified, it saves few-shot examples and a recipe cache entry. If the build is not verified, it saves nothing.

With `--optimize`, `route_finish_to_next` then sends the run to `optimize_node`. See [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/).

`main.py` then writes the outputs and exits with 0 for a verified port, or 3 when no riscv64 output is proven. With `--package`, a packaging failure gives exit code 2. Performance mode never changes the exit code. See [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/) for the verdicts.

## What happens at an escalation?

`escalate_node` makes no LLM call. It sets `build_status` to `ESCALATED` and writes an escalation report into `context_cache["escalation_report"]`. The report has these parts:

- A summary: repository, status, attempts, cost and duration.
- The last error, with its category and severity.
- The last 5 fix attempts.
- Up to 5 `high` or `critical` architecture findings.
- A recommendation from `should_escalate()`.
- The last 5 error records.

`main.py` then prints the last error and the last 10 audit events, and exits with 1. See [Exit codes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/exit-codes/).

## Related pages

- [Agent state](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/)
- [Scripted operations](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/scripted-ops/)
- [Recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/)
- [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/)
- [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/)
- [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/)

# Agent state

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/

Eclipse Atesor™ keeps everything about one port in a single `AgentState` dataclass, defined in `src/state.py`. Every node reads it and writes it, and every routing decision comes from its fields. Read this page before you change a node, a routing function or an error pattern.

## Why is the state the contract between nodes?

The graph in `src/graph.py` is a `StateGraph(AgentState)`. All nodes receive the same `AgentState` object, change it in place, and return it. No node calls another node. A node tells the next node what happened through state fields.

The routing functions read only state fields, for example `build_status`, `last_error_category` and `attempt_count`. The final report, the exit code, the zip manifest and the learning gate also read the state. At the end of a run, `main.py` writes the full state to `<repo>_state_<timestamp>.json`.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` states the rule: `AgentState` is the single source of truth. Mutate it in place inside every node, and never construct a fresh one. In a run, `create_initial_state(repo_url, max_attempts, optimize, emulate_cpu, cached_recipe)` makes the only instance. It rejects a URL that is not a plain `http(s)` URL, derives `repo_name`, and sets `repo_path` to `/workspace/repos/<repo_name>`. The last 3 arguments come from the performance mode flags and default to off.

## What are the main field groups?

The source groups the fields with comments. This table shows the important fields in each group.

| Group | Important fields | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| Repository | `repo_url`, `repo_name`, `repo_path`, `repo_tree` | `create_initial_state`, `init_node` |
| Task planning | `package_analysis`, `task_plan`, `current_phase` | `analyst_node`, `cached_recipe_node`, all nodes |
| Build | `build_system_info`, `build_plan`, `build_status` | `init_node`, planners, all nodes |
| Dependencies | `dependencies` | `init_node` |
| Architecture | `arch_specific_code` | `init_node` |
| Execution tracking | `attempt_count`, `max_attempts`, `last_successful_phase` | `add_error()`, `builder_node`, `fixer_node` |
| Error handling | `last_error`, `last_error_category`, `last_error_severity`, `error_history`, `fixes_attempted` | `add_error()`, `fixer_node` |
| Cost tracking | `api_calls_made`, `api_cost_usd`, `api_tokens_in`, `api_tokens_out`, `scripted_ops_count`, `execution_start_time` | `log_api_call()`, `log_scripted_op()` |
| Caches | `context_cache`, `file_content_cache`, `command_results_cache` | all nodes |
| Heuristic plan facts | `scout_build_system_result`, `scout_deps_result`, `scout_arch_issues_result` | `heuristic_plan_node` |
| Outputs | `patches_generated`, `porting_recipe`, `build_artifacts`, `curated_artifacts`, `artifact_verification`, `package_tests` | `fixer_node`, `cached_recipe_node`, `verify_node`, `finish_node` |
| Performance mode | `optimize_requested`, `emulate_cpu`, `cached_recipe`, `machine_profile`, `optimization` | `create_initial_state`, `cached_recipe_node`, `optimize_node` |
| Audit | `audit_trail`, `current_agent`, `messages` | `log_event()`, `@agent_node`, `main.py` |

Some fields need a short note:

- `task_plan` is a fixed structural record from `create_default_plan()`. No LLM writes it, and no routing function reads its content.
- `build_status` takes one of 8 `BuildStatus` values: `PENDING`, `PLANNING`, `SCOUTING`, `BUILDING`, `FIXING`, `SUCCESS`, `FAILED` and `ESCALATED`.
- `last_successful_phase` lets the builder resume at the phase that failed.
- `command_results_cache` keys each command by its MD5 hash. The builder skips a command that already has a cached success.
- `artifact_verification` holds the last scan verdict: `verified`, `wrong_arch` or `unverified`. It is `None` until `verify_node` runs.
- `package_tests` holds the non-gating test result. It is `None` until `finish_node` runs. Performance mode runs the same test command again in each tune tree.
- `optimize_requested` is true only with `--optimize`. `route_finish_to_next` reads it.
- `emulate_cpu` holds the QEMU CPU model for performance mode on the QEMU target, or `None`.
- `cached_recipe` holds a verified recipe cache entry. `main.py` sets it only with `--optimize` and without `--force`. `route_init_to_next` reads it, and `cached_recipe_node` sets it to `None` when the entry has no command.
- `machine_profile` and `optimization` are `None` until `optimize_node` runs. The `status` of `optimization` is `accepted`, `no gain`, `not confirmed`, `not measured`, `checked`, `skipped` or `error`. See [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/).
- `tests_run` and `subgraph_outcome` are declared, but no code on `main` sets them.

The state also uses these dataclasses: `CommandResult`, `ErrorRecord`, `FixAttempt`, `ArchSpecificCode`, `BuildPhase`, `BuildPlan`, `DependencyInfo`, `TaskPhase`, `TaskPlan`, `BuildSystemInfo` and `PackageAnalysis`. The [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/) page describes `PackageAnalysis`.

## How does the state count attempts?

`add_error(error)` is the only place that increments `attempt_count`. It also appends the record to `error_history` and copies its message, category and severity into the `last_error*` fields. So an attempt is one recorded error, not one fix.

These events record an error and use one attempt:

- A build command that fails after all recovery heuristics.
- A wrong-architecture verdict from `verify_node`.
- A scout failure that uses the fallback plan.
- A fixer response that is not valid.
- A clone that fails in `init_node`.
- An exception that `@agent_node` catches.

`max_attempts` is 5 by default. The `--max-attempts` (`-m`) flag changes it.

## What is the error taxonomy?

`ErrorCategory` has 14 values. `classify_error(message)` assigns one category from the lower-case error text. It checks pattern groups in a fixed order, and the first match wins.

| Order | Category | Example patterns |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `RATE_LIMIT` | `rate limit`, `too many requests`, `429`, `quota exceeded` |
| 2 | `DEPENDENCY` | package manager lock messages, for example `unable to lock database` |
| 3 | `DISK_SPACE` | `no space left`, `virtual memory exhausted`, `exit 137` |
| 4 | `NETWORK` | exit status 124, `timed out` |
| 5 | `CONFIGURATION` | `repository '...' not found` |
| 6 | `NETWORK` | `could not read username`, `authentication failed`, `connection`, `unreachable` |
| 7 | `CONFIGURATION` | a stale `config.guess` or `config.sub` that does not know `riscv64` |
| 8 | `ARCHITECTURE` | `immintrin.h`, `cpuid.h`, `unsupported architecture`, `-march=native`, `invalid instruction mnemonic`, `sse`, `avx`, `neon` |
| 9 | `LINKING` | `relocation truncated to fit`, `r_riscv_hi20`, `__atomic_load_`, `undefined reference`, `cannot find -l` |
| 10 | `DEPENDENCY` | `cmake error` with `could not find <name>` |
| 11 | `DEPENDENCY` | `no package '<name>' found`, `unable to locate package`, `has no installation candidate` |
| 12 | `MISSING_TOOLS` | `command not found`, `cmake: not found` |
| 13 | `CONFIGURATION` | `possibly undefined macro`, `autoreconf: error` |
| 14 | `CONFIGURATION` | `configure` with `syntax error` |
| 15 | `COMPILATION` | Rust `error[E0000]` codes, `could not compile`, `undeclared`, `implicit declaration` |
| 16 | `CONFIGURATION` | `configure: error`, `no rule to make target`, `no required module provides`, `inconsistent vendoring` |
| 17 | `DEPENDENCY` | `cannot find`, `not found`, `no such file`, `module not found` |
| 18 | `PERMISSION` | `permission denied`, `access denied`, `forbidden` |
| 19 | `DISK_SPACE` | a line that is only `killed` |
| 20 | `CONFIGURATION` | Python exception names, for example `keyerror` |
| 21 | `CONFIGURATION` | `empty repository` |
| 22 | `MISSING_TOOLS` | `go.mod requires go >=`, `requires rust version` |
| 23 | `UNKNOWN` | no match |

The other 3 categories are `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE` and `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE`. No code path on `main` sets them. They exist for the severity and escalation checks.

:::note
The builder reports a failed command as `Build command failed: <command> (exit <code>) - <output>`. An OOM kill (out-of-memory kill) therefore contains `exit 137`, which matches `DISK_SPACE`. `DISK_SPACE` is a fundamental blocker, so the supervisor escalates the run the next time it routes. The builder tries a serialized retry before it records that error. See [Recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/).
:::

## How does Atesor infer severity?

`FailureSeverity` has 3 values: `low`, `medium` and `high`. `create_error_record()` calls `infer_failure_severity(category, command, message)` when the caller gives no severity. The function checks these rules in this order:

1. The command starts with `which `: `low`.
2. The category is `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE`, `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE`, `PERMISSION` or `DISK_SPACE`: `high`.
3. The command contains `git clone`, `git pull`, `apt-get update`, `apt update`, `apk update` or `apk add`: `high`.
4. The category is `CONFIGURATION`, `DEPENDENCY`, `COMPILATION`, `LINKING`, `NETWORK`, `RATE_LIMIT`, `MISSING_TOOLS` or `ARCHITECTURE`: `medium`.
5. The message contains `not found` and `which `: `low`.
6. All other errors: `medium`.

`init_node` sets `high` explicitly for a failed clone. The routing functions read the category, not the severity. Atesor writes the severity to the error record, the escalation report and the final terminal output.

## When does a run escalate?

`should_escalate(state)` returns `(True, reason)` for the first check that matches:

1. `attempt_count` is `max_attempts` or more: `Maximum attempts (N) reached`.
2. The run is in an error loop: `Stuck in error loop with no progress`.
3. `last_error_category` is `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE`, `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE`, `PERMISSION` or `DISK_SPACE`: `Fundamental blocker: <category>`.
4. `api_cost_usd` is more than 1.0: `API cost limit ($1.0) exceeded`.

`route_supervisor_to_next` calls `should_escalate()` after it checks for `SUCCESS` and `ESCALATED`. A `SUCCESS` therefore always goes to `finish_node`, also at the attempt or cost limit. The subgraph routing functions also stop at `max_attempts`. The [overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/) shows the full order of checks.

The LLM calls of the optimizer agent also add to `api_cost_usd`. They run in `optimize_node`, after `finish_node`, so no escalation check follows them.

`is_in_error_loop()` compares the last 3 records in `error_history`. Each record gets a signature: its category plus one normalized error line. The function picks the first line that contains a marker such as `error`, `fatal` or `undefined reference`. When no line has a marker, it picks the first line. It then replaces paths with `<path>`, line and column numbers with `:<n>`, hex values with `<hex>`, and other numbers with `<n>`. The run is in a loop when the 3 signatures are the same.

## Which helper methods change the state?

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_error(error)` | Appends to `error_history`, keeps the last 200, sets the `last_error*` fields, adds 1 to `attempt_count`. |
| `add_fix_attempt(fix)` | Appends a `FixAttempt`. The builder later marks it as a success. |
| `log_api_call(cost, tokens_in, tokens_out, calls)` | Adds calls, cost and tokens. |
| `log_scripted_op(operation)` | Adds 1 to `scripted_ops_count` and writes an audit event. |
| `log_event(type, data)` | Appends to `audit_trail` and keeps the last 2000 events. |
| `cache_command_result()`, `get_cached_command_result()`, `forget_command_result()` | Manage `command_results_cache`. |
| `add_build_artifact(filepath, type, architecture)` | Appends to `build_artifacts`. |
| `is_verified_success` | True only for `SUCCESS` with the verdict `verified`. |
| `to_dict()`, `save_to_json(path)` | Serialize the state. Enums become their values. |

The caps of 200 errors and 2000 audit events keep a long escalated run from growing the state JSON without limit.

`state.py` also has `get_next_action_recommendation(state)`. `tests/test_state.py` uses it, but the graph routing does not call it.

---

# Scripted operations

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/scripted-ops/

Eclipse Atesor™ does all repository inspection with deterministic Python code before any LLM sees the package. This layer lives in `src/scripted_ops.py` and `src/evidence.py`. It costs no LLM tokens, and it gives the same result for the same repository every time.

## Why does this layer exist?

Every LLM call costs tokens, money and time, and the result can change from one call to the next. Many facts about a repository need no reasoning. File names show the build system, `go.mod` lists the Go modules, and a regular expression finds `#include <immintrin.h>`. The scripted layer collects these facts with no LLM cost.

The facts have three uses:

- `heuristic_plan_node` writes a default build plan from them. For a recognized build system, the run then needs no scout LLM call.
- The analyst, scout and fixer prompts include them, so the model reads real evidence and does not guess file names.
- The deterministic fallbacks use them when an LLM call fails. The analyst fallback and the fallback build plan come from scripted detection.

`init_node` runs this layer through `ScriptedOperations.clone_or_update_repository()` and `quick_analysis()`. It records these operations as `scripted_op` events in the audit trail.

## How does Atesor clone and update a repository?

`clone_or_update_repository(url, name)` works inside the sandbox, so file ownership stays correct. It first rejects a name outside `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`, a name that starts with a dot, and a URL that is not `http://` or `https://`. Then it does these steps:

1. **Sandbox health check.** It runs `git --version` and installs `git` if it is missing. On Debian and Ubuntu it runs `apt-get update`. If that fails with a `Release file` error, it deletes files in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d` that changed in the last 1440 minutes, then runs `apt-get update` again.
2. **Existing clone.** If the clone exists, it compares the `origin` URL with the requested URL after normalization. A different URL gets a fresh clone.
3. **Reset.** For a matching clone, it runs `git fetch --depth 1 origin && git reset --hard FETCH_HEAD && git clean -fdx`. This removes any file that an earlier run changed. If the reset fails, it makes a fresh clone.
4. **Fresh clone.** It removes the directory and runs `git clone --depth 1`. After an authentication error, it tries again without the token. If the clone still fails, it tries URL variants.
5. **Safe directory.** It runs `git config --global --add safe.directory <path>` for the clone.
6. **Submodules.** If the repository has a `.gitmodules` file, it runs `git submodule update --init --recursive` with a 300 second limit. A failure is only a warning.

The URL variants are, in this order: `/cgit/` changed to `/git/`, the URL with `.git` added, and 4 homepage rules. The homepage rules map `gnu.org/software/<name>` and two GNU Savannah URL forms to `git.savannah.gnu.org/git/<name>.git`, and `dev.yorhel.nl` to `code.blicky.net/yorhel/<name>.git`.

Every git command gets a fail-fast environment: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, `GIT_ASKPASS=/bin/echo`, and an SSH command with `BatchMode=yes`. A GitHub token is optional. When `GIT_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` is set and the URL starts with `https://github.com/`, Atesor adds a bearer header. It sends the header through `GIT_CONFIG_*` environment variables, only for the git commands of that clone or update. It never writes the token to the git configuration in the sandbox.

## Which build systems does Atesor detect?

`detect_build_system(repo_path)` returns a `BuildSystemInfo` with a type, a confidence from 0 to 1, the primary file and a `module_dir`. It detects 11 build systems from files at the repository root:

| Type | Marker files |
|---|---|
| `cmake` | `CMakeLists.txt` |
| `autotools` | `configure.ac`, `configure.in`, `configure` |
| `make` | `Makefile`, `GNUmakefile` |
| `meson` | `meson.build` |
| `cargo` | `Cargo.toml` |
| `npm` | `package.json`, only with `package-lock.json` or a `build` script |
| `pip` | `setup.py`, `pyproject.toml` |
| `go` | `go.mod` |
| `gradle` | `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts` |
| `maven` | `pom.xml` |
| `bazel` | `BUILD`, `BUILD.bazel`, `WORKSPACE` |

The confidence rules are these:

- `CMakeLists.txt`, `Cargo.toml`, `configure.ac` and `go.mod` give 0.95.
- `configure` gives 0.85.
- Each other marker adds 0.3, up to 0.9.
- When both `go` and `npm` match, `npm` gets a lower confidence than `go`.
- The type with the highest confidence wins.

When no marker is at the root, the detector tries these fallbacks in order:

1. A `go.mod` in a subdirectory gives `go` at 0.90. The detector skips vendored and test directories. The detector prefers a directory with `main.go`, a `cmd/` directory or a `package main` file. Else a `Cargo.toml` in a subdirectory gives `cargo` at 0.90.
2. A nested build file, in a directory up to 2 levels below the root, gives 0.75. The detector searches for `CMakeLists.txt`, `meson.build`, `configure.ac`, `configure.in`, `Makefile` and `GNUmakefile`. The shallowest file wins.
3. `.go` files with no `go.mod` (a GOPATH-style project) give `go` at 0.65.
4. If nothing matches, the type is `unknown` with confidence 0.0.

When the primary file is in a subdirectory, `module_dir` holds that directory. The scout prompt shows it. The [build systems reference](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/build-systems/) lists what each build system gets after detection.

For Go, `find_go_main_package()` also finds the main package. It prefers `cmd/<repo name>`, then other `cmd/` directories, then the root. It gives 0 points to directories such as `gen`, `examples`, `test`, `internal`, `tools` and `vendor`. It returns a `build_command` such as `go build ./cmd/<name>`, and it sets `needs_go_init` for a project with no `go.mod`.

## How does Atesor extract dependencies?

`extract_dependencies()` reads the package files of the detected build system. It returns a `DependencyInfo` with `system_packages`, `libraries` and `build_tools`.

| Build system | Source | What it extracts |
|---|---|---|
| `cmake` | `CMakeLists.txt` in `module_dir` | `find_package()` names, plus `pkg_check_modules()` and `pkg_search_module()` modules. 8 CMake names map to distro packages, for example `OpenSSL` to `openssl` and `ZLIB` to `zlib`. |
| `make` | root `Makefile` | `-l<name>` flags. `ssl` and `crypto` map to `openssl`, `z` to `zlib`, and `pthread`, `dl` and `m` to `musl-dev`. |
| `go` | `go.mod` | Module paths from single-line and block `require` statements. |
| `cargo` | `Cargo.toml` | The keys of `[dependencies]`. |
| `pip` | `requirements.txt` | Package names before the version operator. |
| `npm` | `package.json` | `dependencies` and `devDependencies` keys. |

For `cmake` and `make`, the active platform profile resolves each mapped name to the distro package name. There is no extractor for `autotools`, `meson`, `gradle`, `maven` or `bazel`. For those, the analyst LLM is the only source of dependencies.

## What does the architecture scan find?

`find_architecture_specific_code()` walks the repository and returns `ArchSpecificCode` findings. It skips vendored, test, example and documentation directories. It keeps at most 40 findings, and at most 8 in each category. Each finding has a file, a line, a code snippet, a severity and a suggested fix.

| Category | Severity | What matches |
|---|---|---|
| `intrinsic_header` | high | `#include` of an x86 or ARM intrinsic header, for example `immintrin.h`, `cpuid.h` or `arm_neon.h` |
| `inline_asm` | high | `__asm__`, `__asm` or `asm volatile` in a source file |
| `hardcoded_arch_flags` | high | x86 or ARM flags in a build file, for example `-msse4.2`, `-mavx2`, `-m64` or `-march=native` |
| `stale_autotools` | high | A `config.guess` or `config.sub` with a timestamp before 2018-02-22 |
| `arch_dispatch` | high or medium | x86 or ARM macros such as `__x86_64__`, in a file with no `__riscv` or with an `#else` that leads to an `#error`. The `#error` case is `high`. |
| `assembly_source` | medium | A `.S`, `.s` or `.asm` file |
| `go_build_constraints` | medium | A `//go:build` or `// +build` line that holds for linux/amd64 or linux/arm64 but not for linux/riscv64 |
| `go_arch_files` | medium | A directory with `_amd64.go` or `_arm64.go` files and no Go file that builds for linux/riscv64 |

For Go, the scan evaluates the build constraint expressions and the file-name suffix rules. A file such as `x_amd64.go` builds only for amd64. A line such as `//go:build !amd64` is a riscv64 fallback, so it is not a finding.

The findings have these uses. `heuristic_plan_node` sends the run to the LLM scout when there is a `critical` finding or 3 or more `high` findings. The scout prompt lists up to 10 findings. The fixer prompt and the escalation report list up to 5 `high` or `critical` findings.

`detect_arch_specific_build_files()` is a second, smaller check. It searches the content of `*.mak` and `*.mk` files for per-architecture names, such as `makefile.x86_64` or `build_arm64`. It reports whether a RISC-V variant already exists.

## What does Atesor probe in the sandbox?

`get_system_info(tools)` runs `which <tool>` inside the sandbox for each tool and `uname -m` for the architecture. Each tool is `Available in PATH` or `Not installed`.

- `init_node` probes `gcc`, `make`, the detected build-system type and the build tools from the dependencies. It stores the result in `context_cache["system_info"]` and the missing tools in `context_cache["missing_tools"]`.
- `scout_node` probes the default list and puts it in its prompt. The default list is `gcc`, `g++`, `cmake`, `make`, `ninja`, `meson`, `automake`, `autoconf`, `python3`, `go`, `rustc` and `cargo`.

`quick_analysis()` also collects the commit and branch, a compact repository tree, and up to 10 documentation files. `init_node` reads the first 5 documentation files, up to 500 lines each, into `file_content_cache`.

On the native target, the build tree is on the remote machine. The scripted layer refreshes a local mirror of that repository and reads the mirror. See [Native RISC-V](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## What is in an evidence bundle?

`src/evidence.py` puts real file content into prompts. It has two functions, and both have size limits.

`collect_build_evidence(repo_path)` builds the evidence for the analyst and the scout:

1. A listing of the top-level entries, up to 60.
2. Excerpts of the build files that exist, in this order: `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `configure.ac`, `configure.in`, `meson.build`, `Makefile.am`, `Makefile`, `makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `package.json`. Each excerpt has at most 2500 characters.
3. One documentation excerpt of at most 2000 characters, from the first file found: `README.md`, `README.rst`, `README`, `README.txt`, `INSTALL`, `INSTALL.md`, `BUILDING.md`, `BUILD.md` or `docs/BUILD.md`.

The total bundle has at most 14000 characters.

`error_context_excerpts(error_text, repo_path)` builds the evidence for the fixer. It finds `file:line` references in the error text, for files with source or build extensions such as `.c`, `.go`, `.rs`, `.m4` or `.cmake`. For up to 3 files inside the repository, it shows 12 lines before and after the referenced line, with line numbers. It ignores absolute paths and paths with `..`.

## Related pages

- [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/)
- [Recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/)
- [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/)
- [Build systems](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/build-systems/)

# Recovery heuristics

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/

Eclipse Atesor™ repairs many common build failures with fixed rules before it asks the LLM fixer. The builder in `src/graph.py` applies 23 of these LLM-free heuristics: 7 rewrites before a command runs and 16 retries after a command fails. They cost no tokens, and they work when the LLM provider is rate-limited.

## How does the builder use the heuristics?

`builder_node()` runs the phases of the build plan in order. It skips each phase up to `last_successful_phase`, and each command that has a cached success. For each other command, it does these steps:

1. It applies the rewrites 1 to 7 to the command.
2. It runs the rewritten command in the sandbox.
3. If the command fails, it checks the retries 8 to 23 in table order. Each check reads the result of the last retry.
4. When a retry succeeds, the builder goes to the next command.
5. When no retry succeeds, the builder classifies the error, records it, and sets `build_status` to `FAILED`. While attempts remain, the subgraph then sends the run to the LLM fixer.

The count of 23 comes from `builder_node()` on `main`. Other LLM-free recovery steps outside the builder are in the last section.

The Limit column uses these terms:

- **Each run**: the rule applies every time the command runs.
- **Each attempt**: the rule has no memory. It can fire again on each build attempt while its condition is true.
- **Once per command**: `_builder_retry_allowed()` stores a key in `context_cache["builder_retry_keys"]`. The rule fires one time for that key in the whole run.

## Which rewrites run before a command?

These rewrites change the command that runs. They do not change the command in the build plan.

| # | Heuristic | Trigger | Action | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Go VCS flag | `go build` or `go install` without `-buildvcs=false` | Adds `-buildvcs=false` | Each run |
| 2 | Go flag cleanup | `-buildvcs=false` in a Go command that is not `go build` or `go install` | Removes the flag | Each run |
| 3 | gettext rewrite | `autoreconf` in the command, and `m4/gettext.m4` in the repository | Replaces the command with the gettext sequence | Each run |
| 4 | Autotools bootstrap | `./configure` in the command, and no `configure` file at the root | Prepends a bootstrap command (see below) | Each run |
| 5 | Make root redirect | The command starts with `make`, has no ` -C` or ` -f`, and the root has no makefile | Prepends `cd <dir> &&` for the shallowest directory with a makefile | Each run, 2 levels below the root at most |
| 6 | `top_builddir` fix | The command starts with `make`, or a configure phase ends | Adds `top_builddir = <relative path>` to subdirectory Makefiles that use `$(top_builddir)` and do not define it | Each run, 30 second limit |
| 7 | npm script guard | `npm run <script>`, and `package.json` does not declare `<script>` | Runs the first declared script of `build`, `prod`, `compile`, `dist`, or skips the command | Each run |

The gettext sequence is this command:

```bash
cp /usr/share/gettext/m4/*.m4 m4/ 2>/dev/null || true && aclocal -I m4 -I /usr/share/aclocal && autoconf
```

`autoreconf` runs `autopoint`, and `autopoint` reverts a fix to `gettext.m4`. The gettext sequence copies the system macros first and does not run `autopoint`.

The autotools bootstrap (rule 4) picks the first match in this list:

1. `sh autogen.sh`, `sh buildconf`, `sh buildconf.sh` or `sh bootstrap`, for the first script that exists.
2. The gettext sequence, when `configure.ac` or `configure.in` exists and `m4/gettext.m4` exists.
3. `autoreconf -fi`, when `configure.ac` or `configure.in` exists.

If none matches, the command does not change.

The make root redirect (rule 5) skips `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `testdata`, `test`, `tests`, `examples`, `example`, `third_party`, `contrib` and `__pycache__`. When two directories have the same depth, the first in alphabetical order wins.

The `top_builddir` fix (rule 6) handles old gettext `po/Makefile.in.in` templates. A failure of the fix is only a warning. A lost sandbox connection escalates the run.

## Which retries run after a command fails?

| # | Heuristic | Trigger (in the error output) | Action | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | Go VCS retry | A Go build fails with `dubious ownership`, `error obtaining VCS status` or `Use -buildvcs=false` | Retries with `-buildvcs=false` | Each attempt, only without the flag |
| 9 | Go output collision | A Go build fails with `already exists and is a directory` and `build output` | Retries with `-o ./.atesor-bin/<name>` | Each attempt |
| 10 | Go vendoring | A Go build fails with `inconsistent vendoring` | Retries with `-mod=mod` | Each attempt, only without the flag |
| 11 | Go module tidy | A Go build fails with `no required module provides` | Runs `go mod tidy` in the same directory, then retries | Each attempt |
| 12 | autopoint failure | An `autoreconf` command fails with `autopoint` and `no such file` | Runs the gettext sequence | Each attempt |
| 13 | Missing header | `fatal error: <name>.h` or `'<name>.h' file not found` | Installs the matching distro package, then retries | Once per command and package set |
| 14 | CMake with bare make | `no targets specified and no makefile found`, and `CMakeLists.txt` in the command directory | Retries with `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build -j1` | Once per command |
| 15 | go.mod in a subdirectory | `go.mod file not found`, and no `go.mod` at the root | Retries with `cd <dir> &&` for the first subdirectory with a `go.mod` | Once per command |
| 16 | CMake compiler cache | A `cmake` command fails with `not a full path to an existing compiler tool` | Removes `build/` and adds explicit compiler paths, or prefixes `CC` and `CXX` | Once per command |
| 17 | Missing Python module | `No module named '<name>'` | Runs `pip install <names>`, then retries | Once per command and module set |
| 18 | Suspected OOM | Exit code 137, or a parallel build that fails with no output | Retries the command single-threaded | Once per command |
| 19 | Go submodules | `no required module provides package`, and a `.gitmodules` file | Runs `git submodule update --init --recursive`, then retries | Once per command |
| 20 | Missing git | `command not found`, and `git` in the command | Installs `git`, then retries | Once per command |
| 21 | Old Go toolchain | A toolchain version error with `go.mod requires go <version>` | Installs that Go version from go.dev, then retries | Once per command |
| 22 | RISC-V relocation | `relocation truncated` and `R_RISCV` | Retries with `CFLAGS='-mcmodel=medany' CXXFLAGS='-mcmodel=medany'` | Once per command |
| 23 | Package not found | `unable to locate package`, `unable to select packages`, `no such package` or `has no installation candidate` | Installs each package alone and keeps the ones that install | Once per command |

When a retry succeeds, some heuristics also put the working command into the build plan. The recipe then shows that command. These are rules 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18 and 22, and rule 23 when some packages did not install. The other retries leave the plan command as it is.

### Notes on the retries

**Missing header (13).** The builder maps the header name to a canonical library name, for example `png.h` to `libpng` and `ft2build.h` to `freetype`. It also tries the bare name and `lib<name>`. It installs a package only when the name is in the package map of the active platform profile. It never guesses a package for an unknown or project-local header.

**CMake compiler cache (16).** This failure happens when CMake cached a compiler path that does not exist in the riscv64 image. When the command creates `build/` and the directory exists, the builder removes it in the sandbox. It then adds `-DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/usr/bin/gcc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/usr/bin/g++` to the `cmake` call. Otherwise it prefixes `CC=/usr/bin/gcc CXX=/usr/bin/g++`.

**Missing Python module (17).** Most modules install under their top-level name. A short map handles the exceptions, for example `yaml` to `pyyaml`, `serial` to `pyserial` and `google` to `protobuf`.

**Suspected OOM (18).** OOM means out of memory. Under QEMU emulation, parallel builds and downloads sometimes stop with exit code 137 when no emulated memory remains. The builder treats exit code 137 as OOM for every command. For a parallel command, it also treats a failure with no output as OOM. The parallel commands are `go build`, `go install`, `go test`, `make`, `ninja`, `cargo build`, `cargo install`, `cargo test`, `cargo fetch`, `cargo update`, `pip install`, `npm install`, `npm ci` and `npm run`. The serialized form depends on the tool:

| Tool | Serialized form |
|---|---|
| Go | Adds `-p 1` and `env GOMAXPROCS=1` |
| make | Changes `-j$(nproc)`, `-j<N>` and `--jobs` to `-j1`, and adds `env MAKEFLAGS=-j1` |
| ninja | Adds `-j1` when the command has no `-j` |
| cargo | Adds `-j 1` to `build`, `install` and `test`, and adds `env CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1` |
| pip | Adds `env MAKEFLAGS=-j1` |
| npm | Adds `--jobs 1` |

The builder keeps a leading `cd <dir> &&` in place. If the serialized form is the same as the original command, the builder does not retry.

**Old Go toolchain (21).** The builder reads the version from the error, and changes a short version such as `1.25` to `1.25.0`. It then runs one command in the sandbox:

1. It downloads `https://go.dev/dl/go<version>.linux-riscv64.tar.gz`.
2. It checks the archive against the SHA-256 from `https://dl.google.com/go/<archive>.sha256`.
3. It unpacks the archive into `/usr/local/.go-staging` and runs the staged `go version`.
4. It moves the new toolchain to `/usr/local/go`. If that move fails, it restores the old toolchain.

The version must match a plain Go version pattern, because the builder puts it in a shell command. Atesor builds this command itself, so it runs outside the LLM command whitelist.

**Package not found (23).** The builder reads the package list from an `apk add` or `apt-get install -y` command. It installs each package with its own command. If at least one package installs, the phase continues. If some packages failed, the plan command changes to install only the good ones. If no package installs, the builder records the failure.

## What other recovery is LLM-free?

These steps are outside `builder_node()`, so they are not in the count of 23:

- **Clone recovery.** A failed clone retries without the GitHub token after an authentication error, then tries URL variants. See [Scripted operations](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/scripted-ops/).
- **Sandbox health check.** Before a clone, Atesor installs a missing `git`. On Debian and Ubuntu it also removes recent apt source files that break `apt-get update`.
- **Forced re-scout.** `route_supervisor_to_next` sends the run to the scout again for a new plan, one time per run for each of 6 error signatures: `no required module provides`, `already exists and is a directory`, `does not appear to contain cmakelists.txt`, `unable to locate package`, `inconsistent vendoring` and `./configure: no such file or directory`.
- **Fix command rewrite.** The fixer replaces an `autoreconf` command with a gettext sequence when `m4/gettext.m4` exists.
- **Rewind after a fix.** After the fixer changes the tree, `_rewind_after_verify_failure()` makes sure the builder compiles again. When every phase already passed, it rewinds to the first phase with a build step, or to the last phase when no phase has one. It forgets the cached results from there. Earlier phases such as `go mod init` do not run again.
- **Deterministic fallbacks.** The analyst, the scout, the summarizer and the artifact curator each have a fallback for a failed LLM call. See [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/).
- **Rate-limit retry.** `@agent_node` runs a node again after a rate-limit exception, 3 runs at most. See [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/).

To add a heuristic, see [Add a heuristic](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-heuristic/).

---

# Verification

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/

Eclipse Atesor™ does not accept a port because its build commands passed. It reads the ELF header of every build output and accepts the port only when the outputs are real riscv64 machine code. This page describes that check, the artifact ranking, the "not verified" result and the package tests.

## Why is a passed build not enough?

A build can pass and still prove nothing. A header-only library or a script package produces no binary. A build can also produce an x86-64, aarch64 or riscv32 output next to riscv64 ones. Atesor checks the output files themselves, so these cases do not count as a port.

`verify_node` runs after every successful `build_node` in the build-fix subgraph. The scan sets `artifact_verification` in the [agent state](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/). The report, the exit code, the zip manifest and the learning gate read that field.

## What does the artifact scanner read?

ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the file format of Linux executables, shared libraries, objects and core dumps. Its header holds the architecture of the code.

`ArtifactScanner.scan()` in `src/artifact_scanner.py` runs one Python program inside the sandbox with `python3 -c`. Every sandbox image has `python3`. The program walks the repository and prints one JSON document, and the host computes the verdict from it. The scan has a 900 second limit and reads at most 20000 candidate files.

The program skips `.git` and `node_modules`. A file is a candidate when all of these conditions are true:

- It is a regular file, not a symbolic link.
- It is 52 bytes or larger.
- It has an execute bit, or its name ends in `.a` or `.so`, or contains `.so.`.

For each candidate, the program reads the ELF header fields `EI_CLASS`, `EI_DATA`, `e_type`, `e_machine` and `e_flags`. Atesor does not parse the text output of `file(1)`.

A file is riscv64 when `e_machine` is 243 (`EM_RISCV`), `EI_CLASS` is 64-bit, and the data is little-endian. A 32-bit RISC-V file is `riscv32`, and a riscv32 output is not a riscv64 port. The scanner names other machines from their `e_machine` value, for example `x86-64`, `aarch64`, `arm`, `ppc64` or `s390x`.

## How does Atesor check static archives?

A static library (`.a` file) is an archive of object files. The program reads the archive member headers and the ELF header of every member. It skips the symbol index members.

- An archive is riscv64 only when every ELF member is riscv64.
- An archive with members of more than one architecture gets the label `mixed(<a>+<b>)`, and it counts as a foreign output.
- A thin archive holds no member data, so it is not evidence.
- The verdict ignores core dumps (`e_type` 4).

## Which outputs are prebuilt?

The program asks git which files are committed, with `git ls-files`, also in submodules. It also asks which committed files the build modified, with `git ls-files -m`. A file that is committed and not modified is prebuilt, for example a vendored blob or a test fixture.

Prebuilt files never decide the verdict. A committed riscv64 binary does not prove the port. A committed x86-64 binary does not fail it. The verdict lists committed foreign binaries in `prebuilt_foreign`, because the build must not link or run them.

## How does Atesor decide the verdict?

`evaluate_scan()` checks these conditions in this order:

| Order | Condition | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One or more build outputs are not riscv64 | `wrong_arch` |
| 2 | The scan stopped at its file limit | `unverified` |
| 3 | One or more build outputs are riscv64 | `verified` |
| 4 | No ELF build output, or the scan could not run | `unverified` |

One foreign output fails the port, also when all other outputs are riscv64. The `reason` field names up to 5 foreign outputs with their architecture.

A truncated scan cannot prove the port, because an unread output can be foreign. When the scan cannot run, for example when `python3` is missing, the status is `unverified` and `scan_error` holds the cause. A failed scan never gives `verified`.

The verdict also has `abi_warnings`. A warning names each riscv64 output whose ABI is not `lp64d`, the ABI of the Alpine, Debian and Ubuntu riscv64 ports. A warning does not change the status.

After the list holds 3000 entries, the program only counts more riscv64 outputs, in `unlisted_riscv64`. It always lists foreign outputs. The state records at most 60 riscv64 outputs, with expected names first. The verdict keeps the full counts.

## What happens on a wrong-architecture verdict?

`verify_node` sets `build_status` to `FAILED` and adds an `ARCHITECTURE` error: `Artifact verification failed: <reason>`. `route_verify_result` sends this error to `fix_node` while attempts remain. The fixer gets the reason as its error text. After a fix that changes the tree, the builder compiles again from the first phase with a build step, and `verify_node` scans again. The latest scan always replaces the earlier result.

## Where does Atesor search for expected artifacts?

The analyst writes `expected_artifacts` in the `PackageAnalysis`: the binary and library file names that a good build must produce. The scanner uses up to 10 of these names. It drops a name that is not a plain file name.

`make install`, `go install` and `cargo install` can put the outputs outside the repository. The program therefore also searches these directories for the expected names:

- `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/local/sbin`, `/usr/local/lib`, `/usr/local/lib64`
- `/root/go/bin`, `/root/.cargo/bin`

A file matches when its name is an expected name, or starts with the expected name and a dot. The search goes 3 directory levels below each directory. It ignores a file that is older than the run start minus 600 seconds. An earlier package in a shared sandbox therefore cannot prove this port.

The host uses these matches only when the repository holds no build output at all. Then a riscv64 match gives `verified`, and the reason ends with `(installed outside the repository)`. A foreign match gives `wrong_arch`.

If the result is still `unverified`, `expected_missing` lists the expected names that the search did not find.

## What does "not verified" mean?

An `unverified` verdict is a `SUCCESS` that proves nothing. The build commands passed, but Atesor found no riscv64 output. Common causes are a header-only library, a script-only package, a truncated scan or a scan that could not run.

For an unverified build, Atesor does these things:

- `finish_node` runs and writes the recipe. The summarizer prompt and the fallback recipe include the verification verdict.
- The terminal shows `PORTING FINISHED, NOT VERIFIED` and the reason.
- The report status is `SUCCESS, NOT VERIFIED (no riscv64 output proven)`.
- `main.py` exits with code 3.
- Atesor does not write a recipe cache entry and does not save few-shot examples.

A recipe cache hit also exits with code 3 when its entry has no `verified` verdict. Entries from before the verification feature have no verdict. See [Exit codes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/exit-codes/) and [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

`batch_test.py` counts exit code 3 as `UNVERIFIED`, apart from a pass. See [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

## How does the curator rank artifacts?

The scanner returns every riscv64 executable and library. That list holds compiler probes, libtool shims and test programs, next to the real deliverables. `src/artifact_curator.py` ranks the list. It runs in `finish_node`, after the recipe, when the state holds build outputs. Atesor stores the result in `curated_artifacts`. The recipe cache entry and the zip manifest use the roles from that list.

The curator gives each output one role:

- **primary**: the headline deliverable, for example the binary with the package name, or the main shared or static library.
- **secondary**: useful outputs that are not the headline, for example tests, examples and tools.
- **drop**: build-system internals and probes.

It does these steps:

1. It removes hard noise first, with no LLM. Hard noise is any path that contains `/CMakeFiles/`, `/_deps/`, `/.libs/`, `/conftest`, `/CompilerId`, `/meson-private/`, `/autom4te.cache/`, `/build-aux/` or a similar marker.
2. It asks the summarizer model to put each numbered path into `primary`, `secondary` or `drop`, with a 60 second limit.
3. An output that the model does not classify becomes `secondary`, so no real deliverable disappears.
4. It puts the primary outputs first.

The curator uses deterministic rules in 4 cases: no model, a failed call, JSON that does not parse, or a response that drops every output. The rules make every library and every binary with the package name primary. A path under `/test/`, `/tests/`, `/examples/`, `/bench/`, `/tools/` or a similar directory is secondary. All other outputs are primary.

## When do package tests run?

`finish_node` runs the package's own test suite one time after a successful build, verified or not. The tests never fail the port. Atesor writes the result to `state.package_tests`, the report, the recipe prompt and the zip manifest, with the label "not gating".

`_detect_test_command()` picks the first row that matches, from the top of this table. It checks `build/`, `_build/` and `builddir/` in that order, and for each directory it checks CTest before Meson.

| Condition | Command |
|---|---|
| The build directory has `CTestTestfile.cmake` | `ctest --test-dir <dir> --output-on-failure` |
| The build directory has `meson-info` | `meson test -C <dir> --print-errorlogs` |
| `go.mod` exists, and the build system is `go` or there is no `Makefile` | `go test ./...` |
| `Cargo.toml` exists, and the build system is `cargo` or `rust` or there is no `Makefile` | `cargo test --release` |
| The top `Makefile` has a `check:` target | `make check` |
| The top `Makefile` has a `test:` target | `make test` |

The test phase has a time limit:

- The default limit is 600 seconds.
- `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT` sets a different limit. The value `0` disables the phase.
- When `ATESOR_RUN_DEADLINE` (epoch seconds) is set, the limit ends 420 seconds before that time. The summarizer and curator calls, the outputs, the native mirror copy and the zip need that time.
- A limit under 60 seconds skips the phase.

The result `status` is one of these values:

- `passed`: the exit code is 0.
- `failed`: the exit code is not 0.
- `timeout`: the command was killed, with exit code 137 or -1, and it used the time limit minus 35 seconds or more.
- `skipped`: the phase is disabled, has no time left, or found no test suite.
- `error`: the phase could not run.

The result also keeps the framework, the command, the exit code, the duration and the last 3000 characters of output. See [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/).

Performance mode reuses the detected test command. It runs that command again in each tune tree, with the same time limit rules, as its second gate.

## How does performance mode check a tune?

Performance mode (`--optimize`) runs only after a `verified` verdict, and it never changes that verdict or the verified tree. It checks each tune with its own gates:

- The tune must build the libraries of the package and the program that the workload runs. When there is neither, it must build every artifact of the verified build. Every ELF file and static archive of the tune must have `e_machine` 243.
- The package tests must pass in the tune tree when they passed for the verified build.
- The workload output of the tune must equal the output of the baseline.

The gates also scan the code of each tune for instructions from extensions that the machine lacks. A match is a warning, not a failure. See [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/).

## Related pages

- [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/)
- [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/)
- [Read the output](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/read-the-output/)
- [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/)
