# LLM layer

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/

Eclipse Atesor™ uses an LLM in 5 graph nodes: the analyst, the scout, the fixer, the finish node and the optimize node. This page describes model selection, response checks, fallbacks, prompts, few-shot learning and the call log.

## Which providers does Atesor support?

On `main`, `src/models.py` supports 4 providers. The `LLM_PROVIDER` environment variable selects one. The default is `gemini`.

| `LLM_PROVIDER` | API key variable | Client class |
|---|---|---|
| `gemini` (default) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | `ChatGoogleGenerativeAI` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `ChatOpenAI` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `ChatOpenAI` with the OpenRouter base URL |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ChatAnthropic` from the `langchain-anthropic` package |

`check_api_keys()` fails when the key is missing or is the placeholder `your_key_here`. It also fails for an unknown provider name. For `anthropic`, it also fails when the `langchain-anthropic` package is not installed. `requirements.txt` lists that package. See [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

Two more variables apply to all providers:

- `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` sets the output token cap. The default is 8192. For `anthropic`, the cap also covers the thinking tokens of the reply.
- `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` sets the HTTP timeout in seconds. The default is 120.

`invoke_llm()` runs each call in a separate thread with a wall timeout of `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` plus 15 seconds. The provider timeout therefore fires first and releases the connection. The artifact curator uses a wall timeout of 60 seconds. The optimizer agent uses a wall timeout of 240 seconds for a harness, because a harness is a full source file.

## Which model does each role use?

`MODEL_CONFIG` maps each provider and agent role to a model and a temperature.

| Role | Temperature | `gemini` | `openai` | `openrouter` | `anthropic` (effort) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `planner` | 0.1 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` (`medium`) |
| `scout` | 0.1 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` (`medium`) |
| `fixer` | 0.2 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o` | `openai/gpt-oss-120b:free` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` (`medium`) |
| `summarizer` | 0.1 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` (`low`) |
| `supervisor` | 0.0 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-haiku-5-5` (`low`) |
| `builder` | 0.0 | `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | `gpt-4o-mini` | `qwen/qwen3-coder:free` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` (`medium`) |

The `anthropic` entries send no temperature, because both Claude models reject it. Each entry sends an `effort` value instead, as `output_config`. The effort sets the depth of the adaptive thinking of the model. A Claude reply can contain `thinking` parts. `extract_content()` keeps only the `text` parts, so a thinking part cannot break the JSON parse.

These nodes call a model:

- `analyst_node` uses the `planner` role.
- `scout_node` uses the `scout` role.
- `fixer_node` uses the `fixer` role.
- `finish_node` uses the `summarizer` role for the recipe and for the artifact curator.
- `optimize_node` uses the `builder` role when the optimizer agent writes a harness, and the `planner` role when it chooses a program run.

The `supervisor` role has entries, but no node calls a model with it. The supervisor routes by rules. The `builder` role has no model call in the build itself: the builder runs commands, and only the optimizer agent uses the builder model, for harness code.

## How do model fallbacks work?

`create_llm_pool(role)` returns the primary model and its fallbacks. For `gemini`, `openai` and `anthropic`, the pool holds only the primary model.

For `openrouter`, the pool adds these models after the primary, in this order:

1. The models in `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS`, a comma-separated list. When it is not set, Atesor uses 6 default free models.
2. `openrouter/free`, the OpenRouter free models router, always last.

The primary model does not appear a second time in the pool.

Each OpenRouter request also carries a `models` array, so OpenRouter can try other models in the same request. The array holds the first 2 named fallbacks and `openrouter/free`, because OpenRouter accepts at most 3 entries.

## How does Atesor validate a JSON response?

The analyst, the scout, the fixer and the optimizer agent use `llm_call_with_validation()` in `src/llm_helpers.py`. The function does not raise for a failed model call. It does these steps for each attempt:

1. It sends the messages to the active model and logs the response.
2. It takes the text from the first `{` to the last `}` and parses it as JSON. The top level must be an object.
3. It runs the node's validator on the object.
4. A valid object ends the call.
5. After a validation failure, it appends a critique message with the reason and asks again.

The nodes and the optimizer agent allow 2 critique retries. Three other failures rotate to the next model in the pool first. They use a critique retry only when no other model remains:

- **Provider error**, for example `404`, `429`, `402`, `rate limit`, `502` or `upstream`.
- **Empty response**.
- **JSON parse failure**.

Some provider errors get special handling:

- **`Retry-After` of 65 seconds or less**: wait one time per model, then try the same model again.
- **HTTP 402 with `can only afford N`**: lower the token cap of every pool model to 90% of N, at least 256, and try the same model again.
- **`use this slug instead: <id>`**: add that model to the pool.
- **`free-models-per-day`**: stop at once. This OpenRouter daily cap covers every free model on the account, so a rotation cannot help.

The total number of attempts is at most the critique retries plus 1, plus the pool size, plus 1 for each added model. The result is an `LLMCallOutcome` with the data, the attempt count, the last error, the token counts and the cost.

The optimizer agent also sets `rotate_on_timeout=True`. A timeout then rotates to the next model in the pool. A timeout on the last model ends the call, because the same model would cost one more full timeout. When no model of the role answers in time, the agent asks the models of the other role one time: the `planner` pool for a harness, and the `builder` pool for a program run.

### What does each validator check?

- **Analyst**: `purpose` is a non-empty string, `build_system` is an object with a `type`, `dependencies` is an array, and `needs_custom_plan` is a JSON boolean.
- **Scout**: `phases` is a non-empty array, and each phase has a `name` and a non-empty list of string commands. `validate_build_plan()` then rejects a build step that hides its failure, such as `make || true`. It also rejects placeholder paths such as `/path/to/`, a guessed `/home/` path and the cross-compiler prefix `riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc`. It rejects a Go subcommand used as a package name, and `cmake` commands that make a nested build directory. After validation, `scout_node` removes test commands, such as `ctest`, `make check`, `go test` or `cargo test`, because `finish_node` runs the package tests. A plan with only test commands counts as a scout failure.
- **Fixer**: the response has strategies, and the recommended strategy has actions. A `create_file` action needs a path and content, and the path must stay inside the repository. A `patch` path must stay inside the repository. A `command` action must pass `validate_fix_command()`. That function blocks commands such as `rm -rf /`, `git push`, `git reset --hard` and `touch` of a source file. It then applies the single-command check of `CommandValidator`.
- **Optimizer agent**: a program run must name one of the built programs and pass the strict command grammar of `check_workload_command()`. A harness must be a complete source file of at most 32000 bytes. It must print an `ATESOR-CHECK` line and must not use a forbidden call, such as `system`, `rand`, `time.Now` or `std::net::`. A C or C++ harness must call an exported function of the library, a Go file must define `BenchmarkAtesor`, and a Rust example must use the crate. See [Performance mode internals](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/).

## What happens when every attempt fails?

Each node has its own fallback, so the run continues when all attempts fail.

| Node | Fallback |
|---|---|
| `analyst_node` | `_fallback_analysis()` builds a `PackageAnalysis` from scripted detection, with `llm_grounded=False`. It sets `needs_custom_plan` when the detection confidence is under 0.5. |
| `scout_node` | `create_fallback_build_plan()` writes a fixed plan for `go`, `cmake`, `make`, `cargo`, `meson` or `autotools`, or a discovery plan. It also records a `Scout failed` error. |
| `fixer_node` | No deterministic fix. It records `FIXER proposed invalid fix` and sets `FAILED`. |
| `finish_node` | A short recipe with the build steps and the verification verdict. |
| Artifact curator | Rule-based ranking. See [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/). |
| Optimizer agent | No deterministic answer. That workload source gives no workload, and performance mode tries the next source. |

## How does Atesor count cost?

`cost_for_usage(model_id, input_tokens, output_tokens)` computes the cost from the token usage that the provider reports. A model ID that ends in `:free`, or `openrouter/free`, costs $0. Paid models use this table, in USD per 1 million tokens:

| Model | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `gpt-4o` | 2.50 | 10.00 |
| `gpt-4o-mini` | 0.15 | 0.60 |
| `gemini-flash-lite-latest` | 0.10 | 0.40 |
| `gemini-flash-latest` | 0.30 | 2.50 |
| `claude-haiku-5-5` | 0.10 | 0.50 |
| `claude-sonnet-5-5` | 2.00 | 10.00 |

A paid model that is not in the table uses 3.00 and 12.00, so an unknown model counts high, not free. The tokens of an attempt that fails validation also count. The supervisor escalates the run when `api_cost_usd` is more than $1.00. The calls of the optimizer agent also add to `api_cost_usd`, but they come after `finish_node`, so no escalation check follows them. See [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).

## How does Atesor build the prompts?

The prompt templates are in `src/graph.py`: `ANALYST_PROMPT`, `SCOUT_PROMPT`, `FIXER_PROMPT` and `SUMMARIZER_PROMPT`. The curator prompt is in `src/artifact_curator.py`. The optimizer agent prompts are in `src/workload.py`: one for a program run, and one each for a C or C++ harness, a Go benchmark and a Rust example. The analyst, scout, fixer and optimizer prompts ask for JSON only and show the JSON shape of the answer.

The analyst, scout and fixer prompts start with a platform banner from `_build_platform_banner()`. The banner names the distro, the libc, the target triplet and the package manager of the active sandbox. It tells the model never to use the package manager of another distro. It also shows one worked install example and one package name correction.

The scout and fixer prompts also include the static knowledge from `get_system_knowledge_summary()` in `src/knowledge.py`. The active platform profile supplies the distro parts. The block has these parts:

- The install command and the map from canonical names to distro packages.
- 7 RISC-V preprocessor macros, for example `__riscv`, `__riscv_xlen` and `__riscv_vector`.
- 9 common porting issues, each with its root cause and first fix. The issues are x86 intrinsics, inline assembly, builtin functions, memory ordering, musl libc, `config.guess`, atomics linking, the code model and the cache line size. The block skips the musl issue in a glibc sandbox.
- Key facts: the libc, the native triplet, no cross-compilation flags, and the weaker RISC-V memory model.
- The package name corrections of the active distro.

The summarizer prompt asks for a Markdown recipe with 6 H2 sections in this order: `Executive Summary`, `Prerequisites`, `Build Instructions`, `Architecture Notes`, `Verification`, and `Known Issues & Recommendations`.

## What does the analyst produce?

`analyst_node` makes one validated LLM call. It reads the evidence bundle from `collect_build_evidence()` and the scripted detection summary. It writes a `PackageAnalysis`:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `purpose`, `language` | What the package is, and its main language |
| `build_system`, `build_system_confidence`, `build_system_reasoning` | The build system, with the file that proves it |
| `dependencies` | Up to 15 entries of a canonical name and the file evidence |
| `riscv_risks` | Up to 10 RISC-V risks that the evidence shows |
| `build_strategy` | 2 to 3 sentences on how to build |
| `expected_artifacts` | Up to 10 binary or library names |
| `needs_custom_plan` | True when a standard recipe for the build system will fail |
| `complexity` | 1 to 10 |
| `llm_grounded` | True for an LLM result, False for the fallback |

Later nodes use the analysis:

- `heuristic_plan_node` reads `needs_custom_plan`, the build system and the dependencies.
- The scout and fixer prompts include a compact text form of the analysis.
- `verify_node` uses `expected_artifacts`.
- The optimizer agent prompts use `purpose`.

With `--optimize` and a verified recipe cache entry, `cached_recipe_node` writes the analysis instead of the analyst, with `llm_grounded=False`.

The analyst replaced an earlier LLM planner. `task_plan` is now a fixed record from `create_default_plan()`, with no LLM call.

## What evidence does the fixer get?

`fixer_node` gives the model this evidence:

- The failed command and the first 3000 characters of the error.
- Source excerpts around the `file:line` references in the error, for up to 3 files, from `error_context_excerpts()`.
- The package analysis.
- The last 5 fix attempts, with the instruction not to repeat them.
- The first 500 characters of the repository tree, and up to 5 `high` or `critical` architecture findings.
- The build system and the completed phases.
- The platform banner, the static knowledge and up to 2 few-shot examples.

The fixer can ask for one bounded investigation round. In the first round, the model can return `{"investigate": {"commands": [...]}}` instead of a fix. Atesor then runs the commands with these limits:

- At most 4 commands.
- Each command is a single command. Its first word must be one of `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `ls`, `find`, `grep`, `egrep`, `file`, `stat`, `wc`, `pkg-config`, `readelf`, `nm`, `ldd`, `go` or `which`.
- No `<` or `>` redirection.
- Atesor keeps the first 1500 characters of each output.

Atesor puts the outputs into the prompt and asks again. In the second round the model must return a fix.

Atesor applies the actions of the recommended strategy. A `create_file` action writes through a sandbox command that resolves every symbolic link first and refuses a target outside the repository. A `patch` action must also stay in the repository. A `command` action must pass `validate_fix_command()` again. Atesor records the fix as a `FixAttempt`. The builder marks it as a success after the next successful build.

## How does few-shot memory work?

A few-shot example is a short record of an earlier, verified solution that Atesor puts into a prompt. `src/memory.py` keeps one JSON file per agent in the `examples` folder of the data directory:

- `scout_examples.json`: build plans. The scout prompt uses them.
- `fixer_examples.json`: error patterns and fixes. The fixer prompt uses them.
- `builder_examples.json`: build phases. Atesor saves them, but no prompt uses them.

`supervisor_examples.json` is a legacy file that no code reads. On the first run, Atesor copies the bundled example files into the writable data directory.

**Sandbox scope.** Each example has a `sandbox` key, for example `alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64`. Retrieval removes examples from another sandbox before it scores. An example with no `sandbox` key counts as `alpine-riscv64`. If no example matches the active sandbox, the prompt gets no examples.

**Ranking.** `_calculate_relevance()` adds these weights and caps the score at 1.0:

| Signal | Weight |
|---|---|
| Same build system | +0.5 |
| The fixer `error_pattern` regex matches the error | +0.4 |
| Each example tag found in the error | +0.15 |
| Same `has_main` | +0.1 |
| Same `module_dir` | +0.15 |
| Both have a `module_dir`, but they differ | +0.05 |
| CGO context and a `cgo` tag | +0.2 |
| Same sandbox | +0.25 |
| Different sandbox | -0.35 |

Only examples with a positive score appear. The scout and fixer prompts get at most 2 examples and 2000 characters.

**Learning.** An unverified port saves no examples. After a verified port, `finish_node` saves these examples:

- A scout example with the build plan.
- A fixer example for each successful fix, with the escaped first 80 characters of its error as the `error_pattern`.
- A builder example with the phases.

**Cap and deduplication.** A new example is a duplicate when it has the same sandbox and the same repository and build system. A fixer example with the same `error_pattern` and build system is also a duplicate. So is a scout or builder example with the same commands. Each file keeps at most 100 examples. When a file has more, Atesor keeps the manual examples and removes the oldest auto-learned examples first. Learned examples get IDs such as `scout-auto-001`. Writes use a file lock and an atomic file replace.

See [Few-shot examples](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/few-shot-examples/) to add examples by hand.

## What does the LLM audit log record?

`src/llm_logger.py` writes every LLM call to a log file in the logs directory. `main.py` switches the file to `agent-call_<repo>.log` for each repository, so parallel batch runs do not mix their logs.

Each entry has these fields:

- A call ID and a timestamp.
- The agent role and the model. The optimizer agent logs its calls under the role label `optimizer`.
- The cost in USD, with 6 decimals, and the input and output token counts.
- Metadata as JSON, for example the repository, the attempt number and the pool index. An optimizer call also has a `phase`, for example `optimize-harness-c` or `optimize-workload-program`.
- The prompt and the response, each limited to 10000 characters, with a note on the dropped length.

A validated call logs every attempt that returns a response, also when the response fails validation. The entry shows the full message thread, with the critique messages. The logger is a thread-safe singleton. It also keeps the last 1000 call records in memory. See [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/).

---

# Performance mode internals

Section: Architecture
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/optimize/

Eclipse Atesor™ performance mode (`--optimize`) builds tuned copies of a verified port, checks them, and times them against the verified build on native riscv64 hardware. The code is in `src/optimize.py`, `src/machine.py`, `src/workload.py` and `src/bench.py`. Read this page before you change how Atesor builds, checks, measures or accepts a tune. For the user steps, see [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

This page uses these terms:

- A **tune** is the verified build with other compiler or toolchain settings. The console calls them `Tune-1`, `Tune-2` and so on.
- The **baseline tree** is a copy of the verified build, rebuilt the same way as each tune. Atesor compares each tune with it.
- A **gate** is a check that a tune must pass before Atesor times it.
- A **workload** is a command that does the same, fixed amount of work in every run, so its run time shows the speed of the build.

## Where does performance mode hook into a run?

Performance mode adds 2 nodes to the parent graph, `cached_recipe_node` and `optimize_node`. It works in these steps:

1. `main.py` sets `optimize_requested` in the initial state. `--optimize` skips the recipe cache fast path, because performance mode needs a real build tree.
2. Without `--force`, `main.py` reads the recipe cache. A verified entry goes into `state.cached_recipe`, and `cached_recipe_node` turns it into the build plan with no planning LLM call.
3. The port runs as usual. After `finish_node`, `route_finish_to_next` sends the run to `optimize_node`.
4. `optimize_node` calls `run_optimization()` in `src/optimize.py`. It passes the optimizer agent and a function that runs the detected package test command in a given tree.
5. `optimize_node` writes the result to `state.optimization`. It then calls `record_optimization()`, which stores a native measured result in the recipe cache.

`optimize_node` catches every exception itself. An error becomes `state.optimization` with the status `error`, and the port keeps its result and its exit code. `run_optimization()` stops at once with the status `skipped` when the verdict of the port is not `verified`. The [architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/) shows both nodes in the graph.

## What does the pipeline look like?

```text
finish_node (SUCCESS)
  |  route_finish_to_next: optimize_requested
  v
optimize_node --> run_optimization()
  |
  |-- verdict is not verified ----------------------------> skipped
  |
  1. probe_machine()          src/machine.py      no LLM
  2. check_integrity()        native only         no LLM
  |    a CPU gives wrong data ----------------------------> not measured
  3. profile_package()        src/workload.py     no LLM
  4. replay_commands(), build_ladder()            no LLM
  |    no tune, no command or no artifact ----------------> skipped
  5. baseline tree <repo>.opt/base, gate 1        no LLM
  |    the baseline does not build -----------------------> error
  6. choose_workload()        src/workload.py     LLM for a program
  |                                               run or a harness
  |    no workload on native -----------------------------> not measured
  7. for each tune, Tune-1 to Tune-6:
  |      build in <repo>.opt/<id>
  |      gate 1 --> gate 2 --> gate 3
  |      bench.measure()      native only         no LLM
  8. PGO tune on top of the best tune             no LLM
  9. second check of the fastest tune, then the next one
  10. copy the accepted artifacts to <repo>.opt/accepted,
      remove every other tree
  v
state.optimization["status"]:
  accepted | no gain | not confirmed | not measured
  checked (QEMU) | skipped | error
```

## What does the machine probe read?

`probe_machine()` runs one Python program in the sandbox, with a limit of 600 seconds. The program prints raw facts as one JSON document. `evaluate_probe()` on the host turns the facts into a `MachineProfile`. The probe reads these facts:

- **ISA extensions** from 3 sources: `/proc/cpuinfo`, the `riscv_hwprobe` system call (Linux 6.4 or later), and test instructions. A test instruction runs in a child process for `zba`, `zbb`, `zbs`, `zicond`, `zfa`, `zfhmin` and `v`. A child that stops with SIGILL marks the extension as absent. The test instructions win over the other 2 sources.
- **The core**, from the device-tree `compatible` string, the `uarch` line of `/proc/cpuinfo`, or `mvendorid` and `marchid` together. The core table in `src/machine.py` has 5 entries: `sifive-u74`, `sifive-p550`, `spacemit-x60`, `thead-c906` and `thead-c910`. Atesor matches a core on the native target only.
- **Misaligned access speed**, from `riscv_hwprobe`. When `riscv_hwprobe` gives no answer on the native target, a load-timing test decides. A misaligned 8-byte load that costs at most 4 aligned loads is `fast`. A load that costs 40 or more is `emulated`, and a load between the two is `slow`. A test that stops with SIGBUS gives `unsupported`.
- **Compilers**: `gcc`, `clang` and `clang-19` to `clang-22`, when they are installed. For each compiler, the probe records the `-march` extensions and `-mtune` names that it accepts. It also tests `-mstrict-align`, `-flto=auto` and `-ffat-lto-objects`, and whether the compiler really emits Zba and Zbb instructions.
- **Go and Rust**: the Go version, the `rustc` version, the target CPUs of `rustc` and their target features.
- **The board**: the allowed CPUs, the memory, the kernel, the libc, the cpufreq governor and frequency, the temperatures and the caches.

Under QEMU with no named CPU model, the extension set is the QEMU `max` CPU, which matches no real board. Atesor then builds no ISA tune. `--emulate-cpu` (or `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`) names a model. Atesor passes it as `QEMU_CPU` to the probe, the builds and the runs. `--probe` runs the same probe alone and writes `machine_profile_<kind>.json` to the output directory.

## How does the machine check work?

On the native target, `check_integrity()` runs after the probe and before any build. It does these steps:

1. It starts one child process for each allowed CPU, all at the same time, and pins each child to its CPU.
2. Each child compresses and decompresses the same 8 MiB buffer 10 times with zlib.
3. Each child counts the round trips that do not give the buffer back. A child that crashes counts as a failure.

One failure on any CPU stops performance mode with the status `not measured`, before any build. Unchanged code that gives wrong data makes every timing on that machine meaningless. When the check cannot run, Atesor adds a warning and continues.

## How does Atesor profile the package?

`profile_package()` in `src/workload.py` reads the curated artifacts of the verified build, or the raw list when the curator wrote none. It uses only paths inside the repository tree:

- An artifact of type `library_static` or `library_shared` is a library.
- A program in a directory such as `test`, `tests`, `example`, `bench`, `demo`, `sample` or `fuzz` is a helper program.
- Every other program is one of the package's own programs.

The kind of the package is `library`, `program`, `library+programs` or `unknown`. `language_of()` gives the language from the build system of the plan: `go` for Go, `rust` for `cargo` or `rust`, and `c` for C and C++ in all other cases.

## How does Atesor build the baseline and each tune?

Each tree is a copy, so the verified tree never changes. `replay_commands()` reads the commands that really ran in the verified build from `command_results_cache`. These commands include the rewrites and the successful retries of the builder. `replayable()` splits each command at `&&` and drops these parts:

- Package installs, for example `apt-get`, `apk`, `pip install` or `rustup`.
- Install steps, for example `make install`, `cmake --install`, `go install`, `cargo install` or `ldconfig`.
- Source control and download steps, for example `git clone`, `git apply`, `patch`, `wget` or `curl`.
- Copies and outputs to a path outside the tree. A `cd` out of the tree drops the rest of its chain.

The result lists up to 20 dropped parts as `not repeated: <part>`. For each tree, `prepare_tree()` and `build_variant()` do these steps in the sandbox:

1. Copy the patched tree to `<repo>.opt/<id>` with `cp -a`.
2. Remove the compiled outputs that git does not track. These are top-level build directories such as `build`, `_build` or `target`, CMake and Meson build directories, ELF files, static archives, and files such as `CMakeCache.txt` or `*.lo`.
3. Write 2 compiler wrappers, `.atesor/cc` and `.atesor/cxx`. Each wrapper logs the call to `.atesor/cc.log`. It then runs the real compiler with the arguments of the call first and the tune flags last, so a tune flag wins over a repeated project flag such as `-O` or `-march`.
4. Run the replayed commands with `CC`, `CXX` and `MAKEFLAGS` set to the wrappers, plus the tune environment, for example `GORISCV64` or `RUSTFLAGS`. Each command has a limit of 1800 seconds, capped at the remaining time budget, with a floor of 60 seconds.

The baseline tree is `<repo>.opt/base`. For C and C++, it builds with `gcc` through the wrappers and no tune flag. The baseline must pass gate 1. Atesor then compares the code of its artifacts with the code of the verified artifacts. A difference gives a warning that the build is not reproducible, and every tune still uses the baseline tree. When the baseline does not build, performance mode stops with the status `error`.

## How does Atesor choose the workload?

`strategies()` gives the workload sources in this order. `choose_workload()` uses the first source that gives a usable workload.

| Order | Source | When it applies | What it gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `go-benchmarks` | A Go package | The module's own benchmarks |
| 2 | `program` | The package builds its own programs | One program run that the optimizer agent proposes |
| 3 | `harness` | The package builds a library, or is a Go package | A harness that the optimizer agent writes |
| 4 | `helper-program` | The package has helper programs | One run of a helper program that uses the library |
| 5 | `tests` | Always | The package tests, a weak signal |

- **Go benchmarks.** `go test -list '^Benchmark' ./...` finds the package with the most benchmarks. Atesor builds its test binary with `go test -c` in each tree. It runs the binary with a fixed iteration count (`-test.benchtime <N>x`), so the baseline and the tune do the same work. This source compares no output.
- **Program run.** The agent gets the programs with the first 20 lines of their `--help` output and returns one command template. In the template, `{bin}` is the program, `{input}` is the generated input file and `{output}` is an output file. `check_workload_command()` applies a strict grammar. Each pipe stage starts with `{bin}` or a helper such as `gzip`, `sha256sum` or `wc`. `<` reads only `{input}` or `/dev/null`, and `>` writes only `{output}` or `/dev/null`. Outside quotes, the template has no `;`, `$`, backtick, parenthesis, absolute path or `..` path.
- **Harness.** A harness is a small driver program that calls the library API. For C and C++, `library_api()` collects the exported functions and the headers that declare them, and the agent writes one source file. The harness links the shared libraries of the tree with an `rpath`, and `ldd` must show that it loads the library of the tree, not a system copy. Without shared libraries, it links the static ones. For Go, the agent writes `atesor_bench_test.go` with `BenchmarkAtesor`. For Rust, it writes the Cargo example `atesor_bench`. A harness reads its input one time, does the work N times, and prints one `ATESOR-CHECK` line.
- **Helper program.** Atesor uses only the helper programs that call into the package library, from an `nm` check. The agent then proposes a run, as for a program run.
- **Package tests.** Atesor uses the detected test command only when the tests passed in the port. Go tests are not timed, because `go test` caches results.

Every candidate runs on the baseline tree first:

- A harness must build, exit 0, and print the same `ATESOR-CHECK` line in 2 runs. The module's own Go benchmarks must build and exit 0, and they compare no output. For both, `size_by_iterations()` scales N so that one run takes about 2 seconds. On native hardware, one run must take 0.5 to 5 seconds.
- A program run compares its whole output in 2 runs. `size_by_input()` scales the input from 1 to 512 MiB, so that one run takes about 2 seconds. A run under 0.5 seconds is still usable, and a run over 5 seconds fails.
- A package test run must take 5 seconds or less on native hardware.
- A run that exits 0 and still writes to stderr fails.
- Under QEMU, the input of a program run is at most 4 MiB, and no time limit applies.

`write_input()` writes deterministic input data of kind `binary`, `text`, `json` or `csv` from the fixed seed `atesor-measure`. A crash of the baseline during this check, for example with SIGILL or SIGSEGV, is a fault of the port, and the report says so. Without a workload, a native run builds no tune and stops with the status `not measured`. Under QEMU, the tunes still build and pass gates 1 and 2.

## Which tunes does Atesor try, and in which order?

`build_ladder()` makes the list from the probe and the language, and keeps at most 6 tunes. One PGO tune can follow, so `MAX_VARIANTS` is 7.

For C and C++, `c_ladder()` gives this order:

1. **Core tuning**: `-mtune=<name>` for the probed core, with the first name that the compiler accepts.
2. **Machine ISA**: `-march=rv64gc_<extensions>`. The extensions come from `zicond`, `zfa`, `zfhmin`, `zba`, `zbb` and `zbs`, only when the machine has them and the compiler accepts them.
3. **Vector ISA**: `-march=rv64gcv_<extensions>`, only when the machine has V and the compiler accepts it.
4. **Optimization level**: `-O3`.
5. **Link-time optimization**: `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects`, when GCC accepts both flags.
6. **Compiler**: the newest probed clang that emits bitmanip instructions, with its own `-mtune`, `-march` (with V when the machine has it) and `-O3`.

Each GCC tune keeps the flags of the GCC tunes before it. Each tune also gets `-mstrict-align` when misaligned access is not `fast` and the compiler accepts the flag. A tune whose precondition fails is left out, for example for an unknown core. Without GCC in the probe, the list is empty. Atesor skips the `-O3` tune when every source compile of the baseline already uses `-O3`. It skips the LTO tune when a source compile already uses `-flto`. It reads these facts from the wrapper log of the baseline, and it ignores configure checks.

For Go, `go_ladder()` gives one tune, the `GORISCV64` level:

- `rva23u64` needs Go 1.25 or later and the extensions `zba`, `zbb`, `zbs`, `v`, `zicond` and `zfa`.
- `rva22u64` needs Go 1.23 or later and `zba`, `zbb` and `zbs`.
- A machine that lacks only Zbs can get `rva22u64` with Go 1.23 to 1.26, because those releases emit no Zbs instruction. Gate 2 then decides.
- `rva20u64` is the Go default, so it gives no tune.

For Rust, `rust_ladder()` gives this order:

1. `RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=<core>`, when `rustc` knows the core and the machine has every feature of that CPU model. Otherwise `-C target-feature=` with the probed `+zba`, `+zbb` and `+zbs`.
2. Fat LTO with one codegen unit, on top of tune 1.

When the build sets `RUSTFLAGS` itself, only the LTO tune remains.

## How does PGO work?

PGO (profile-guided optimization) builds the code with instrumentation, runs it on a training input, and builds it again with the recorded profile. `_pgo_variant()` adds one PGO tune on top of a base tune. The base tune is the fastest `faster` tune, else the `no change` tune with the lowest time ratio, else the last tune that built under QEMU. PGO applies to C, C++ and Go only. It needs a workload, and for Go the workload must be a Go benchmark: the module's own benchmarks or the `BenchmarkAtesor` harness.

For C and C++, PGO does these steps:

1. A training build adds `-fprofile-generate=<dir>` and sets `CCACHE_DISABLE=1`. GCC also gets `-fprofile-update=atomic` and `-fprofile-prefix-path=<tree>`, so the profile names do not depend on the tree.
2. The training run uses a second input from the seed `atesor-train` when the workload reads an input. It runs 3 times.
3. For clang, `llvm-profdata merge` writes `merged.profdata`.
4. The final build adds `-fprofile-use` with the profile. It then passes the gates and the timing as every other tune.

For Go, the baseline tree records a CPU profile with `-test.cpuprofile` during a 1 second benchmark run. The PGO tune builds with `GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false -pgo=<profile>`, and gate 1 checks that the binary records `-pgo`. The profile directory is `<repo>.opt/pgo-<id>`, outside the tune trees, because Atesor removes the training tree before the final build.

## What do the gates check?

**Gate 1** (`gate_build_facts()`) reads the artifacts of the tune in the sandbox with `inspect_tree()`. It applies these checks:

- The libraries of the package and the program that the workload runs must exist. When there is neither, every artifact of the verified build must exist. A missing other artifact is a warning.
- Every ELF file and static archive must have `e_machine` 243 (riscv64).
- For C and C++, the wrapper log must show at least one compiler call. This proves that the flags reached the compiler.
- For Go, one binary or more must record the `GORISCV64` level of the tune in `go version -m`, and a PGO tune must record `-pgo`.
- When every artifact has the same code as the baseline, the verdict is `no effect`. The code hash covers the executable sections only, so an embedded build path is not a change.

Gate 1 also counts the instructions of each extension class in the executable sections. On native, it reads up to 8 artifacts and 32 MiB of code in each. Under QEMU, it reads up to 4 artifacts and 1 MiB in each. An instruction from an extension that the machine lacks, and that the baseline does not have, gives a warning, not a failure. Runtime dispatch (ifunc, `riscv_hwprobe`) can contain such code, so gates 2 and 3 decide. The RISC-V unaligned access attribute on a machine without fast misaligned access also gives a warning.

**Gate 2** (`gate_tests()`) applies when the package tests passed for the verified build. The tests must then pass in the tune tree. Atesor copies the tune artifacts to `.atesor/keep` before the tests and puts back each artifact that the tests rebuilt. When the tests did not pass for the verified build, gate 2 is not decisive and passes.

**Gate 3** requires the workload output of the tune to equal the output of the baseline. A run must also not change its input file. The runner hashes stdout, or only the `ATESOR-CHECK` lines for a harness, plus the output file. On native hardware, `bench.measure()` checks this after its first session. Under QEMU, `check_once()` runs each build one time and compares the outputs. A workload that compares no output, such as Go benchmarks or the package tests, has no gate 3 under QEMU.

A tune whose artifacts have the same code as an earlier tune gets the result of that tune, with no new measurement.

## How does Atesor measure a tune?

`bench.measure()` times the baseline (B) and the tune (V) on native hardware only. One runner program in the sandbox runs every timed run, so SSH and podman start-up never enter a measurement. Each run is pinned to one CPU, the highest allowed CPU. Each run also gets an `ATESOR_PAD` environment variable with a random length of 0 to 4096 characters. The padding moves the stack, so one lucky stack layout cannot favor the same build in every round.

The protocol has these steps:

1. The first session runs 3 warm-up runs of each build, then 10 calibration runs of B. The coefficient of variation (CV) of the calibration times gives the noise.
2. The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is `2.8 * CV * sqrt(2 / rounds)`. Atesor uses 20 rounds, or 40 rounds when 20 rounds cannot detect a 2% change.
3. The second session runs 1 warm-up run of each build, then the rounds. Each round runs B and V in a random order.
4. The comparison uses the per-round ratio V/B. It computes the median ratio, its 95% bootstrap interval from 2000 resamples of whole rounds, and the two-sided Mann-Whitney p-value of the two sets of times.

The verdict follows from the interval and the p-value:

- `faster`: the upper bound of the interval is below 0.98, and p is below 0.05.
- `slower`: the lower bound of the interval is above 1.02, and p is below 0.05.
- `no change`: all other results.

Atesor handles noise with these rules:

- A session is `unstable`, with no verdict, when the CPU frequency changes between the start and the end, or a temperature reaches 75 C.
- A warning shows when other work uses more than 0.5 CPU at the start, when the cpufreq governor is not `performance`, or when the MDE is above 2%.
- A warning shows when other Atesor containers run on the machine.
- A measurement with fewer than 5 complete rounds fails.
- A measurement starts only when the budget covers it: 56 runs (2 times 3 warm-ups, 10 calibration runs, 2 times 20 rounds) times the run time.
- Each run has a limit of 300 seconds.
- When the unchanged baseline fails in 2 measurements, Atesor times no later tune, because the machine or the workload gives wrong results.

## When does Atesor accept a tune?

One `faster` verdict is not enough. After all tunes and the PGO tune, Atesor sorts the `faster` tunes by time ratio. It gives the best tune a second check:

- **C and C++**: Atesor builds the tune again with `-falign-functions=64`, and builds the baseline one time with the same flag. The flag changes the code layout but not the code.
- **Rust**: the same check with `-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=6`.
- **Go**: a second measurement session of the same builds.

The tune must be `faster` again. The first tune that passes the second check is accepted, and the other `faster` tunes get `not checked`. A tune that fails the second check gets `not confirmed`, and the next `faster` tune gets its check.

The time budget is `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` seconds, with a default of 3600. A step starts only when 300 seconds or more remain. Once a tune is faster, a later tune starts only when the budget still covers the longest tune so far plus the second check of the best tune. For the PGO tune, Atesor counts the longest tune 2 times, because PGO builds and runs twice. These rules give the final status:

- `accepted`: a tune passed the second check.
- `no gain`: no tune was faster, or no gain held in its second check.
- `not confirmed`: a gain got no time for its second check.
- `not measured`: the machine check failed, there is no workload, the budget is shorter than one step, or no tune got a timing.
- `checked`: a QEMU run. The tunes built and passed the gates, with no timing.
- `skipped`: the port is not verified, no tune applies, or the verified build has no repeatable command or artifact.
- `error`: the probe, the inspection of the verified tree or the baseline build failed, or an exception occurred.

## Which steps call a model?

Only the workload choice calls a model. The probe, the tunes, the gates, the timing and the verdicts use no LLM.

| Phase | Source | Role | Wall timeout |
|---|---|---|---|
| `workload-program` | Program run, helper program | `planner` | `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` plus 15 seconds |
| `harness-c` | C or C++ harness | `builder` | 240 seconds |
| `harness-go` | Go benchmark | `builder` | 240 seconds |
| `harness-rust` | Cargo example | `builder` | 240 seconds |

These limits apply:

- Each question goes through `llm_call_with_validation()` with 2 critique retries and model rotation, also after a timeout.
- When no model of the role answers in time, the models of the other role get the question one time.
- `_agent_rounds()` tries each answer on the baseline tree and sends the error back. It runs 3 rounds, and up to 8 rounds while each round gives a new error. From round 3 on, an error that an earlier round gave stops the rounds.
- The rounds stop when less than 600 seconds of the budget remain.
- Each call adds to `api_cost_usd`. See [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/).

## What does performance mode write?

- **`state.optimization`**: the result record, with the status, the reason, the machine label, the package profile, the baseline, the workload, one record per tune, the warnings and the notes. The state JSON contains it.
- **`state.machine_profile`**: the `MachineProfile` of the probe.
- **`<repo>.opt/accepted`**: the artifacts of the accepted tune. Atesor removes every other tree under `<repo>.opt`.
- **The report**: a `## Performance Mode (--optimize)` section with one row per tune, and the source of the harness when the agent wrote one.
- **The console**: one line for each step, then a summary that starts with `Optimized: YES`, `Optimized: NO` or, under QEMU, `Optimized: NOT TIMED`.
- **The zip** (with `--package`): the accepted artifacts under `optimized/`, and a manifest with `schema_version` 3 and the `machine` and `optimization` sections.
- **The recipe cache**: `record_optimization()` stores a native result with a workload and the status `accepted` or `no gain`. It writes under `optimizations` in the verified entry, with the core name or the ISA label as the key. It never creates an entry. It keeps only the settings that a later run can repeat, so it drops the `-fprofile` flags and the `GOFLAGS` and `CCACHE_DISABLE` variables.

On the native target, `_run_native()` removes `<repo>.opt` from the machine after the run. With `--package`, Atesor first copies it to the local mirror for the zip.

## Related pages

- [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/)
- [Architecture overview](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/overview/)
- [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/)
- [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/)
- [Native RISC-V](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/)

# Command-line options

Section: Reference
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/cli/

Eclipse Atesor™ has one command. The `.deb` package installs it as `atesor-ai`, and a source checkout runs it as `python3 main.py`. Both forms take the same options and return the same [exit codes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/exit-codes/). This page lists every option that `main.py` accepts, with its argument, its default and its effect, and the order in which Atesor processes them.

## What is the command syntax?

The usage text in `main.py` is:

```text
atesor-ai --repo URL [options]
       atesor-ai --setup-only | --cleanup | --clean-workspace
```

A port needs `--repo`. These commands do not need it:

- `--setup-only`
- `--rebuild` without `--repo`
- `--cleanup` and `--clean-image`
- `--clean-workspace`
- `--preflight`
- `--probe`

If you give no `--repo` and none of these commands, Atesor prints `ERROR: --repo argument is required`, prints the help, and exits with code 1.

The built-in help puts the options in four groups: `porting`, `performance`, `sandbox` and `other`. After the options, the help prints example commands and a short list of environment variables. This page groups the options by task.

## Input

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-r`, `--repo` | `URL` | none | The repository to port. |

Rules for `--repo`:

- The URL must start with `http://` or `https://`.
- After the scheme, the URL can use only letters, digits and the characters `._~:/?#@!+,=%-`.
- Atesor rejects any other value with `ERROR: unsupported or unsafe repository URL` and exit code 1.

Atesor derives the repository name from the last segment of the URL and removes a `.git` suffix. For a generic last segment, Atesor adds the owner in front: `cli`, `core`, `src`, `app`, `main`, `client`, `server` and `lib`. For example, `https://github.com/cli/cli` gives `cli-cli`. The clone directory, the recipe cache key, the log files and the [output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) all use this name.

## Platform and target

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--platform` | `NAME` | `auto` | The sandbox distribution: `alpine`, `debian`, `ubuntu` or `auto`. |
| `--target` | `NAME` | `ATESOR_TARGET`, else `qemu` | Where the builds run: `qemu` or `native`. |
| `--container` | `NAME` | the container name of the profile | The sandbox container name. Batch runs use it. |

### `--platform`

- A value other than `auto` sets `ATESOR_PLATFORM` for the run. The flag wins over `.env`.
- `ubuntu` uses the same profile as `debian`. The image, the container and the package names are the same.
- With `auto` on the `qemu` target, Atesor uses a valid `ATESOR_PLATFORM` first.
- Without one, Atesor reads `/etc/os-release` in the sandbox container. The container is `ATESOR_CONTAINER`, else `atesor-ai-sandbox`.
- If that read fails or gives an unknown distribution, Atesor uses `alpine`.
- The `native` target does not detect the platform. Set `--platform` or `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, or preflight rung 1 fails.

| Platform | Image | Container | Dockerfile (`qemu`) | Dockerfile (`native`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `alpine` | `atesor-ai-sandbox:latest` | `atesor-ai-sandbox` | `Dockerfile` | `Dockerfile` |
| `debian`, `ubuntu` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian:latest` | `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian` | `Dockerfile.debian` | `Dockerfile.native` |

### `--target`

- `main.py` reads `--target` before it parses the other options, because `src/config.py` computes the workspace paths at import time.
- The flag sets `ATESOR_TARGET` and wins over `.env`. Both `--target native` and `--target=native` work. When you give the flag two times, the last one wins.
- Write the flag in full. The parser also accepts a short form such as `--targ native`, but the early read does not. When the two values differ, Atesor prints `ERROR: write --target in full, for example --target native.` and exits with code 1.
- The `native` target needs the SSH settings. Refer to [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/) and [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

### `--container`

The flag sets `ATESOR_CONTAINER` for the run. `--setup-only`, `--cleanup`, `--clean-image` and the port all use this container name. `batch_test.py` gives each worker its own container with this flag, for example `atesor-ai-sandbox-debian-w1`.

## Run control

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-m`, `--max-attempts` | `N` (integer) | `5` | The number of attempts before Atesor escalates the run. |
| `--force` | none | off | Ignore the recipe cache and run the full pipeline. |
| `--rebuild` | none | off | Rebuild the sandbox image before the run. |

### `--max-attempts`

Atesor counts each recorded error as one attempt. When the count reaches `N`, the supervisor escalates the run and the exit code is 1. A build that succeeds always goes to the finish step, also when the count is at `N`. A value that is not an integer gives a parser error and exit code 2.

### `--force`

Without `--force`, Atesor looks in the recipe cache before it checks the API key and before it starts the sandbox. A matching entry ends the run: Atesor writes `<repo>_recipe.md` from the cache and makes no LLM call. The entry must match the repository name and the sandbox. When the entry stores a repository URL, that URL must also match. With `--force`, Atesor skips this check and builds again. Refer to [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

`--optimize` also skips this check, because performance mode needs a real build tree. Without `--force`, a cache entry with a `verified` verdict then becomes the build plan of the port. With `--force`, the agents plan the build again.

### `--rebuild`

The flag sets `REBUILD_IMAGE=true`.

- With `--repo`, Atesor rebuilds the image of the active platform, then ports the repository.
- The cache check comes first. A cache hit ends the run before the rebuild. Add `--force` to rebuild and port. `--optimize` also skips the cache check.
- Without `--repo`, Atesor rebuilds the image and exits.
- On the `qemu` target with `--platform auto` and no `--container`, a rebuild without `--repo` rebuilds the `alpine` sandbox, then the `debian` sandbox.
- On the `native` target, podman builds the image on the machine.

## Output

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--package` | none | off | After a successful build, write a zip with the recipe and the source tree. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | none | off | Show the activity of the agents on the console. |

### `--package`

- Atesor writes the zip when the final status is `SUCCESS`. This includes a build that is not verified (exit code 3). The manifest in the zip records the verdict.
- The zip goes to the `packages/` directory of the workspace. Refer to [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/).
- With `--optimize`, the manifest has schema version 3. When performance mode accepts a tune, the zip also holds the files of that tune in `optimized/`.
- If the zip step fails, Atesor prints `Packaging FAILED` and exits with code 2.
- On a cache hit, Atesor skips `--package` and prints a note, because no fresh source tree exists. Add `--force` to build and package.

### `--verbose`

Without the flag, the console shows the step and status lines, and log records of level `ERROR` only. With the flag, the console also shows log records of level `DEBUG` and the messages of each agent. The log file always records level `DEBUG`. The lines of the optimize step always show on the console, also without `--verbose`.

## Performance mode

Performance mode tries faster builds of a verified port for the machine that runs the build. Each candidate build is a "tune": the verified build with other compiler flags or toolchain settings. Refer to [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--optimize` | none | off | After a verified port, build, check and measure tunes. |
| `--emulate-cpu` | `MODEL` | `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`, else none | The `QEMU_CPU` model for `--optimize` and `--probe` on the `qemu` target. |
| `--probe` | none | off | Probe the machine in the sandbox, print the result, then exit. |

### `--optimize`

- The optimize step runs after the finish step, so only a port with the status `SUCCESS` reaches it. A port that fails or escalates does not.
- The step needs the verdict `verified`. For a port that is not verified, Atesor records the status `skipped` and the reason.
- The verified build stays the result of the port. Performance mode never changes the exit code of the port.
- Atesor skips the recipe cache check. Without `--force`, a verified cache entry of the package becomes the build plan. Then the analyst and the scout make no LLM call.
- Atesor applies the patches of that cache entry first. When the build fails, the fixer and the re-plan loop continue as usual.
- Atesor measures speed only on the `native` target. On `qemu`, Atesor builds and checks each tune, but makes no speed claim.
- `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` sets the time limit of the optimize step, in seconds. The default is 3600.
- The console summary starts with a line `Optimized:` that gives the answer, for example `YES:` or `NO:`.
- On `native`, Atesor removes the `<repo>.opt` tree from the machine when the command ends. Add `--package` to keep the files of an accepted tune.
- `batch_test.py` never passes `--optimize`.

### `--emulate-cpu`

- The value is a QEMU CPU model, for example `rva22u64`. A model can also have properties, for example `rv64i,m=true,a=true,f=true,d=true,c=true,zba=true`.
- The value must start with a letter. It can use only letters, digits and the characters `_.,=+-`, up to 512 characters in total.
- For another value, Atesor prints an `ERROR:` line that says the value is not a QEMU CPU model, and exits with code 1.
- Atesor uses and checks the value only with `--optimize` or `--probe`. Without them, Atesor ignores the flag.
- On `qemu`, the flag wins over `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`.
- The value `max`, or no value, gives QEMU's `max` CPU. Atesor then builds no ISA tune, because no real board has that set of extensions.
- On `native`, Atesor ignores the flag and prints a warning. It ignores `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` on `native` with no warning.
- On a native machine, `--probe` prints a `QEMU model:` line. That line gives an `--emulate-cpu` value that models the machine under QEMU.

### `--probe`

- `--probe` runs alone. With `--repo`, Atesor prints `ERROR: --probe runs alone. Remove --repo, or remove --probe to port the repository.` and exits with code 1.
- Atesor does not check the API key for this command.
- Atesor sets up the sandbox first. On `native`, preflight rungs 2 to 11 run before the setup.
- The probe reads `/proc` and `/sys`, runs compiler checks, and runs test instructions in child processes. It does not change the machine.
- Atesor prints the machine facts and the settings that performance mode derives from them. Then it writes `machine_profile_<target>.json` to the `output/` directory, where `<target>` is `qemu` or `native`.
- The exit code is 0 when the probe ran, else 1. On `native`, the container stops when the command ends.
- With `--rebuild`, Atesor rebuilds the sandbox image before the probe.
- Exception: on `qemu` with `--platform auto` and no `--container`, `--probe --rebuild` rebuilds both sandboxes and exits with no probe.

## Setup and cleanup

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--setup-only` | none | off | Build the sandbox image if it is missing, start the container, then exit. |
| `--cleanup` | none | off | Stop and remove the sandbox container, then exit. |
| `--clean-image` | none | off | Also remove the sandbox image. It implies `--cleanup`. |
| `--clean-workspace` | none | off | Show the workspace size and delete the parts that you select. |

### `--setup-only`

- Atesor does not check the API key for this command.
- `--setup-only` wins over `--repo`. Atesor sets up the sandbox and does not port.
- On `qemu`, Atesor first looks for the `qemu-riscv64` handler in `/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc`. If the handler is missing, Atesor runs `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64` one time.
- On `qemu`, Docker builds the image for `linux/riscv64`. Atesor creates the container with the memory limit `8g` and mounts the workspace at `/workspace`.
- On `native`, preflight rungs 2 to 11 run first. Podman builds the image on the machine, with a time limit of 5400 seconds. The container stops when the command ends.

### `--cleanup` and `--clean-image`

- Atesor uses the container name from `--container` or `ATESOR_CONTAINER`, else the name of the profile.
- With `--repo` and without `--rebuild`, Atesor prints a `NOTE` that it does not port the repository.
- With `--rebuild`, Atesor continues after the teardown.
- On `native`, preflight rungs 2 to 8 run first. Then podman on the machine removes the container, and the image for `--clean-image`.

### `--clean-workspace`

1. Atesor prints the workspace location, the total size and the number of files.
2. Atesor prints the size of each of these directories that exists: `repos`, `output`, `logs`, `.cache` and `patches`.
3. Atesor asks for one choice: `1` (`repos/`), `2` (`output/`), `3` (`logs/`), `4` (`.cache/`), `5` (all five directories) or `q` (quit).
4. Atesor deletes each selected directory and creates it again, empty.

Without an interactive terminal, Atesor cancels the cleanup. On `native`, a choice that includes `repos` also removes the cloned repositories in the work directory on the machine. Preflight rungs 2 to 10 run before that removal. This command always exits with code 0.

## Debugging and help

| Flag | Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--preflight` | none | off | Check the native machine, then exit. |
| `--version` | none | off | Print `atesor-ai <version>`, then exit. |
| `-h`, `--help` | none | off | Print the help, then exit. |

- `--preflight` runs all 11 preflight rungs and prints each result. The exit code is 0 when all rungs pass, else 1. On the `qemu` target, Atesor prints a message and exits with code 1.
- `--version` prints the value of `__version__` in `src/__init__.py`. The release workflow writes the tag version into that file before it builds the `.deb`.
- `--help` and `--version` exit with code 0.

## In what order does Atesor process the options?

1. Atesor loads the `.env` files and copies `--target` into `ATESOR_TARGET`.
2. `--platform` (other than `auto`) sets `ATESOR_PLATFORM`. `--container` sets `ATESOR_CONTAINER`.
3. Atesor compares `--target` with the early read. Then preflight rung 1 checks the target settings. It runs for every command except `--help` and `--version`, also on `qemu`.
4. With `--optimize` or `--probe`, Atesor checks the `--emulate-cpu` or `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` value.
5. `--probe` together with `--repo` stops with code 1.
6. `--preflight` runs and exits.
7. Atesor checks the `--repo` URL.
8. `--cleanup` and `--clean-image` run. They exit, unless `--rebuild` is set.
9. `--clean-workspace` runs and exits.
10. Without `--repo`, a setup command or `--probe`, Atesor exits with code 1.
11. A rebuild of both `qemu` sandboxes runs and exits, when it applies.
12. The recipe cache check runs, unless `--setup-only`, `--force` or `--optimize` is set. A hit exits.
13. On `native`, preflight rungs 2 to 11 run.
14. `--probe` sets up the sandbox, probes the machine and exits.
15. Atesor checks the API key of the LLM provider. This step runs only for a port.
16. Atesor sets up the sandbox. `--setup-only`, and `--rebuild` without `--repo`, exit here.
17. The agents port the repository. With `--optimize`, the optimize step follows a successful port.

## Example commands

These examples use only real flags. Replace `atesor-ai` with `python3 main.py` in a source checkout.

```bash
# Build the sandbox one time (the platform comes from auto-detection)
atesor-ai --setup-only

# Port zlib and show the agent activity
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --verbose

# Port SQLite in the Debian sandbox and write a zip
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/sqlite/sqlite --platform debian --package

# Ignore the recipe cache and allow 3 attempts
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --force --max-attempts 3

# Check a native riscv64 machine
atesor-ai --target native --platform debian --preflight

# Show what the native machine supports and save the profile
atesor-ai --target native --platform debian --probe

# Port zlib on the native machine, try faster builds, and keep them in a zip
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --target native --platform debian --optimize --package

# Build and check the tunes under QEMU with a modelled CPU (no timing)
atesor-ai --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --optimize --emulate-cpu rva22u64

# Remove the Debian sandbox container and its image
atesor-ai --platform debian --clean-image
```

## How does the `atesor-ai` launcher map to `main.py`?

The `.deb` package installs `/usr/bin/atesor-ai`, a POSIX shell script. The script does these steps:

1. It checks that `/opt/atesor-ai/venv/bin/python3` exists and can run. If not, it prints `atesor-ai: bundled interpreter missing at /opt/atesor-ai/venv/bin/python3.` and a reinstall command, then exits with code 1.
2. It exports `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, so Python writes no bytecode files into `/opt`.
3. It puts `/opt/atesor-ai/app` first in `PYTHONPATH`.
4. It runs `exec /opt/atesor-ai/venv/bin/python3 /opt/atesor-ai/app/main.py "$@"`.

The launcher passes all arguments to `main.py` unchanged. Thus `atesor-ai ARGS` and `python3 main.py ARGS` take the same options and return the same exit codes. These items are different:

| Item | Source checkout | `.deb` package |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `python3 main.py` | `atesor-ai` |
| Python | your interpreter and packages | the bundled virtualenv in `/opt/atesor-ai/venv` |
| Application files | the checkout | `/opt/atesor-ai/app` |
| State home | the checkout root | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai`, default `~/.local/share/atesor-ai` |
| First `.env` search | the checkout root and its parents | `/opt/atesor-ai/app` and its parents |

`ATESOR_HOME` changes the state home for both forms. Refer to [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) and [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/).

:::caution
The `.deb` build copies `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.debian` into `/opt/atesor-ai/app`, but not `Dockerfile.native`. A native image build for the `debian` or `ubuntu` platform reads `Dockerfile.native`. Use a source checkout for that image build.
:::

The package does not contain `.github/scripts/batch_test.py`. Batch runs need a source checkout. Refer to [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

---

# Environment variables

Section: Reference
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/

Eclipse Atesor™ reads its settings from environment variables and from `.env` files. This page lists every variable that the code reads, with its default, what it controls, and the file that reads it. Some command-line flags set a variable for one run. Refer to [Command-line options](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/cli/).

## How does Atesor load `.env` files?

`main.py` loads the `.env` files at start-up, before it imports the other modules. It loads them in this order:

1. The first `.env` that python-dotenv finds. A call to `load_dotenv()` with no path starts the search in the directory of `main.py`, then goes up through each parent directory. It does not start in the current directory.
2. `$ATESOR_HOME/.env`, when `ATESOR_HOME` has a value. A value from step 1 also counts.
3. `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atesor-ai/.env`. The default is `~/.config/atesor-ai/.env`.
4. `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai/.env`. The default is `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/.env`.

No file replaces a variable that already has a value. Thus a variable in the process environment wins over all files, and an earlier file wins over a later file.

:::note
For the `.deb` package, step 1 searches `/opt/atesor-ai/app` and its parent directories, not your current directory. Put your `.env` in `~/.config/atesor-ai/`, or set the variables in the environment. The package installs the template at `/opt/atesor-ai/app/.env-example`.
:::

## LLM provider and keys

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LLM_PROVIDER` | `gemini` | The LLM provider: `gemini`, `openai`, `openrouter` or `anthropic`. Case does not matter. | `src/models.py` |
| `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | none | The API key for `gemini`. | `src/models.py`, Google SDK |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | none | The API key for `openai`. | `src/models.py`, OpenAI SDK |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | none | The API key for `openrouter`. Atesor sends it to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`. | `src/models.py` |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | none | The API key for `anthropic`. | `src/models.py`, Anthropic SDK |
| `GIT_TOKEN` | none | A token to clone private GitHub repositories. | `src/scripted_ops.py` |
| `GH_TOKEN` | none | The same as `GIT_TOKEN`. Atesor uses it when `GIT_TOKEN` is empty. | `src/scripted_ops.py` |

- Only the key of the selected provider is necessary.
- The placeholder value `your_key_here` counts as a missing key.
- Atesor checks the key only for a port, after the recipe cache check. A missing key, or a provider name that Atesor does not know, gives exit code 1.
- The `anthropic` provider also needs the Python package `langchain-anthropic`. Without it, the key check fails with exit code 1. `requirements.txt` lists the package.
- Atesor sends the git token only to `https://github.com/` URLs. It adds the header `Authorization: bearer <token>` to each clone through `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0` and `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`. It does not write the token to the git configuration of the sandbox.

Refer to [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

## Models and LLM calls

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS` | six free models, listed below | The fallback model IDs for `openrouter`, separated by commas, in order. | `src/models.py` |
| `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` | `8192` | The output-token limit of each LLM call. For `anthropic`, the limit also covers the thinking tokens of the reply. | `src/models.py` |
| `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` | `120` | The HTTP timeout of each LLM request, in seconds. | `src/models.py` |

The default fallback list is:

```text
qwen/qwen3-coder:free
openai/gpt-oss-120b:free
openai/gpt-oss-20b:free
meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free
qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct:free
nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free
```

- Atesor always adds `openrouter/free` at the end of the fallback list.
- Each OpenRouter request also sends a `models` array: the first two fallbacks that are not the primary model, then `openrouter/free`.
- `src/graph.py` and `src/llm_helpers.py` stop the wait for one LLM call after `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` plus 15 seconds.
- Exception: when the optimizer agent of `--optimize` writes code, the wait is 240 seconds. `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` does not change this value.
- `ATESOR_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` and `ATESOR_LLM_TIMEOUT` must be integers. `src/models.py` reads them at import time, so another value stops Atesor at start-up with a Python error.

No environment variable selects the model of an agent role. The models, temperatures and, for `anthropic`, the effort levels come from `MODEL_CONFIG` in `src/models.py`. Refer to [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/).

## Cost

No environment variable sets the cost limit. `should_escalate()` in `src/state.py` escalates a run when its LLM cost is more than 1.0 USD. Atesor calculates the cost of each call from its token usage. Free models cost 0. Refer to [Cost control](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/cost-control/).

Only the supervisor checks this limit, during the port. The limit does not stop the LLM calls of the optimize step. The cost of those calls still goes into the run total of the report.

## Target and native machine

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_TARGET` | `qemu` | Where the builds run: `qemu` or `native`. `--target` sets it. | `src/target.py`, `src/config.py` |
| `ATESOR_PLATFORM` | none (detection) | The sandbox distribution: `alpine`, `debian` or `ubuntu`. `--platform` sets it. | `src/platforms.py`, `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_CONTAINER` | the container name of the profile | The sandbox container name. `--container` sets it. | `src/platforms.py` |
| `REBUILD_IMAGE` | none | The value `true` forces a rebuild of the sandbox image. `--rebuild` sets it. | `main.py` |
| `ATESOR_SSH_HOST` | none | Alias mode: the ssh destination, as you type it after `ssh`. | `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_SSH_HOSTNAME` | none | Field mode: the address of the machine. | `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_SSH_PORT` | `22` | Field mode: the SSH port, from 1 to 65535. | `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_SSH_USER` | the ssh default | Field mode: the login user. | `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_SSH_IDENTITY_FILE` | none | Field mode: the path to the private key file. | `src/target.py` |
| `ATESOR_REMOTE_WORKDIR` | `~/atesor-ai` | The work directory on the machine. | `src/target.py` |

Rules for these variables:

- A value of `ATESOR_TARGET` other than `qemu` or `native` makes preflight rung 1 fail. An empty value means `qemu`.
- On `qemu`, Atesor ignores an unknown `ATESOR_PLATFORM` value and writes a warning to the log.
- On `native`, `ATESOR_PLATFORM` is necessary. Rung 1 fails without it.
- Atesor reads the `ATESOR_SSH_*` keys and `ATESOR_REMOTE_WORKDIR` only on the `native` target.
- Set alias mode (`ATESOR_SSH_HOST`) or field mode (`ATESOR_SSH_HOSTNAME` and the other field keys), not both.
- Field mode needs `ATESOR_SSH_HOSTNAME`.
- Any other `ATESOR_SSH_*` key with a value makes rung 1 fail. Atesor supports key login only.
- `ATESOR_SSH_HOST` must be one destination with no spaces and no leading `-`.
- `ATESOR_SSH_IDENTITY_FILE` must have no spaces, no quotes and no `%`.
- `ATESOR_REMOTE_WORKDIR` can use only letters, digits and the characters `.`, `_`, `/`, `~` and `-`.

In field mode, Atesor writes the SSH settings to `ssh_config` in the cache directory, with mode `0600`. Refer to [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## Paths

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_HOME` | none | The state home: the base directory for all runtime state. It also adds `$ATESOR_HOME/.env` to the `.env` search. | `src/config.py`, `main.py` |
| `XDG_DATA_HOME` | `~/.local/share` | The parent of the default state home `atesor-ai/`, and of one `.env` location. | `src/config.py`, `main.py` |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | `~/.config` | The parent of the `atesor-ai/.env` location. | `main.py` |
| `XDG_CACHE_HOME` | `~/.cache` | The parent of `atesor-ai/`, which holds the native `ssh_config`. | `src/target.py` |
| `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` | none | When this directory exists, `atesor-ai/` in it holds the ssh control sockets. Else the cache directory holds them. | `src/target.py` |

`src/config.py` selects the state home in this order:

1. `$ATESOR_HOME`, when it has a value.
2. `/workspace`, when Atesor itself runs in a container.
3. The source checkout root, when it has `.git` or `tests/` and you can write to it.
4. `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai`. The default is `~/.local/share/atesor-ai`.

Refer to [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/) for the directories under the state home.

## Package tests and run time

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT` | `600` | The time limit of the package tests, in seconds. | `src/graph.py` |
| `ATESOR_RUN_DEADLINE` | none | The kill time of the run, in epoch seconds. | `src/graph.py` |

- A limit under 60 seconds skips the package tests. Thus `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT=0` turns them off.
- A value of `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT` that is not an integer gives 600.
- With `ATESOR_RUN_DEADLINE`, the tests must end 420 seconds before that time. `batch_test.py` sets it for each child run.
- When the port ran a test command, performance mode runs the same command in each tune tree, with the same time limit.

## Performance mode

`ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` applies to `--optimize`. `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` applies to `--optimize` and `--probe`. Refer to [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET` | `3600` | The time limit of the optimize step, in seconds. | `src/optimize.py` |
| `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` | none | The `QEMU_CPU` model for `--optimize` and `--probe` on the `qemu` target. `--emulate-cpu` wins over it. | `main.py` |

Rules for `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET`:

- The time counts from the start of the optimize step, not from the start of the port.
- Atesor checks the remaining time before each step. Each tune build gets the remaining time, with a minimum of 60 seconds and a maximum of 1800 seconds.
- A value that is not a number gives 3600.
- One step needs at least 300 seconds. With less time left, Atesor skips the step. A budget under 300 seconds stops before the baseline build, with the status `not measured`.
- When the budget ends before the second check of a faster tune, the result is `not confirmed`. The report then advises a larger `ATESOR_OPTIMIZE_BUDGET`.

Rules for `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU`:

- Atesor reads it only with `--optimize` or `--probe`, and only on the `qemu` target. On `native`, Atesor ignores it.
- The value follows the rules of `--emulate-cpu`. Another value gives exit code 1.
- The value `max`, or no value, gives QEMU's `max` CPU. Atesor then builds no ISA tune.

## Logging and tracing

No Atesor variable sets the log level. Use `--verbose` for the console. The log file always records level `DEBUG`.

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2` | none | LangSmith tracing. | LangChain SDK, not Atesor code |
| `LANGCHAIN_API_KEY` | none | The LangSmith API key. | LangChain SDK, not Atesor code |

## CI only

These rows describe how the scripts in `.github/scripts/` read a variable. The `ATESOR_PLATFORM` row gives the default of `batch_test.py` only. `main.py` reads that variable as the [Target and native machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/#target-and-native-machine) table says.

| Variable | Default | What it controls | Read in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATESOR_PLATFORM` | `debian` | The default platform of a batch run. | `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` |
| `ATESOR_SETUP_STREAM` | off | `1`, `true`, `yes` or `on` shows the live output of each worker sandbox setup. | `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` |
| `NO_COLOR` | none | When it is set, the batch output has no color. | `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` |
| `ATESOR_HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT` | `30` | The HTTP timeout of each provider probe, in seconds. | `.github/scripts/check_llm_providers.py` |
| `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` | set by GitHub Actions | The file that receives the regression test summary. | `.github/scripts/report_regression.py` |

- `check_llm_providers.py` also reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `OPENROUTER_FALLBACK_MODELS`. By default, it probes all four providers.
- `batch_test.py` writes `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, `ATESOR_TARGET` (from its `--target` flag) and `ATESOR_RUN_DEADLINE` into the environment of each `main.py` child process.
- `batch_test.py` never passes `--optimize`, so the performance mode variables have no effect on a batch run.
- `release-sandbox.sh` passes `VARIANT`, `EXPLICIT_VERSION`, `BUMP_MAJOR` and `TAGS` to its own embedded Python step. Its command-line flags set them. They are not user settings.

Refer to [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

## Variables that the launcher sets

The `atesor-ai` launcher of the `.deb` package sets two variables before it starts `main.py`:

| Variable | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE` | `1` | Python writes no bytecode files into `/opt`. |
| `PYTHONPATH` | `/opt/atesor-ai/app`, then the old value | Python finds the `src` package. |

## Variables in the sandbox images

The Dockerfiles set these variables in the sandbox. The build commands in the sandbox see them. Atesor code on the host does not read them.

| Variable | Value | Images |
|---|---|---|
| `GOFLAGS` | `-buildvcs=false` | all three |
| `GOTOOLCHAIN` | `local` | all three |
| `GOPROXY` | `https://proxy.golang.org,direct` | all three |
| `GONOSUMCHECK` | `*` | all three |
| `GOPATH` | `/root/go` | all three |
| `CARGO_HOME` | `/root/.cargo` | all three |
| `RUSTUP_HOME` | `/root/.rustup` | all three |
| `CC` | `gcc` | all three |
| `CXX` | `g++` | all three |
| `CCACHE_DIR` | `/workspace/.ccache` | `Dockerfile.debian`, `Dockerfile.native` |
| `DEBIAN_FRONTEND` | `noninteractive` | `Dockerfile.debian`, `Dockerfile.native` |
| `PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES` | `1` | `Dockerfile.native` |
| `PATH` | `/root/.cargo/bin:/root/go/bin:/usr/local/go/bin`, then the base `PATH` | `Dockerfile` |
| `PATH` | `/root/.cargo/bin:/root/go/bin:/usr/local/go/bin:/usr/lib/ccache`, then the base `PATH` | `Dockerfile.debian`, `Dockerfile.native` |

The three images are `Dockerfile` (Alpine), `Dockerfile.debian` (Ubuntu jammy) and `Dockerfile.native` (Debian trixie). Refer to [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/).

## Variables that performance mode sets in the sandbox

Performance mode sets these variables for its own commands in the sandbox. They are not user settings. Do not set them yourself.

| Variable | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `QEMU_CPU` | the `--emulate-cpu` or `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` model | On `qemu`, the probe, the tune checks and the workload runs use this CPU model. |
| `CC`, `CXX` | the wrapper scripts `cc` and `cxx` in `<tree>/.atesor/` | A C or C++ tune builds through the wrappers. |
| `MAKEFLAGS` | `CC=<tree>/.atesor/cc CXX=<tree>/.atesor/cxx` | A `CC = gcc` line in a Makefile cannot replace the wrappers. |
| `ATESOR_REAL_CC`, `ATESOR_REAL_CXX` | the compiler of the tune, for example `gcc` and `g++` | The wrappers run this compiler. |
| `ATESOR_CC_FLAGS` | the flags of the tune | The wrappers add these flags after the flags of the project. |
