| `ATESOR_CC_LOG` | `<tree>/.atesor/cc.log` | The wrappers log each compiler call. |
| `GORISCV64` | the Go ISA level from the probe | The Go ISA tune. |
| `GOFLAGS` | `-buildvcs=false -pgo=<profile>` | The Go profile-guided optimization (PGO) tune. |
| `RUSTFLAGS` | a target CPU or target features from the probe | The Rust ISA or target CPU tune. |
| `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO`, `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS` | `fat`, `1` | The Rust link-time optimization (LTO) tune. |
| `CCACHE_DISABLE` | `1` | The C and C++ PGO builds do not use ccache. |
| `ATESOR_PAD` | 0 to 4096 `x` characters, random for each run | Each timed run gets another stack layout. |
| `ATESOR_INPUT` | the input file, or `/dev/null` | A Go benchmark that the optimizer agent writes reads its input from this file. |

`<tree>` is the copy of the repository that one tune builds in, for example `/workspace/repos/zlib.opt/tune2`. Refer to [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/).

---

# Exit codes

Section: Reference
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/exit-codes/

Eclipse Atesor™ returns an exit code that tells a script or a CI job how a command ended. Code 0 means success with proven riscv64 output, and code 3 means that the build commands passed but no riscv64 output is proven. This page lists every code that `main.py` returns, and the code paths that return it.

## Which exit codes can Atesor return?

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Success. For a port, the artifact scan proved riscv64 output. |
| `1` | Failure: a build that failed or escalated, a setup error, a configuration error, a failed machine probe, or a missing API key. |
| `2` | The build succeeded, but `--package` could not write the zip. The argument parser also uses code 2 for a usage error. |
| `3` | Not verified. The build commands passed, but no riscv64 output is proven. |
| `130` | You interrupted the agent run with Ctrl+C. |

The `atesor-ai` launcher passes the code of `main.py` through unchanged. The launcher itself returns 1 when its bundled interpreter is missing.

The optimize step of performance mode (`--optimize`) never changes the exit code of the port that it follows. But `--optimize` skips the recipe cache check, so a port with `--optimize` always builds, and the build decides the code. Refer to [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

## When does Atesor return 0?

- A port ends with status `SUCCESS`, and the artifact scan gives the verdict `verified`. The console shows `PORTING SUCCESSFUL! (riscv64 output verified)`. This is also true when the optimize step that follows finds no faster build or stops with an error.
- A recipe cache hit has an entry with a `verified` verdict. The console shows `CACHED (not rebuilt)`.
- `--setup-only` completes, or `--rebuild` without `--repo` completes.
- `--probe` probes the machine and writes `machine_profile_<target>.json`.
- `--cleanup` or `--clean-image` ends without `--rebuild`. The code is 0 also when the container or the image does not exist. When Docker or podman fails during the teardown, Atesor prints the error and still returns 0.
- `--clean-workspace` ends. The code is 0 also when you cancel or select an option that is not valid.
- `--preflight` passes all 11 rungs.
- `--help` or `--version` prints its text.

## When does Atesor return 1?

Configuration and arguments:

- `--target` in a short form gives a value that differs from the early read of the flag.
- Preflight rung 1 fails. For example, `ATESOR_TARGET` has a value that is not valid, or the native settings are incomplete.
- With `--optimize` or `--probe`, the `--emulate-cpu` value is not a QEMU CPU model. On `qemu` without the flag, Atesor checks the `ATESOR_QEMU_CPU` value in the same way.
- `--probe` and `--repo` are in the same command.
- `--preflight` runs on the `qemu` target, or a rung fails.
- The `--repo` URL is not a plain `http://` or `https://` URL.
- The command has no `--repo`, no setup command and no `--probe`.
- The API key of the selected provider is missing, or `LLM_PROVIDER` names an unknown provider.
- `LLM_PROVIDER` is `anthropic`, and the `langchain-anthropic` package is not installed.

Sandbox setup:

- Docker does not run or does not answer.
- The `qemu-riscv64` binfmt_misc handler is missing, and the automatic registration fails.
- The image build fails, or the native image build reaches its time limit of 5400 seconds.
- The container does not start after 2 attempts, or it fails the health check.
- The distribution in the container does not match the selected platform.
- On `native`, the container reports an architecture other than `riscv64`.
- The rebuild of both `qemu` sandboxes fails.
- On `native`, preflight rungs 2 to 11 fail before setup, or rungs 2 to 8 fail before a cleanup.

Machine probe (`--probe`):

- The sandbox setup fails, for one of the causes in the list above.
- The probe program gives no result. The console shows `ERROR: the machine probe failed:` and the cause.

Port:

- The run ends with a status other than `SUCCESS`, for example `ESCALATED` or `FAILED`. The console shows `PORTING STOPPED / FAILED`, the last error and the last 10 audit events.
- The agent run raises an error that it does not handle. The console shows `ERROR:` and the error text.

A port escalates when one of these conditions is true:

- The number of recorded errors reaches `--max-attempts`.
- The last 3 errors have the same signature.
- The last error has one of the categories `LICENSE_INCOMPATIBLE`, `REQUIRES_HARDWARE`, `ARCHITECTURE_IMPOSSIBLE`, `PERMISSION` or `DISK_SPACE`.
- The LLM cost of the run is more than 1.0 USD.

A verdict of `wrong_arch` sets the build to `FAILED` and sends it to the fixer. If no fix succeeds, the run ends with code 1.

## When does Atesor return 2?

- The port ends with status `SUCCESS`, `--package` is set, and the zip step raises an error. The console shows `Packaging FAILED`. Atesor wrote the recipe, the report and the state file before the zip step.
- The argument parser rejects the command line. Examples: an unknown option, a `--platform` or `--target` value that is not in the list, a `--max-attempts` value that is not an integer, or an option without its argument.

For a script, check the console output to know which of the two causes applies.

## What does exit code 3 mean?

Exit code 3 means "not verified". The build commands passed, but Atesor cannot prove that the build produced riscv64 machine code. Atesor returns 3 in two cases:

1. A port ends with status `SUCCESS`, but the artifact scan gives the verdict `unverified`. The console shows `PORTING FINISHED, NOT VERIFIED` and the reason.
2. A recipe cache hit has an entry without a `verified` verdict. The console shows `CACHED (not rebuilt), NOT VERIFIED` and `Exit code 3: no riscv64 output is proven for this entry.`

The artifact scan gives `unverified` in these cases:

- The build produced no riscv64 output, for example a header-only library or a package of scripts.
- The scan stopped at its file limit before it read every build output.
- The scan could not run.

Atesor never writes an unverified result to the recipe cache or to the few-shot store. With `--package`, Atesor still writes the zip, and the manifest records `"verified": false`. With `--optimize`, the optimize step records the status `skipped`, because an unverified build gives no baseline. Re-run a cached entry with `--force` to build and verify it again. Refer to [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/).

## When does Atesor return 130?

The agent run catches `KeyboardInterrupt`, prints `Interrupted by user`, and returns 130. The agent run includes the optimize step of `--optimize`. After an interrupt, Atesor writes no recipe, report or state file for the run. The `--clean-workspace` prompt also catches the interrupt, but it cancels the cleanup and returns 0. No other step of `main.py` catches the interrupt. An interrupt during the sandbox setup or the machine probe, for example, goes to Python.

## How does `batch_test.py` count the codes?

`.github/scripts/batch_test.py` maps the exit code of each `main.py` run to a status:

| Exit code | Batch status |
|---|---|
| `0` | `PASS` |
| `3` | `UNVERIFIED` |
| `130`, or a shutdown request | `CANCELLED` |
| any other code | `FAIL` |

A run that reaches the time limit of the batch gets the status `TIMEOUT`. Only `PASS` counts as a success. Refer to [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

---

# Output files

Section: Reference
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/

Eclipse Atesor™ writes its results, logs and caches under one state home. This page lists every file and folder that a run writes, where it goes, its format, and its main fields or sections. Use it to find a result, to parse a file in a script, or to clean up disk space.

## Where does Atesor write its files?

All runtime state goes under the state home. `src/config.py` selects the state home in this order:

1. `$ATESOR_HOME`, when it has a value.
2. `/workspace`, when Atesor itself runs in a container.
3. The source checkout root, when it has `.git` or `tests/` and you can write to it.
4. `$XDG_DATA_HOME/atesor-ai`. The default is `~/.local/share/atesor-ai`.

The workspace is a directory under the state home. Its name depends on the target:

| Target | Workspace |
|---|---|
| `qemu` | `<state home>/workspace` |
| `native` | `<state home>/workspace-native` |

Exception: when Atesor runs in a container on the `qemu` target and `ATESOR_HOME` has no value, the workspace is `/workspace`.

Common locations:

| How you run Atesor | State home | Workspace on `qemu` |
|---|---|---|
| `python3 main.py` in a source checkout | the checkout root | `<checkout>/workspace` |
| `atesor-ai` from the `.deb` | `~/.local/share/atesor-ai` | `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/workspace` |
| Either form, with `ATESOR_HOME` | `$ATESOR_HOME` | `$ATESOR_HOME/workspace` |

The results of the two targets never mix. They use different workspaces, different recipe cache keys and different zip names.

## Which directories does Atesor create?

`main.py` imports `src/config.py` at start-up, for every command. That import creates these directories when they are missing:

| Directory | Content |
|---|---|
| `<state home>/data/` | The recipe cache and the few-shot examples. |
| `<workspace>/repos/` | The cloned repositories, one directory for each repository name. With `--optimize`, also the `<repo>.opt/` tree. |
| `<workspace>/output/` | The recipe, the report, the state file and the patches of each run, and the machine profile of `--probe`. |
| `<workspace>/logs/` | The agent logs, the LLM call logs and the setup lock file. |
| `<workspace>/packages/` | The zip files from `--package`. |
| `<workspace>/.cache/` | Atesor creates it, but the code writes no files to it. |

On the `qemu` target, the sandbox container mounts the workspace at `/workspace`. A path such as `/workspace/repos/zlib` in a log is `<workspace>/repos/zlib` on your computer.

`--clean-workspace` also lists a `patches/` directory when it exists. The sandbox images create `/workspace/patches`, but the code writes no files to it. Atesor writes patches to `output/`.

## Which files does a run write?

| File | Directory | When Atesor writes it | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<repo>_recipe.md` | `output/` | A port that ends with `SUCCESS`, or a recipe cache hit | Markdown |
| `<repo>_report_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.md` | `output/` | The end of each agent run, for each final status | Markdown |
| `<repo>_state_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.json` | `output/` | The end of each agent run, for each final status | JSON |
| `<repo>_patches_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/` | `output/` | The end of a run in which the fixer applied a patch | Folder of `.patch` files |
| `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip` | `packages/` | `--package`, after a port that ends with `SUCCESS` | Zip |
| `machine_profile_<target>.json` | `output/` | `--probe` | JSON |
| `<repo>.opt/accepted/` | `repos/` | `--optimize`, when performance mode accepts a tune | Folder of riscv64 artifacts |
| `agent_<repo>.log` | `logs/` | Each command with `--repo` | Text log |
| `agent.log` | `logs/` | A command without `--repo` that passes the first checks, for example `--setup-only` or `--probe` | Text log |
| `agent-call_<repo>.log` | `logs/` | Each LLM call of a port | Text log |
| `agent-call.log` | `logs/` | Atesor creates it with a header when it first loads the LLM logger | Text log |
| `.container_setup.lock` | `logs/` | Each sandbox setup | Lock file |
| `recipe_cache.json` | `<state home>/data/` | A verified port, and a measured run of `--optimize` on `native` | JSON |
| `examples/<agent>_examples.json` | `<state home>/data/` | A verified port | JSON |

`<repo>` is the repository name that Atesor derives from the URL. `<target>` is `qemu` or `native`. Refer to [Command-line options](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/cli/).

When the agent run raises an error or you interrupt it, Atesor writes no recipe, report, state file or patches for that run. This rule also applies during the optimize step of `--optimize`.

## What is in the recipe?

`<repo>_recipe.md` is the replayable porting guide. Atesor writes the same file name on each run, so a new run replaces the old recipe. The file has one of three forms.

### Recipe from the summarizer

After a successful build, the summarizer agent writes the recipe with an LLM. Its prompt asks for these H2 headings, in this order:

```markdown
## Executive Summary
## Prerequisites
## Build Instructions
## Architecture Notes
## Verification
## Known Issues & Recommendations
```

- `Executive Summary`: the status and a short portability verdict.
- `Prerequisites`: the package install commands for the sandbox distribution.
- `Build Instructions`: shell commands in fenced `bash` blocks, one block for each step, in order.
- `Architecture Notes`: the arch-specific items that the project needed. The LLM can omit this section.
- `Verification`: how to check that the binaries are riscv64, with `file` or `readelf -h`.
- `Known Issues & Recommendations`: open concerns and ideas for upstream changes.

The summarizer gets the build steps that ran, the artifacts, the verification verdict and the package test result. An LLM writes this text, so Atesor does not check that the output has each heading.

### Fallback recipe

When the summarizer call fails, Atesor writes a short recipe from the build plan:

```markdown
# RISC-V Porting Recipe: <repo>

The build commands succeeded. Artifact verification: <verdict>.

### <phase name>
```

Each phase has a `bash` block with its commands. When the run has artifacts, a `### Build Artifacts Generated` list follows. The text ends with an `**Artifact verification:**` line and a `**Package tests (not gating):**` line.

### Recipe from the cache

On a cache hit, Atesor writes the recipe again from the cache entry. When the entry stores the original Markdown, Atesor copies it unchanged. Else Atesor builds a recipe from the entry fields:

- A `# RISC-V Porting Recipe: <repo>` title.
- Bullets for the repository, the build system, the architecture, the sandbox and the last build time.
- A note that the recipe comes from the cache, and that `--force` makes a full guide from a fresh build.
- `## Dependencies`, `## Build Steps` (one `###` heading and one `bash` block for each phase), `## Patches / Fixes Applied` and `## Build Artifacts`, when the entry has data for them.

## What is in the report?

`<repo>_report_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.md` describes one agent run. Atesor writes a new report for each run, also for a failed run. The report has these sections:

1. `# RISC-V Porting Report: <repo>`.
2. `## Executive Summary`: the status, the target (`qemu` or `native`), the repository URL and the time of the report.
3. `## Metrics`: a table with the build status, the total duration, the attempts, the API calls, the scripted operations, the LLM tokens (in and out) and the cost in USD.
4. `## Artifact Verification`: the verdict, the reason and the source commit. A table gives the counts of riscv64 outputs, other-arch outputs and committed foreign files. Lists show up to 20 items of each kind, the ABI warnings and the expected artifacts that the build did not produce.
5. `## Package Tests (not gating)`: the result, the command with its exit code and duration, the reason, and the last 1500 characters of the output.
6. `## Machine Profile`: the facts of the machine probe and the settings that follow from them, in a code block.
7. `## Performance Mode (--optimize)`: the result of performance mode. Refer to [Performance mode section](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/#what-is-in-the-performance-mode-section-of-the-report).
8. `## Build System Analysis`: the build system and each build phase with its commands. A `### Dependencies` part lists the build tools and the system packages.
9. `## Architecture-Specific Code`: up to 5 findings, each with its file, line and code snippet.
10. `## Patches Applied`: each patch, cut at 500 characters.
11. `## Error Resolution History`: each recorded error with its category and the first 300 characters of the message.
12. `## Recommendations`: next steps for the final status.

Atesor writes sections 6 and 7 only after the optimize step of `--optimize`. Section 6 needs a machine probe that ran. Atesor omits sections 9 to 11 when they have no data. The status text is one of these:

- `SUCCESS (riscv64 output verified)`
- `SUCCESS, NOT VERIFIED (no riscv64 output proven)`
- The final status of a run that did not succeed, for example `ESCALATED` or `FAILED`.

## What is in the state file?

`<repo>_state_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.json` is the full `AgentState` at the end of the run, as indented JSON. Enum values appear as strings, for example `"SUCCESS"`. Dates appear as strings. The top-level keys are:

| Group | Keys |
|---|---|
| Repository | `repo_url`, `repo_name`, `repo_path`, `repo_tree` |
| Planning | `task_plan`, `package_analysis`, `current_phase` |
| Build | `build_system_info`, `build_plan`, `build_status`, `tests_run` |
| Dependencies | `dependencies` |
| Architecture | `arch_specific_code` |
| Attempts | `attempt_count`, `max_attempts`, `last_successful_phase` |
| Errors | `last_error`, `last_error_category`, `last_error_severity`, `error_history`, `fixes_attempted` |
| Usage | `api_calls_made`, `api_cost_usd`, `api_tokens_in`, `api_tokens_out`, `scripted_ops_count`, `execution_start_time` |
| Caches | `context_cache`, `file_content_cache`, `command_results_cache` |
| Plan facts | `scout_build_system_result`, `scout_deps_result`, `scout_arch_issues_result` |
| Graph | `subgraph_outcome`, `messages`, `current_agent` |
| Results | `patches_generated`, `porting_recipe`, `build_artifacts`, `curated_artifacts`, `artifact_verification`, `package_tests` |
| Performance mode | `optimize_requested`, `emulate_cpu`, `cached_recipe`, `machine_profile`, `optimization` |
| Audit | `audit_trail`, `created_at`, `last_updated` |

`error_history` keeps the last 200 errors. `audit_trail` keeps the last 2000 events. The performance mode keys have these values:

- `optimize_requested`: `true` with `--optimize`.
- `emulate_cpu`: the `QEMU_CPU` model of the run, or `null`.
- `cached_recipe`: the verified recipe cache entry that became the build plan, or `null`.
- `machine_profile` and `optimization`: `null` until the optimize step runs. Refer to [Performance mode outputs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/#which-files-does-performance-mode-write).

Two keys hold the main verdicts of the port:

- `artifact_verification`: `status` (`verified`, `wrong_arch` or `unverified`), `verified`, `reason`, `source_commit`, `counts` (`riscv64`, `foreign`, `prebuilt_foreign`), the lists `riscv64`, `foreign` and `prebuilt_foreign` (up to 200 items each), `abi_warnings`, `examined`, `truncated`, `scan_error` and `expected_missing`. Each listed artifact has `path`, `type`, `arch`, `abi`, `size` and `prebuilt`.
- `package_tests`: `status` (`passed`, `failed`, `timeout`, `skipped` or `error`). After a test run, it also has `framework`, `command`, `exit_code`, `duration_seconds`, `timeout_seconds` and `output_tail` (the last 3000 characters). A `skipped` or `error` result has a `reason` instead.

Refer to [Agent state](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/agent-state/) and [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/).

## What is in the patches folder?

`<repo>_patches_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/` holds one file for each patch that the fixer applied with success: `patch_1.patch`, `patch_2.patch` and so on. Each file holds the patch text that the fixer agent wrote, in the order of application. Atesor creates the folder only when the run applied at least one patch.

## Which files does performance mode write?

`--probe` and `--optimize` write the files in this part. Refer to [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) for the steps of the optimize step.

### Machine profile

`--probe` writes `machine_profile_<target>.json` to `output/`, as indented JSON. A new probe on the same target replaces the file. The optimize step does not write this file. It keeps the same data in the `machine_profile` key of the state file. The fields are:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `native` or `qemu`. |
| `emulated_cpu` | The `QEMU_CPU` model, or `null`. |
| `extensions` | The ISA extensions that the machine runs, in lower case. |
| `vlen` | The vector register length in bits, or `null` without the V extension. |
| `core` | The identity facts: `mvendorid`, `marchid`, `mimpid`, `uarch`, `model` and `compatible`. |
| `core_name` | The name of the known core that matched, or `null`. |
| `misaligned` | The speed of misaligned scalar access: `fast`, `slow`, `emulated`, `unsupported` or `unknown`. |
| `misaligned_source` | `hwprobe`, `timing test` or `none`. |
| `misaligned_test` | The result of the timing test. |
| `cores`, `allowed_cpus` | The number of usable CPUs, and the CPU numbers that the sandbox can use. |
| `mem_kib` | The total memory in KiB, or `null`. |
| `kernel`, `libc` | The kernel release, and `glibc <version>`, `musl` or `null`. |
| `board` | The governor, the frequencies, the temperatures, the perf settings, the load and the caches. |
| `toolchains` | The facts of each compiler, plus `go` and `rust`. |
| `label` | A short ISA label, for example `rv64gc+zba+zbb`. |
| `sources` | The sources that gave facts: `cpuinfo`, `hwprobe` and `tests`. |
| `tests` | The result of each test instruction: `present`, `absent` or `error`. |
| `warnings` | Warnings in plain language. |

### The `<repo>.opt` tree

The optimize step works in `/workspace/repos/<repo>.opt/` in the sandbox, next to the clone. Before the baseline build, Atesor removes the tree of an earlier step. During the step, the tree holds these directories:

- `base/`: a copy of the verified build, built again. Atesor compares each tune with this copy.
- `tune1/`, `tune2/` and so on: one copy of the patched tree for each tune.
- In each copy, `.atesor/` holds the compiler wrappers `cc` and `cxx`. A C or C++ build logs each compiler call to `.atesor/cc.log`.
- Work directories for the second check, the PGO profiles, the generated input files and the run outputs.

At the end of the step, Atesor copies the riscv64 artifacts of the accepted tune to `accepted/`, at their paths in the tree. Then it removes the other directories. When the tree is empty at the end, Atesor removes it. The verified build in `repos/<repo>/` never changes.

Where `accepted/` stays:

- On `qemu`, the sandbox mounts the workspace. The files stay in `<workspace>/repos/<repo>.opt/accepted/` on your computer.
- On `native`, the tree is on the machine. When the command ends, Atesor removes `/workspace/repos/<repo>.opt` from the machine.
- On `native` with `--package`, Atesor first copies the tree into the local mirror, `<state home>/workspace-native/repos/<repo>.opt/`. The zip holds the files in `optimized/`.

### The optimization record

The `optimization` key of the state file holds the result of the optimize step. Its main fields are:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `status` | `accepted`, `no gain`, `not confirmed`, `not measured`, `checked` (on `qemu`), `skipped` or `error`. |
| `headline` | The answer in one line, for example `YES: ...` or `NO: ...`. The console summary shows it after `Optimized:`. |
| `reason`, `advice` | Why the step ended with this status, and a fix when Atesor has one. |
| `kind`, `machine_label`, `machine_check` | The target, the ISA label, and on `native` the result of the machine check. |
| `budget_seconds`, `duration_seconds` | The time limit and the time used, in seconds. |
| `language`, `package` | `c`, `go` or `rust`, and the package profile: `kind`, `libraries`, `programs` and more. |
| `baseline` | `build_seconds`, `same_code` and `artifacts` of the baseline copy. |
| `build_flags` | C and C++ only: `compiles`, `levels` and `lto` of the compiler calls of the baseline copy. |
| `workload` | The workload: `mode`, `command`, `description`, `origin`, and the source `files` of a harness. |
| `variants` | One record for each tune: `variant` (the settings), `verdict`, `reason`, `ratio`, `measurement` and `second_check`. |
| `accepted`, `accepted_label`, `accepted_title`, `accepted_ratio` | The accepted tune. `accepted` is `null` when no tune is accepted. |
| `accepted_dir`, `accepted_artifacts` | The sandbox path of `accepted/` and the files in it. |
| `warnings`, `notes` | Warnings and notes in plain language. |

A field that does not apply is missing or `null`. For example, a step that stops before the baseline build has no `baseline`.

### What is in the performance mode section of the report?

The report adds `## Machine Profile` with the facts of the probe and the settings that follow from them, in a code block. Then `## Performance Mode (--optimize)` has these items:

- `**Optimized**:` the headline. `**Result**:` the status and the reason. `**Fix**:` the advice, when there is one.
- `**Machine**:` the target, the ISA label, the core and the misaligned access speed.
- `**Package**:` the package type, the language, the build system, the libraries and the programs.
- `**Baseline**:` the build time of the baseline copy, and the number of riscv64 artifacts with the same code as the verified build.
- `**Workload**:`, `**Duration**:` and `**Optimized artifacts**:` when they apply.
- A table with one row for each tune. The columns are `Tune`, `Technique`, `Settings`, `Result`, `Time ratio (95% CI)` and `Details`.
- `### Warnings` and `### Notes`, with up to 30 items each.
- `### Workload source:` with the source file of a harness that the optimizer agent wrote.

The section ends with a note on the table. A time ratio below 1 means that the tune ran faster than the baseline. Only native runs measure time.

## What is in the zip package?

With `--package`, Atesor writes a zip after a port that ends with `SUCCESS`. This includes a build that is not verified.

The file name is `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip`:

- `<owner>-<repo>` comes from the last two segments of the URL, in lower case. For example, `https://github.com/madler/zlib` gives `madler-zlib`.
- `<platform>` is the profile name: `alpine` or `debian`. The `ubuntu` platform uses the `debian` profile, so its zip name has `debian`.
- On the `native` target, the platform part ends in `-native`, for example `debian-native`.
- When the file name exists already, Atesor adds `.1`, `.2` and so on before `.zip`.

Atesor writes the zip as `<name>.zip.part` and renames it at the end. A run that stops during the write leaves no partial `.zip` file. The zip holds:

```text
build_recipe.md        copy of <repo>_recipe.md
manifest.json          metadata, see below
<repo>.log             batch log, when batch_test.py wrote one
agent_<repo>.log       agent log, when it exists
optimized/             the files of the accepted tune (--optimize only)
<repo>/                the source tree of the verified build
```

The source tree has no `.git` directories and no symbolic links. On the `native` target, Atesor copies the final tree from the machine before it writes the zip. With `--optimize`, it also copies the `<repo>.opt` tree when performance mode accepted a tune.

`optimized/` holds the riscv64 artifacts of the accepted tune, at their paths in the repository tree: `optimized/<path>` is the tune's build of `<repo>/<path>`. Atesor skips symbolic links and paths outside the accepted directory.

### `manifest.json` fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `2`, or `3` with `--optimize` |
| `repo_name` | The repository name. |
| `repo_url` | The repository URL. |
| `package_stem` | The `<owner>-<repo>` part of the file name. |
| `legacy_package_stem` | The name stem that older releases used. |
| `platform` | The platform part of the file name, for example `debian-native`. |
| `created_at` | The local time, ISO 8601, in seconds. |
| `verification` | `status`, `verified`, `reason`, `source_commit`, `counts`, `abi_warnings`, `expected_missing`, `truncated` and `scan_error`. |
| `artifacts` | The riscv64 outputs that the artifact scan found. |
| `package_tests` | `status`, `framework`, `command`, `exit_code`, `duration_seconds` and `reason`. |
| `recipe_filename_in_zip` | `build_recipe.md` |
| `source_root_in_zip` | The repository name. |
| `logs_in_zip` | The names of the log files in the zip. |
| `machine` | Schema 3 only. `kind`, `emulated_cpu`, `label`, `extensions`, `vlen`, `core_name`, `misaligned`, `kernel` and `libc` from the machine probe. |
| `optimization` | Schema 3 only. The result of performance mode, see below. |

Each item in `artifacts` has `path`, `type`, `arch`, `abi`, `size` and `in_zip`. It can also have these fields:

- `role`, when the artifact curator gave the file a role, such as `primary`.
- `path_in_zip`, when the file is in the repository tree.
- `sha256`, when the file is a regular file in the zip.

An output that the build installed outside the repository tree, for example in `/usr/local/bin`, has `"in_zip": false`.

The `optimization` section of schema 3 has these fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `status` | The status of performance mode, for example `accepted` or `no gain`. |
| `kind` | `native` or `qemu`. |
| `reason` | Why performance mode ended with this status. |
| `workload`, `workload_mode`, `workload_origin` | The description, the mode and the origin of the workload. |
| `accepted`, `accepted_label`, `accepted_ratio` | The ID, the console name and the time ratio of the accepted tune, or `null`. |
| `accepted_variant` | The full settings of the accepted tune, or `null`. |
| `artifacts` | One item for each file in `optimized/`, with `path_in_zip` and `sha256`. |
| `variants` | One item for each tune, with `vid`, `label`, `technique`, `verdict` and `ratio`. |

## What is in the logs?

### Agent log

`agent_<repo>.log` records all log messages of the run from level `DEBUG` up, also without `--verbose`. Each line has this form:

```text
HH:MM:SS [LEVEL] logger.name: message
```

Atesor appends to the file. A new run of the same repository adds to the same log.

### LLM call log

`agent-call_<repo>.log` records each LLM call of a port. Atesor appends one block for each call:

```text
CALL: call_<8 hex characters>
TIMESTAMP: <ISO 8601 time>
AGENT: <role>
MODEL: <model ID>
COST: $<cost in USD>
TOKENS: in=<input tokens> out=<output tokens>
METADATA: <JSON, when present>

--- PROMPT ---
<the first 10000 characters of the prompt>

--- RESPONSE ---
<the first 10000 characters of the response>
```

A line of 80 `=` characters comes before and after each block. When Atesor cuts the prompt or the response, it adds a line with the number of characters that it removed. The calls come from the agents through `src/llm_helpers.py`, from the summarizer and from the artifact curator. With `--optimize`, the optimizer agent adds calls with `AGENT: optimizer`. Their `METADATA` has a `phase` value that starts with `optimize-`.

`agent-call.log` is the file that Atesor creates with a header line `ATESOR AI - LLM CALL LOG` when it first loads the LLM logger. A port switches to `agent-call_<repo>.log` before the first call.

### Setup lock

`.container_setup.lock` is a lock file. Each sandbox setup locks it, so that parallel batch workers do not build the same image at the same time.

## What is in the cache files?

On the first load of `src/memory.py`, Atesor copies the bundled seed files into `<state home>/data/` when they are missing: `examples/*.json` and `recipe_cache.json`. Without a bundled cache, it writes an empty cache. After that, Atesor changes only the copies in `<state home>/data/`.

Atesor writes to these files only after a verified port. A build that is not verified, or a build that fails, does not change them. Each write holds a lock file next to the data file, for example `recipe_cache.json.lock`. Atesor writes a temporary file, then renames it. Performance mode also writes to `recipe_cache.json`, as the `optimizations` field below tells.

### `recipe_cache.json`

```json
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "packages": {
    "<repo>": {
      "<sandbox>": { "...": "one entry" }
    }
  }
}
```

The sandbox key is `<profile>-riscv64`, for example `alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64`. On the `native` target, the key ends in `-native`. Each entry has these fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `repo_url` | The repository URL. When it has a value, a cache hit needs a matching URL. |
| `build_system` | The build system of the plan. |
| `architecture` | `riscv64` |
| `sandbox` | The sandbox key. |
| `last_built` | The time of the build, ISO 8601. |
| `build_plan` | `phases`, each with `name` and `commands`. |
| `dependencies` | The system packages. |
| `patches` | Up to 10 applied patches. |
| `artifacts` | Up to 20 artifacts, each with `type`, `path` and an optional `role`. |
| `build_duration_seconds` | The duration of the run. |
| `recipe_file` | `output/<repo>_recipe.md` |
| `recipe_markdown` | The full recipe text, when the run made one. |
| `verification` | `status`, `reason` and `source_commit`. |
| `optimizations` | Results of performance mode, one for each machine. Present only after a measured run of `--optimize`. |

Atesor reads entries in an older flat format and moves each one under its sandbox key, with `alpine-riscv64` as the default key. Refer to [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

The `optimizations` field follows these rules:

- Atesor adds a result only on the `native` target, only when the run had a workload, and only for the status `accepted` or `no gain`.
- Atesor adds a result only to an entry that exists already. Performance mode never creates an entry.
- The key is the core name from the machine probe, else the ISA label, else `unknown`. Results from different boards stay apart.
- Each result has `date`, `machine`, `status`, `accepted`, `ratio` and `workload`. An accepted tune adds `variant`: `label`, `technique`, `title`, `compiler`, `flags`, `env` and `pgo`.
- `variant` keeps only the settings that a later run can repeat. It drops the `-fprofile` flags and the `GOFLAGS` and `CCACHE_DISABLE` values, and keeps `pgo` as `true` or `false`.
- A new verified port of the package replaces the entry, and the old `optimizations` field with it. When that port runs with `--optimize`, Atesor adds the new result after the port.

### Few-shot example files

`<state home>/data/examples/` holds `scout_examples.json`, `fixer_examples.json`, `builder_examples.json` and `supervisor_examples.json`. After a verified port, Atesor adds learned examples:

- One scout example with the build plan.
- One builder example with the build phases.
- One fixer example for each fix that succeeded.

Each learned example gets an `id` such as `scout-auto-001`, `"source": "auto"`, a `timestamp` (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and a `sandbox` such as `debian-riscv64`. Atesor skips a duplicate example. Each file keeps up to 100 examples. When a file has more, Atesor removes the oldest learned examples first and keeps the manual ones. Refer to [Few-shot examples](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/few-shot-examples/).

## Which files does the native target add?

| File or directory | Location | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `ssh_config` | `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/atesor-ai/`, default `~/.cache/atesor-ai/` | The field-mode SSH settings, mode `0600`. Atesor writes it again on each run. |
| `cm-<process ID>-<hash>` | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/atesor-ai/` when that directory exists, else the cache directory | The ssh control socket of one Atesor process. Atesor closes it when the command ends. |
| `repos/<repo>/` | `<state home>/workspace-native/` | The local mirror. rsync copies the tree from the machine for local reads. |
| work directory | `ATESOR_REMOTE_WORKDIR` on the machine, default `~/atesor-ai` | The container mounts it at `/workspace`. |

Atesor creates `repos`, `output`, `logs` and `patches` in the work directory on the machine. After each port, Atesor removes `/workspace/repos/<repo>` on the machine. The local mirror keeps its copy. With `--optimize`, Atesor also removes `/workspace/repos/<repo>.opt`. The local mirror has a copy of that tree only after `--package`. Refer to [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

## Which other files can appear?

- `.ccache/`: `Dockerfile.debian` and `Dockerfile.native` set `CCACHE_DIR=/workspace/.ccache`. The compiler cache of the sandbox can write files there. On `qemu`, this is `<workspace>/.ccache/`. On `native`, it is in the work directory on the machine.
- `output/batch_logs/<repo>.log`: `batch_test.py` writes one log for each package, relative to its current directory. `--package` adds this file to the zip when it exists. Refer to [Batch runs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/batch-runs/).

---

# Build systems

Section: Reference
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/build-systems/

Eclipse Atesor™ finds the build system of a repository from marker files, with no LLM call. The build system selects the default build plan, the dependency scan, the package test command and the tunes of performance mode. This page lists each build system that the code detects, how Atesor detects it, the default commands, and the support level.

## What is the support level of each build system?

| Build system | Ecosystem | Support level |
|---|---|---|
| `cmake` | C, C++ | Full |
| `make` | C, C++ | Full |
| `autotools` | C, C++ | Full |
| `go` | Go modules, and GOPATH-style Go | Full |
| `meson` | C, C++ | Fallback |
| `cargo` | Rust | Fallback |
| `npm` | Node.js | Guarded |
| `pip` | Python | Detected only |
| `gradle` | JVM | Detected only |
| `maven` | JVM | Detected only |
| `bazel` | multi-language | Detected only |

The levels mean this:

- **Full**: Atesor has a default build plan that needs no LLM call. It also has a fallback plan and a package test command.
- **Fallback**: The LLM scout writes the build plan. If the scout fails, Atesor uses a built-in fallback plan. Atesor finds the package test command.
- **Guarded**: The LLM scout writes the build plan. Detection and the builder have extra checks for this ecosystem. If the scout fails, Atesor uses the discovery plan.
- **Detected only**: Atesor detects the build system and tells the LLM scout. The scout writes the plan. If the scout fails, Atesor uses the discovery plan.

All levels share the same sandbox, the same build and fix loop, and the same artifact verification. Refer to [How it works](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/how-it-works/).

## How does Atesor detect the build system?

`ScriptedOperations.detect_build_system()` in `src/scripted_ops.py` looks for these files in the repository root, in this order:

| Build system | Marker files |
|---|---|
| `cmake` | `CMakeLists.txt` |
| `autotools` | `configure.ac`, `configure.in`, `configure` |
| `make` | `Makefile`, `GNUmakefile` |
| `meson` | `meson.build` |
| `cargo` | `Cargo.toml` |
| `npm` | `package.json` |
| `pip` | `setup.py`, `pyproject.toml` |
| `go` | `go.mod` |
| `gradle` | `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts` |
| `maven` | `pom.xml` |
| `bazel` | `BUILD`, `BUILD.bazel`, `WORKSPACE` |

Each marker gives a confidence value:

- `CMakeLists.txt`, `Cargo.toml`, `configure.ac` and `go.mod` give 0.95.
- `configure` gives 0.85, but never lowers a value that is already higher.
- Each other marker adds 0.3 to its build system, up to 0.9.

Rules for the result:

- The build system with the highest confidence wins. On a tie, the build system that comes first in the table wins.
- `package.json` counts only when the root also has `package-lock.json`, or `package.json` declares a `build` script.
- When Atesor finds both `go` and `npm`, `go` wins.
- When the primary marker file is in a subdirectory, Atesor records that directory as `module_dir`. The scout and the builder use it.

### What if the root has no marker file?

Atesor tries these steps in order, and stops at the first match:

1. Atesor searches all subdirectories for `go.mod` and `Cargo.toml`. It skips vendored and test directories such as `vendor`, `third_party`, `node_modules`, `test`, `tests`, `examples` and `docs`. A Go module wins over a Cargo module. Confidence: 0.90.
2. Atesor searches the directories 1 and 2 levels below the root for `CMakeLists.txt`, `meson.build`, `configure.ac`, `configure.in`, `Makefile` and `GNUmakefile`. It skips the same vendored and test directories. The shallowest file wins, then the first file in this list. Confidence: 0.75.
3. Atesor looks for `.go` files without a `go.mod`. A match gives `go` (GOPATH style), and the plan adds `go mod init`. Confidence: 0.65.
4. No match gives `unknown`, with confidence 0.0.

For a Go module in a subdirectory, Atesor prefers the directory with the strongest signs of a program: a `main.go` file, a `cmd/` directory, and a `.go` file with `package main`.

## When does Atesor use the default plan?

After detection, the analyst agent reads the build files with an LLM. Then `heuristic_plan_node()` in `src/graph.py` decides between the default plan and the LLM scout. Atesor uses the default plan only when all of these conditions are true:

- The build system is `cmake`, `make`, `autotools` or `go`.
- The confidence is 0.5 or more.
- The analyst did not set `needs_custom_plan`.
- The scan found no `critical` arch-specific code, and fewer than 3 `high` findings.

The analyst can replace the detected build system and confidence with its own. This happens when the analyst read the files with an LLM, names a build system other than `unknown`, and has a confidence equal to or higher than the detection confidence. In all other cases, the LLM scout writes the plan.

:::note
A root `Makefile` alone gives a confidence of 0.3, which is below 0.5. The default `make` plan then needs the analyst to confirm `make` with a higher confidence.
:::

With `--optimize`, a verified entry in the recipe cache replaces this decision. The cached build plan becomes the plan, with confidence 1.0. The analyst, the default plan and the scout do not run before the first build. When the entry has no command, Atesor plans as usual. `--force` turns this off. Refer to [Command-line options](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/cli/).

## What are the default build commands?

Each plan starts with a `setup` phase. It runs one install command for the active sandbox: `<update> && <install> <packages>`. The packages come from canonical names that the platform profile maps to distribution packages. The default plan also adds the dependencies that the analyst and the scan found, when the profile knows them. The setup command has up to 15 names in total. The fallback plans install only the packages in their table.

### Default plans (no LLM)

| Build system | Setup packages (canonical) | Configure | Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cmake` | `cmake`, `gcc` | `mkdir -p build && cd build && cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` | `cd build && make -j$(nproc)` |
| `make` | `gcc` | none | `make -j$(nproc)` |
| `autotools` | `gcc`, `autotools`, `pkgconfig` | `./configure` | `make -j$(nproc)` |
| `go` | `git` | none | `go mod tidy`, then the Go build command |

The Go build command comes from the search for the `main` package:

- `go build -buildvcs=false ./<dir>` for a `main` package in a subdirectory of the module. Atesor prefers `cmd/<repository name>`, then the other `cmd/` directories, then the module root.
- `go build -buildvcs=false .` for a `main` package in the module root, for a GOPATH-style repository, and when the search finds no `main` package.
- `go build -buildvcs=false ./...` when Atesor has no search result, for example when the analyst changes the build system to `go`.
- For a repository without `go.mod`, the phase starts with `go mod init <module>` and `go mod tidy`. `<module>` is the repository URL without `https://`.

### Fallback plans (after a scout failure)

When the LLM scout gives no valid plan, `create_fallback_build_plan()` in `src/graph.py` uses the detected build system:

| Build system | Setup packages (canonical) | Configure | Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cmake` | `gcc`, `cmake` | `mkdir -p build`, then `cd build && cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` | `cd build && make -j$(nproc)` |
| `make` | `gcc` | none | `make -j$(nproc)` |
| `autotools` | `gcc`, `autotools`, `pkgconfig` | `./configure` | `make -j$(nproc)` |
| `go` | `git` | none | `go mod tidy` (and `go mod init` when needed), then the Go build command |
| `meson` | `gcc`, `meson`, `ninja` | `meson setup builddir` | `ninja -C builddir` |
| `cargo` | `rust` | none | `cargo build --release` |
| other | none | none | `make -j$(nproc)` |

- For `autotools` without a committed `configure`, the configure phase runs `autoreconf -fi` before `./configure`.
- The `autotools` setup phase also copies the gettext `.m4` files into `m4/`.
- In the `go` fallback plan, `go build .` becomes `go build -buildvcs=false ./...`. Another Go build command stays as the search gave it. The sandbox images set `GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`.
- For other build systems, a `discover` phase runs `ls -la` on the build files that exist, or a short `find` for them. Then the plan runs `make -j$(nproc)`.

:::note
Neither platform profile maps the canonical name `rust`, so the `cargo` fallback plan passes `rust` to the package manager unchanged. The sandbox images already contain a Rust toolchain from rustup.
:::

## Which package test command does Atesor run?

After a successful build, Atesor runs the tests of the package one time. The result goes into the report and the zip manifest. It never changes the result of the port. `_detect_test_command()` in `src/graph.py` checks these cases in order:

1. In `build/`, `_build/` or `builddir/`: a `CTestTestfile.cmake` file gives `ctest --test-dir <dir> --output-on-failure`.
2. In the same directories: a `meson-info` directory gives `meson test -C <dir> --print-errorlogs`.
3. A root `go.mod` gives `go test ./...`, when the plan is `go` or the root has no `Makefile`.
4. A root `Cargo.toml` gives `cargo test --release`, when the plan is `cargo` or `rust`, or the root has no `Makefile`.
5. A root `Makefile` with a `check:` target gives `make check`. Else a `test:` target gives `make test`.

Without a match, the result is `skipped`. The time limit is 600 seconds. Refer to [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/) for `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT`.

A build plan from the LLM scout never runs tests. Atesor removes these commands from the scout plan, because the package tests run after the build:

- `ctest`, `pytest` and `python -m pytest`.
- `go test`, `cargo test`, `meson test` and `npm test`.
- `make`, `gmake` or `ninja` with the target `check`, `test` or `tests`.
- `cmake --build` with `--target check`, `--target test` or `--target tests`.

Atesor ignores a leading `cd <dir> &&` and leading `NAME=value` words when it reads a command. A phase that has no command left goes out of the plan. A scout plan with only test commands counts as a scout failure, so Atesor uses the fallback plan.

## What else does Atesor do for each build system?

The scan reads the dependencies of some build systems from their files, with no LLM call:

| Build system | Dependency scan |
|---|---|
| `cmake` | `find_package()`, `pkg_check_modules()` and `pkg_search_module()` in `CMakeLists.txt` |
| `make` | `-l<name>` flags in `Makefile` |
| `go` | `require` lines in `go.mod` |
| `cargo` | `[dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml` |
| `npm` | `dependencies` and `devDependencies` in `package.json` |
| `pip` | `requirements.txt` |
| `autotools`, `meson`, `gradle`, `maven`, `bazel` | none |

The builder also changes or retries some commands with no LLM call. This table shows examples for each build system. Refer to [Recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/) for the full list.

| Build system | Examples of builder adjustments |
|---|---|
| `cmake` | When a bare `make` finds no makefile next to `CMakeLists.txt`, Atesor retries with `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build -j1`. When the CMake cache has a stale compiler path, Atesor deletes `build/` and sets `/usr/bin/gcc` and `/usr/bin/g++`. |
| `make` | When the root has no makefile, a plain `make` runs in the shallowest subdirectory that has one, 1 or 2 levels below the root. |
| `autotools` | When the repository has no committed `configure`, Atesor runs a bootstrap before `./configure`. |
| `go` | Atesor adds `-buildvcs=false` to `go build` and `go install`, and removes it from other Go commands. It retries with `-mod=mod` or after `go mod tidy` for some module errors. |
| `meson` | `ninja` runs with `-j1` after a suspected out-of-memory kill. |
| `cargo` | `cargo` runs with `-j 1` and `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1` after a suspected out-of-memory kill. |
| `npm` | The `npm run <script>` guard. `npm install`, `npm ci` and `npm run` get `--jobs 1` after a suspected out-of-memory kill. |
| `pip` | `pip install` runs with `MAKEFLAGS=-j1` after a suspected out-of-memory kill. |

The autotools bootstrap uses the first case that applies:

1. The repository has `autogen.sh`, `buildconf`, `buildconf.sh` or `bootstrap`. Atesor runs `sh <script>`.
2. The repository has `configure.ac` or `configure.in`, and `m4/gettext.m4`. Atesor copies the gettext `.m4` files into `m4/`, then runs `aclocal -I m4 -I /usr/share/aclocal && autoconf`.
3. The repository has `configure.ac` or `configure.in`. Atesor runs `autoreconf -fi`.

The `npm run <script>` guard works like this:

- When `package.json` does not declare the script, Atesor uses the first declared script of `build`, `prod`, `compile` and `dist`.
- When none of them exists, Atesor skips the command.

After a suspected out-of-memory kill, Atesor also runs `make` with `-j1` and `MAKEFLAGS=-j1`, and Go with `-p 1` and `GOMAXPROCS=1`. Exit code 137 always counts as an out-of-memory kill.

Performance mode (`--optimize`) also reads the build system of the plan. It treats `go` as Go, `cargo` and `rust` as Rust, and every other build system as C or C++. The language selects the tunes:

- C and C++: core tuning (`-mtune`), machine ISA (`-march`), vector ISA, optimization level, link-time optimization and a second compiler, all through wrapper scripts. Then profile-guided optimization on top of the best tune.
- Go: the `GORISCV64` level, then profile-guided optimization.
- Rust: `RUSTFLAGS` with a target CPU or target features, then link-time optimization.

A tune repeats the commands of the verified build in a copy of the tree. It does not repeat package installs, install steps, source control steps and writes outside the tree. Refer to [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

## Which tool packages does each sandbox install?

The platform profiles in `src/platforms.py` map canonical names to distribution packages:

| Canonical name | Alpine | Debian and Ubuntu |
|---|---|---|
| `cmake` | `cmake` | `cmake` |
| `make` | `make` | `make` |
| `ninja` | `ninja` | `ninja-build` |
| `meson` | `meson` | `meson` |
| `autotools` | `automake autoconf libtool` | `autoconf automake libtool` |
| `gcc`, `g++` | `build-base` | `build-essential` |
| `pkgconfig` | `pkgconf` | `pkg-config` |
| `python3` | `python3 py3-pip` | `python3 python3-pip python3-dev` |
| `node` | `nodejs npm` | `nodejs npm` |
| `java` | `openjdk17` | `openjdk-17-jdk` |
| `git` | `git` | `git` |
| `go` | `go` | no entry |
| `rust` | no entry | no entry |

All three sandbox images contain Go 1.26.5 in `/usr/local/go` and Rust 1.99.0 from rustup in `/root/.cargo`. The profiles have no `rust` entry and the Debian profile has no `go` entry, so that a distribution package does not hide the newer toolchain. `Dockerfile.native` also installs `clang-19`, `lld-19`, `llvm-19` and `libclang-rt-19-dev` for the second compiler and the clang profiles of performance mode. Refer to [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/) and [Add a platform](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-platform/).

---

# Development setup

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/development-setup/

This page tells you how to prepare a source checkout of Eclipse Atesor™ for development. You clone the repository, install the Python dependencies, add an LLM key, build the riscv64 sandbox and run a port with `python3 main.py`.

## What do you need?

- A host with Docker. A host that is not RISC-V also needs QEMU emulation for riscv64. See [Requirements](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/requirements/).
- Python 3.10 or later. The CI workflows use Python 3.11.
- `git`.
- An API key for one LLM provider: Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter or Anthropic.

## Get the source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor
cd atesor
```

The project is not a pip package. You run `main.py` from the checkout, and every test command sets `PYTHONPATH=.`.

## Install the Python dependencies

`CONTRIBUTING.md` installs the dependencies with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. A virtual environment isolates these packages from the system Python:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

`requirements.txt` holds the runtime packages (LangChain, LangGraph, the Docker SDK, `filelock` and others) and the development tools `pytest`, `pytest-asyncio`, `black` and `flake8`. The `.dockerignore` file excludes `.venv/` and `venv/`, so the build context of the sandbox image does not include the environment.

## Add an LLM key

Copy the template, then edit `.env`:

```bash
cp .env-example .env
```

Set `LLM_PROVIDER` and the key for that provider. `src/models.py` checks these names:

| `LLM_PROVIDER` | Key variable |
| --- | --- |
| `gemini` (default) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |

For `anthropic`, the key check also needs the `langchain-anthropic` package. `requirements.txt` lists it.

`.gitignore` lists `.env`, so git does not track the file. Never put a key in a tracked file. For the other settings, see [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/) and [Environment variables](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/environment-variables/).

## Install the merge driver for the recipe cache

Run this script one time in each clone:

```bash
sh .github/scripts/setup_git_merge_driver.sh
```

The script changes only your clone: `.git/config` and `.git/info/attributes`. After it, git merges `data/recipe_cache.json` by meaning. When both sides change the same recipe, the newest recipe wins. Without the driver, git stops at a conflict for that file, and `.gitattributes` gives the manual steps.

## Enable RISC-V emulation

On a host that is not RISC-V, register the QEMU handlers one time:

```bash
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all
```

`main.py` checks for the `qemu-riscv64` handler before it prepares the sandbox. If the handler is missing, `main.py` tries one time to register it with `tonistiigi/binfmt --install riscv64`.

## Build the sandbox

```bash
python3 main.py --setup-only                     # Alpine
python3 main.py --setup-only --platform debian   # Debian/Ubuntu
```

Without `--platform` and without `ATESOR_PLATFORM`, Atesor uses the Alpine sandbox. The first image build runs under QEMU emulation, and the code comments give 15 to 45 minutes for it. Later commands use the image again. For the sandbox profiles, see [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/).

## Where does a source checkout keep its state?

A writable source checkout keeps the runtime state in the checkout itself:

- `workspace/` holds the cloned repositories, the outputs and the logs. The native target uses `workspace-native/`.
- `data/examples/` holds the few-shot examples.
- `data/recipe_cache.json` holds the recipe cache.

Set `ATESOR_HOME` to move the state to another directory. Git tracks the files under `data/`, so a verified port changes tracked files. Check `git status` before you commit. Commit these files only when you want to share the result. See [Few-shot examples](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/few-shot-examples/) and [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

## Run a port from source

```bash
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --verbose
```

The bundled recipe cache can hold an entry for the package. A cache hit renders the recipe again and makes no LLM call and no build. Add `--force` to run the full pipeline:

```bash
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --verbose --force
```

For a real riscv64 machine instead of QEMU, see [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/). To run the tests and the lint check, see [Tests and checks](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/tests/).

## Which rules must a change keep?

`CONTRIBUTING.md` lists these architecture rules. A change that breaks one of them can break the graph.

1. `AgentState` is the single source of truth. Each node changes it in place and never makes a new one.
2. Each LangGraph node has the decorator `@agent_node(AgentRole.X)` from `src/graph.py`.
3. Each LLM call uses `invoke_llm(llm, messages, timeout=120)` and then `log_llm_call(...)`. Do not call `llm.invoke()` directly.
4. Each shell command uses `execute_command()` in `src/tools.py`. Do not call `subprocess` directly for sandbox work.
5. Path constants come from `src/config.py`. Do not hardcode `/workspace` or host paths.
6. Distro logic uses `get_active_profile()` in `src/platforms.py`. Do not hardcode `atesor-ai-sandbox`, `apk` or `apt-get`.
7. Writes to the recipe cache and the few-shot files hold a `filelock` lock.
8. Go builds pass `-buildvcs=false`.

## How do you submit a change?

1. Make a branch from `main`, or from `dev` if a maintainer asks for it.
2. Make focused commits with clear messages. `CONTRIBUTING.md` prefers the Conventional Commits style: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`.
3. Run `PYTHONPATH=. pytest` and make sure that all tests pass.
4. Open a pull request on [GitHub](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor). Say what changed and why. List new environment variables, new CLI flags and breaking changes. Add the test output for each new feature.
5. Keep each pull request small. Split a change that touches more than one concern.

## What about PROJECT.md?

`llm.txt` names `PROJECT.md` as the canonical context file of the project. On `main`, `.gitignore` lists `PROJECT.md`, so a fresh clone does not contain the file. Describe each behaviour change in the pull request, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks.

---

# Tests and checks

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/tests/

Eclipse Atesor™ has a pytest suite in `tests/` that needs no LLM key, no sandbox container and no network. This page gives the CI commands, the lint and format tools, and the code that each test file guards.

## How do you run the tests?

Run the tests from the root of the checkout. The project is not a pip package, so every test command sets `PYTHONPATH=.`:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. pytest                                   # full suite
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_graph_routing.py       # one file
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_state.py::TestStateMutation::test_add_error_updates_all_fields_and_attempt
PYTHONPATH=. pytest -k memory                         # by name
```

`pyproject.toml` sets the pytest options:

- `testpaths = ["tests"]`: pytest collects tests only from `tests/`.
- `addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"`: pytest prints a short summary of each test that did not pass, and an unknown marker is an error.

Run the suite in a git clone. A session fixture in `tests/conftest.py` runs `git ls-files data` and fails the run if a test changes a tracked file under `data/`.

Some tests run small programs on the host. `TestHarnessKitOnThisHost` in `tests/test_workload.py` needs `gcc`, `ar`, `nm`, `ldd` and `bash` on the host. Other classes skip when `gcc`, `nm`, `ldd`, `git` or `rsync` is missing.

## What does CI run?

The `Regression Tests` workflow (`.github/workflows/regression-tests.yml`) runs on each push to `main` or `dev`, on each pull request into these branches, and on manual dispatch. It uses Python 3.11 and installs `requirements.txt`. Each test category runs as a separate job:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m pytest <files of the category> -q --junitxml=results-<category>.xml
```

A `report` job then runs this script:

```bash
python3 .github/scripts/report_regression.py --results-dir test-results --tests-dir tests
```

The script prints one results table and also writes it to the run summary. It fails in these conditions:

- A category has a failure or an error.
- A `tests/test_*.py` file is in no category, or in more than one category.
- A category names a file that does not exist.
- The run has no `results-*.xml` file.

The `report` job also fails when one of the category jobs failed.

:::caution
When you add a test file, add it to exactly one category in `.github/workflows/regression-tests.yml`. Otherwise the `report` job fails.
:::

The `Package .deb` workflow (`.github/workflows/package-deb.yml`) builds the release package. Before the build, it runs the full suite and a lint check:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m pytest -q
python3 -m flake8 main.py src/ tests/ .github/scripts/
```

## Which lint and format checks apply?

`CONTRIBUTING.md` sets these coding standards for all Python in the repository:

- PEP 8, with a hard limit of 79 characters for each line.
- Indentation of 4 spaces, with no tabs.
- Double quotes for strings.
- Type hints on each public function and method.
- Google-style docstrings on each public module, class, function and method.
- Import order by isort: standard library, then third-party, then local, with a blank line between the groups.
- `snake_case` for variables, functions and modules, `PascalCase` for classes, `UPPER_SNAKE` for constants.
- Few comments. Add a comment only when the reason for the code is not clear from the code.

Run the checks from the root of the checkout:

```bash
python3 -m flake8 main.py src/ tests/ .github/scripts/
black src/ tests/ main.py
isort src/ tests/ main.py
```

The tools read their settings from the repository:

| Tool | File | Settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| flake8 | `setup.cfg` | `max-line-length = 79`, `docstring-convention = google`, ignores `E203`, `W503` and `D107`, ignores `D102` in `tests/`, excludes `workspace`, `workspace-native`, `artifacts`, `data` and caches |
| black | `pyproject.toml` | `line-length = 79`, `target-version = ["py310"]` |
| isort | `pyproject.toml` | `profile = "black"`, `line_length = 79` |

`requirements.txt` lists `black` and `flake8`. It does not list `isort`, so install it yourself before you use it.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` says that CI does not enforce the linters yet. The `Regression Tests` workflow has no lint step. The `Package .deb` workflow runs `flake8`, so a lint error stops a release build.

## Which test file guards which code?

The table follows the categories of the `Regression Tests` workflow.

| Category | Test file | What it guards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| state-and-routing | `test_state.py` | `AgentState` helpers, enum names, `classify_error` patterns and their order, escalation checks |
| state-and-routing | `test_graph_routing.py` | Routing for init, cached recipe, analyst, heuristic plan, supervisor, finish and the build-fix subgraph, and the heuristic plan node |
| state-and-routing | `test_graph_agent_node.py` | The `agent_node` decorator: rate-limit retry and error escalation |
| graph-agents | `test_graph_agents.py` | The analyst, init, scout, fixer, builder, cached-recipe, optimize and terminal nodes, the read-only investigation of the fixer, expected-artifact checks and the auto-learning step |
| graph-agents | `test_graph_validators.py` | Validators for build plans, fix commands and fixer replies, fallback plans, command rewriters, the package test phase and the helper functions of the builder heuristics |
| execution-tools | `test_tools.py` | Command validation, package-manager helpers, Docker calls and patch application, with mocked subprocesses |
| execution-tools | `test_platforms.py` | Platform profiles: helpers, detection, overrides and name corrections |
| execution-tools | `test_config.py` | Workspace paths and Docker detection in `src/config.py` |
| execution-tools | `test_security_hardening.py` | The command whitelist for each command segment, single fix commands, secret values kept out of the argument list, file writes kept in the repository tree, unsafe repository URLs |
| llm-and-memory | `test_models.py` | API key checks, model pools, OpenRouter fallback lists, cost calculation, the Anthropic provider |
| llm-and-memory | `test_memory.py` | Few-shot examples, auto-learning, the recipe cache, the performance mode results in the recipe cache |
| llm-and-memory | `test_llm_helpers.py` | The validated LLM call with retry and fallback, and the reply format of Claude models |
| llm-and-memory | `test_llm_logger.py` | The LLM audit log, with one log file for each repository |
| llm-and-memory | `test_data_files.py` | The JSON files under `data/`: no duplicate keys, the recipe cache merge and the git merge driver |
| repo-analysis | `test_scripted_ops.py` | The scripted analysis, on small fake repositories on disk |
| repo-analysis | `test_evidence.py` | The repository evidence for LLM prompts |
| repo-analysis | `test_knowledge.py` | The system knowledge text for prompts |
| artifacts-packaging | `test_artifact_scanner.py` | The ELF and archive scan program, which runs with the host `python3` on files with real ELF and ar headers |
| artifacts-packaging | `test_artifact_curator.py` | Rule-based and LLM artifact curation |
| artifacts-packaging | `test_packager.py` | The zip package and its manifest, with the schema 3 sections of performance mode |
| cli-main | `test_main.py` | The CLI in `main.py`: sandbox preparation, reports, cleanup, the native environment, and `--optimize`, `--emulate-cpu` and `--probe` |
| regression-suites | `test_concurrency.py` | Parallel workers: one image build for N workers, the container pool, parallel clones, parallel recipe cache writes |
| regression-suites | `test_masterplan_fixes.py` | Fixes for groups of failed packages, the toolchain pins in the Dockerfiles, and the package URLs in `full.json` |
| regression-suites | `test_plan_remaining.py` | The planner that skips packages that a monthly release already holds, and the helpers `missing_pkgs.py` and `slice_pkgs.py` |
| regression-suites | `test_resource_lifecycle.py` | Log file handles, the Docker client and temporary patch files are closed or removed on each path. The clone token header stays out of command strings and the git config. |
| regression-suites | `test_shard_planning.py` | Shard counts and slices for the batch and retry workflows |
| native-target | `test_target.py` | Target selection and the SSH settings |
| native-target | `test_preflight.py` | The native preflight and its use in `main.py` |
| native-target | `test_sandbox.py` | The exec command line, secrets and transport errors |
| native-target | `test_mirror.py` | The local copy of the repositories on the native machine |
| native-target | `test_batch_test.py` | `batch_test.py`: the native target (worker count, machine probe, `--target`), the toolchain probe, the run deadline, the lock for each repository, the platform choice and the exit code |
| performance-mode | `test_machine.py` | The machine probe in `src/machine.py`, the machine profile, and the rules that turn the profile into flags |
| performance-mode | `test_workload.py` | The package profile and the workload choice in `src/workload.py`: the checks of the agent replies, the sizing on the baseline and the harness build |
| performance-mode | `test_bench.py` | The statistics, the grammar for workload commands, the timing protocol and the runner program in `src/bench.py` |
| performance-mode | `test_optimize.py` | The tunes, the replay of the build, the gates and the full flow in `src/optimize.py`, with a fake sandbox |

## How do you write a test?

- Put the test in the file for the module that you change. `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for one test file for each `src/` module.
- Add a test for each bug fix and for each new public function.
- Most files use `unittest.TestCase`. Some files use plain pytest classes and functions.
- Write files to the `tmp_path` fixture, never to `data/` or `workspace/`.
- Do not start Docker, open a network connection or call an LLM. Mock `execute_command`. The fixture `stub_execute_command` in `tests/conftest.py` replaces it in one module.

The autouse fixtures in `tests/conftest.py` run for each test:

| Fixture | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `_guard_tracked_data_files` | Fails the session if a test changes a tracked file under `data/` |
| `_no_package_test_phase` | Sets `ATESOR_PACKAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT=0`, so `finish_node` runs no package tests |
| `_clear_memory_instances` | Clears the cached few-shot memory before and after each test |
| `_restore_active_profile` | Sets the Alpine profile, so no test runs a real `docker exec` to detect the platform |
| `_reset_target_cache` | Clears the cached target (`qemu` or `native`) |
| `_reset_mirror_state` | Clears the state of the native mirror |
