# Add a platform

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-platform/

A platform profile tells Eclipse Atesor™ how one Linux distribution works inside the riscv64 sandbox. It holds the package manager, the package names, the libc and the Dockerfile. This page shows how to add a profile, from the Dockerfile and the `PlatformProfile` entry in `src/platforms.py` to the tests.

## Which platforms exist today?

`PROFILES` in `src/platforms.py` holds three keys and two profiles:

| Key | Profile | libc | QEMU Dockerfile | Native Dockerfile |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alpine` | `ALPINE_RISCV` | musl | `Dockerfile` | `Dockerfile` |
| `debian` | `DEBIAN_RISCV` | glibc | `Dockerfile.debian` | `Dockerfile.native` |
| `ubuntu` | `DEBIAN_RISCV` | glibc | `Dockerfile.debian` | `Dockerfile.native` |

The `ubuntu` key uses the Debian profile, because the two distributions use the same package names. For how a user selects a platform, see [Sandboxes](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/).

## What is in a platform profile?

`PlatformProfile` is a frozen dataclass. Each field has one job:

| Field | Alpine value | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `"alpine"` | The `PROFILES` key and the `--platform` value. It also gives the sandbox key `<name>-riscv64` for the recipe cache and the few-shot examples. |
| `display_name` | `"Alpine Linux (riscv64, musl)"` | Console output and prompts |
| `libc` | `"musl"` | `src/knowledge.py` adds musl advice only when the value is `musl` |
| `target_triplet` | `"riscv64-alpine-linux-musl"` | Prompts |
| `dockerfile` | `"Dockerfile"` | The image for the QEMU target |
| `native_dockerfile` | `"Dockerfile"` | The image for the native target |
| `image_name` | `"atesor-ai-sandbox:latest"` | The image tag |
| `container_name` | `"atesor-ai-sandbox"` | The default container name |
| `pkg_install` | `"apk add"` | The install command |
| `pkg_update` | `"apk update"` | The index update command |
| `pkg_lock_file` | `"/tmp/apk.lock"` | The `flock` file that puts parallel installs in sequence |
| `package_map` | `{"zlib": "zlib-dev", ...}` | Canonical name to distro package name |
| `name_corrections` | `{"liblzma-dev": "xz-dev", ...}` | A wrong package name to the correct name |
| `extra_notes` | list of strings | Notes for the system knowledge part of the prompts |

Two helper methods use these fields:

- `install_cmd(packages)` returns `"<pkg_update> && <pkg_install> <packages>"`.
- `resolve(canonical)` returns the `package_map` value, or the canonical name when the map has no entry.

The code reads the package map in these places:

- The dependency resolution in `src/scripted_ops.py`.
- The heuristic build plan.
- The missing-header recovery in the builder.
- The prompts.

`execute_command()` in `src/tools.py` applies `name_corrections` to each package command before the command runs.

## Step 1: Write the Dockerfile

Add `Dockerfile.<distro>` in the root of the repository. Use the existing files as models. The sandbox needs these items:

1. A riscv64 base image. Use `FROM --platform=linux/riscv64` with a fully qualified image name. `main.py` also builds with `platform="linux/riscv64"`. Podman on a native machine can have no short-name alias, so the Alpine file uses `docker.io/library/alpine:latest`.
2. The build tools, `git` and `python3`. The artifact scanner runs a `python3` program inside the sandbox.
3. The `flock` and `timeout` commands. `execute_command()` wraps package commands with `flock` and each command with `timeout --signal=KILL`.
4. Go from the go.dev riscv64 tarball, with the `GO_VERSION` and `GO_SHA256` build arguments and a `sha256sum -c -` check. Set `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, `GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false`, `GOPROXY`, `GONOSUMCHECK` and `GOPATH=/root/go`.
5. Rust from rustup, with the `RUST_TOOLCHAIN` build argument, `CARGO_HOME=/root/.cargo` and `RUSTUP_HOME=/root/.rustup`.
6. A `PATH` that holds `${CARGO_HOME}/bin`, `${GOPATH}/bin` and `/usr/local/go/bin`.
7. `WORKDIR /workspace` and the directories `/workspace/repos`, `/workspace/output`, `/workspace/logs` and `/workspace/patches`.
8. `HEALTHCHECK ... CMD gcc --version || exit 1`, and `CMD ["tail", "-f", "/dev/null"]` so that the container does not stop and the agent can use it.

Use the same Go and Rust versions as `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.debian`. The tests check that these two files pin the same versions.

Performance mode (`--optimize`) compares GCC with a second compiler when the image has one. The probe looks for `clang` and `clang-19` to `clang-22`. `Dockerfile.native` installs `clang-19`, `lld-19`, `llvm-19` and `libclang-rt-19-dev` for this comparison. Without a usable clang, performance mode leaves out the clang tune. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).

:::caution
A Dockerfile for the native target must not use `COPY` or `ADD`. The native build sends the Dockerfile with an empty build context.
:::

Do not map `rust` to a distro package. On purpose, the Alpine profile has no `rust` key, and the Debian profile has no `go` key and no `rust` key. The distro packages are older, and they can hide the toolchains of the image on `PATH`.

## Step 2: Add the profile

Add a `PlatformProfile` constant and a `PROFILES` entry in `src/platforms.py`. Use the `ID` value of `/etc/os-release` in the image as the key and as `name`. `detect_platform()` finds that `ID` in `PROFILES`. For an unknown `ID`, it returns the Alpine profile.

This skeleton shows the shape. Replace each `<...>` value:

```python
DISTRO_RISCV = PlatformProfile(
    name="<distro>",
    display_name="<Distro> (riscv64, glibc)",
    libc="glibc",
    target_triplet="<riscv64 target triplet>",
    dockerfile="Dockerfile.<distro>",
    native_dockerfile="Dockerfile.<distro>",
    image_name="atesor-ai-sandbox-<distro>:latest",
    container_name="atesor-ai-sandbox-<distro>",
    pkg_install="<install command>",
    pkg_update="<index update command>",
    pkg_lock_file="/tmp/<distro>.lock",
    package_map={
        "cmake": "cmake",
        "zlib": "<zlib development package>",
    },
    name_corrections={
        "zlib1g-dev": "<zlib development package>",
    },
    extra_notes=[
        "<distro advice for the prompts>",
    ],
)


PROFILES: Dict[str, PlatformProfile] = {
    "alpine": ALPINE_RISCV,
    "debian": DEBIAN_RISCV,
    "ubuntu": DEBIAN_RISCV,
    "<distro>": DISTRO_RISCV,
}
```

Add the new constant to `__all__` too. If the distribution has problems that the LLM must know about, add them to `extra_notes` or to `src/knowledge.py`.

## Step 3: Connect the CLI and the batch runner

The profile alone does not make the platform available everywhere. The docstring of `src/platforms.py` names the minimum: a `PROFILES` entry, a Dockerfile, the `--platform` choices in `main.py` and `target.NATIVE_PLATFORMS`. Change these places:

| File | Place | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main.py` | `--platform` argument | Add the name to `choices=["alpine", "debian", "ubuntu", "auto"]` and to the help text. |
| `src/target.py` | `NATIVE_PLATFORMS` and `_load_native()` | Add the name to the tuple. The native target accepts only the `ATESOR_PLATFORM` values in it. The error text in `_load_native()` names `alpine, debian or ubuntu`. |
| `main.py` | `expected` in `_provision_sandbox_locked()` and `_NATIVE_DISTROS` | These maps list the `os-release` IDs that a container may report for each profile. A profile that is not in a map accepts only its own name. Add an entry only when the container reports another ID. |
| `main.py` | `rebuild_all_sandboxes()` | This function rebuilds `alpine` and `debian` only. Add the platform if `--rebuild --setup-only` must rebuild it too. |
| `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` | `_PLATFORM_CONTAINERS` | Add the base container name. This map also gives the `--platform` choices of the batch runner. |
| `.github/scripts/batch_test.py` | `_MIN_TOOLCHAIN` | Add the minimum Go and Cargo versions. The batch runner rebuilds a worker container that has older toolchains. |

The batch workflows in `.github/workflows/` have jobs for `debian` and `alpine` only. A CI job for a new platform is a separate change.

## Step 4: Check the package manager code

If the distribution uses `apk` or `apt-get`, the code below works without a change. For another package manager, check each of these places:

- `CommandValidator` in `src/tools.py`: the allowed first words include `apt-get`, `apt`, `apk`, `yum` and `dnf`.
- `_is_pkg_command()` in `src/tools.py`: it decides which commands get the `flock` wrapper, the name corrections and the removal of distro Go and Rust packages. It knows `apk`, `apt-get`, `apt` and `dpkg` only.
- `_is_pkg_lock_error()` in `src/tools.py`: it finds lock errors from `apk` and `apt-get` and starts the retry.
- `_strip_bundled_toolchain_packages()` in `src/tools.py`: it removes distro Go and Rust packages from `apt-get`, `apt` and `apk` install commands.
- The missing-package recovery in `builder_node()` in `src/graph.py`: it reads the package list after `apt-get install -y` or `apk add`.
- The sandbox health check in `src/scripted_ops.py`: it runs `apt-get update` only for `debian` and `ubuntu`.

## Step 5: Add the tests

1. In `tests/test_platforms.py`, add tests for the new profile. Copy the pattern of the existing tests: `install_cmd`, `resolve`, `libc`, the detection from `ID=<distro>` in `/etc/os-release`, and the name corrections.
2. In `tests/test_main.py`, add the platform to `expected` in `TestNativeDockerfiles.test_choice_per_platform_and_target`. The test compares each profile with its QEMU and native Dockerfile.
3. In `tests/test_masterplan_fixes.py`, check the Dockerfile tests. `TestRustToolchainBakedIn` and `TestGoToolchainPin` read `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.debian`. `TestPreflightGateTracksImages` maps each `_MIN_TOOLCHAIN` platform to `Dockerfile` for `alpine` and to `Dockerfile.debian` for all others. Change that map when you add a platform to `_MIN_TOOLCHAIN`.
4. In `tests/test_target.py`, `test_platform_is_required_on_native` uses `fedora` as a platform that the native target rejects. Change that value if your new platform is `fedora`.
5. Run the tests:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_platforms.py tests/test_main.py tests/test_masterplan_fixes.py tests/test_tools.py tests/test_target.py
```

If you add a new test file, add it to one category in `.github/workflows/regression-tests.yml`. See [Tests and checks](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/tests/).

## Step 6: Build and try the sandbox

```bash
python3 main.py --setup-only --platform <distro>
python3 main.py --repo https://github.com/madler/zlib --platform <distro> --verbose
```

The new sandbox key `<distro>-riscv64` has no few-shot examples and no recipe cache entries. The first ports on the platform run with no examples in the prompts. Each verified port then adds examples for the new key. To use the platform on a real riscv64 machine, see [Native RISC-V machine](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/native-riscv/).

---

# Add a recovery heuristic

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-heuristic/

A recovery heuristic is a fixed rule in the builder of Eclipse Atesor™. It finds a known failure in the output of a build command, runs a repair, and runs the build command again. It makes no LLM call, so it also works when the LLM provider is rate-limited. This page shows where the heuristics are, the pattern that they follow, and how to test a new one.

## Where are the heuristics?

All heuristics are in `builder_node()` in `src/graph.py`. Their helper functions are module-level functions above `builder_node()`. For the full list with the trigger, the action and the limit of each heuristic, see [Recovery heuristics](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/recovery-heuristics/).

`builder_node()` has two kinds of heuristic:

- **Rewrites before a command runs.** The builder changes `optimized_cmd`, the copy of the command that it runs. Examples: the autotools bootstrap when the repository has no committed `./configure`, and the redirect of `make` to the directory that holds the makefile.
- **Retries after a command fails.** These are in the `if not result.success:` block. Each retry checks the output of the failed command, runs a repair, and runs the command again.

The builder checks the retries in code order. A specific signature must come before a generic one. For example, the suspected-OOM check matches any exit code 137, so a retry for a specific exit-137 failure must come before it.

## Which pattern does a retry follow?

Most retries use the same steps. This template shows them. Replace the `<...>` parts and the helper name:

```python
# In builder_node(), inside `if not result.success:`,
# before the code writes the error record.
if "<signature>" in (result.stderr or "").lower() and (
    _builder_retry_allowed(state, f"<key>:{command}")
):
    retry_command = _my_repair_command(optimized_cmd)
    retry_result = execute_command(retry_command, cwd=state.repo_path)
    state.cache_command_result(retry_command, retry_result)
    state.log_scripted_op("retry_build_command")
    if retry_result.success:
        logger.info("Resolved <failure> by <repair>")
        phase.commands[phase.commands.index(command)] = retry_command
        continue
    result = retry_result
```

Each line has a reason:

1. **The signature check.** Match a text that only this failure prints. Read `result.stderr`, and use `result.exit_code` when the text is not enough.
2. **`_builder_retry_allowed(state, key)`.** The function stores the key in `state.context_cache["builder_retry_keys"]` and returns `True` only the first time. Put the command in the key, so the retry runs one time for each command in the whole run. Some older retries do not use this guard. Use it in each new retry.
3. **`execute_command()`.** Each shell command uses this function. It runs the command in the sandbox and applies the `CommandValidator` whitelist.
4. **`state.cache_command_result()` and `state.log_scripted_op()`.** The result goes in the command cache. The operation goes in the audit trail and in the count of scripted operations in the report. Performance mode (`--optimize`) reads the command cache to find the command that really ran for each plan command. It runs these commands again for the baseline and for each tune.
5. **`phase.commands[...] = retry_command`.** On success, the builder writes the repaired command into the build plan. The recipe cache and the learned examples then hold the command that worked. A retry that installs a package and then runs the same command again leaves `phase.commands` unchanged.
6. **`continue`.** The builder goes to the next command.
7. **`result = retry_result`.** On failure, the later retries and the error record see the newest output.

When no retry succeeds, the builder writes an error record with the category from `classify_error()` in `src/state.py`, sets `build_status` to `FAILED`, and returns. While attempts remain, the LLM fixer then gets the error.

## Which rules apply to the repair command?

- Use `get_active_profile()` from `src/platforms.py` for package names and install commands. `profile.install_cmd(packages)` and `profile.resolve(name)` give the distro form. Do not hardcode `apk` or `apt-get`.
- Keep the command inside the `CommandValidator` whitelist. In `builder_node()`, only the Go toolchain download calls `execute_command(..., validate=False)`. Its comment gives the reason: the code builds that command from a checked version, not from LLM text.
- Use two paths when the heuristic reads files. `_to_host_path(state.repo_path)` gives the host path for a file check. Commands that run in the sandbox need the container path under `/workspace`.
- Go build commands keep `-buildvcs=false`.
- Log the event. Most existing retries write a `logger.warning()` line when they fire and a `logger.info()` line when they succeed.

## How do you test a heuristic?

Test the helper function first. Then test the code in `builder_node()` that calls it. The tests need no Docker and no LLM.

1. Put the detection and the command rewrite in small helper functions. Examples are `_is_suspected_oom()`, `_serialize_build_command()` and `_resolve_header_to_packages()`.
2. Test each helper in `tests/test_graph_validators.py`. The classes `TestSuspectedOOM`, `TestSerializeBuildCommand`, `TestHeaderResolution` and `TestBuilderRetryAllowed` are models.
3. If `execute_command()` validates the repair command, check that the validator accepts it. `TestAutotoolsBootstrap.test_bootstrapped_commands_pass_the_validator` in `tests/test_masterplan_fixes.py` does this with `CommandValidator().is_safe(command)`.
4. Test the code in `builder_node()` with a fake `execute_command`. `TestBuilderCMakeCacheCleanup` in `tests/test_graph_agents.py` is the model. It makes a `BuildPlan` with one phase, patches `graph.execute_command`, `graph._to_host_path` and `graph.predict_build_issues`, calls `graph.builder_node(state)`, and checks the list of commands that ran.
5. Run the tests:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_graph_validators.py tests/test_graph_agents.py tests/test_masterplan_fixes.py
```

## Does the failure also need a new error category?

A heuristic repairs a failure. An error category tells the supervisor how to react when no repair works. To add a category pattern, add a branch to `classify_error()` in `src/state.py`. The order matters: put a specific pattern before a generic one. Add a test for the pattern in `tests/test_state.py`.

For the rules that each change must keep, see [Development setup](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/development-setup/). For the scripted analysis that runs before the build, see [Scripted operations](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/scripted-ops/).

---

# Few-shot examples

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/few-shot-examples/

A few-shot example is a short case that worked before. Eclipse Atesor™ adds the examples that match best to an LLM prompt, so that the model sees a known pattern. Atesor keeps the examples in JSON files under `data/examples/`, one file for each agent, and adds new examples after each verified port.

## Which files are there, and which code reads them?

`src/memory.py` loads the files with the `AgentMemory` class. The schema description is in `data/examples/README.md`.

| File | Format | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scout_examples.json` | v2.0 | The scout prompt in `scout_node()` |
| `fixer_examples.json` | v2.0 | The fixer prompt in `fixer_node()` |
| `builder_examples.json` | v2.0 | No prompt. Runs add examples, but no prompt uses them. |
| `supervisor_examples.json` | legacy v1.0 (`context`, `expected_output`) | No code. The supervisor routes by rules and makes no LLM call. |

Each v2.0 file has the keys `version`, `description`, `general_guidelines` and `examples`. No code in `src/` reads `general_guidelines`.

On `main` at commit `e28f0d0`, the files hold these examples:

| File | Examples | Manual | Auto-learned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scout_examples.json` | 52 | 8 | 44 |
| `fixer_examples.json` | 35 | 12 | 23 |
| `builder_examples.json` | 51 | 6 | 45 |
| `supervisor_examples.json` | 10 | no `source` field | none |

## Where does a run read and write the files?

Atesor uses the `data/examples/` directory under its state home:

- A writable source checkout uses its own `data/examples/`. Git tracks these files.
- An installed `atesor-ai` uses `$ATESOR_HOME/data/examples/`, or `~/.local/share/atesor-ai/data/examples/` when `ATESOR_HOME` is not set.

When `src/memory.py` loads, it copies each bundled file into the state home if the file is not there. It never replaces a file that exists.

## What does an example look like?

All v2.0 examples share these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | A unique name, for example `scout-001`. Auto-learned examples use `<agent>-auto-NNN`. |
| `name` | A readable name |
| `tags` | Words for the relevance score, for example `["go", "cgo"]` |
| `build_system` | The build system, for example `cmake`, `go`, `autotools` or `make` |
| `source` | `manual` or `auto`. A missing value counts as `manual`. |
| `repo_name` | The repository that the example comes from |
| `sandbox` | `alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64` |
| `timestamp` | The date, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `reasoning` | Why the pattern applies |

Each agent adds its own fields:

- **Scout**: `trigger` (for example `build_system`, `has_main`, `main_path`, `module_dir`) and `plan` (a list of `phases`, each with `name` and `commands`).
- **Fixer**: `error_pattern` (a Python regular expression) and `fix` (`analysis`, `strategy`, and `actions` with `type` and `command`).
- **Builder**: `phases` and an optional `timeout_recommendation`.

This fixer example comes from `data/examples/README.md`:

```json
{
  "id": "fixer-001",
  "name": "Missing pkg-config module",
  "tags": ["dependency", "pkgconfig"],
  "build_system": "cmake",
  "sandbox": "debian-riscv64",
  "error_pattern": "No package 'zlib' found",
  "fix": {
    "analysis": "The development package is missing.",
    "strategy": "Install the canonical distro package.",
    "actions": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "apt-get install -y zlib1g-dev"}
    ]
  },
  "reasoning": "zlib1g-dev provides zlib.pc on Debian/Ubuntu."
}
```

## How does Atesor choose the examples for a prompt?

The scout and the fixer call `format_few_shot_examples()` with at most 2 examples and at most 2000 characters. `AgentMemory.get_relevant_examples()` then does these steps:

1. It removes each example from a different sandbox. The sandbox of the run is `<platform>-riscv64`. The `ubuntu` platform uses the Debian profile, so its sandbox is `debian-riscv64`. An example with no `sandbox` counts as `alpine-riscv64`.
2. It gives a score to each example that it keeps. The table below lists the rules.
3. It caps each score at 1.0 and keeps only examples with a score above 0.
4. It returns the examples with the highest scores.

| Match | Score |
| --- | --- |
| Same build system | +0.5 |
| The fixer `error_pattern` matches the error message (case-insensitive) | +0.4 |
| Each tag that occurs in the error message | +0.15 |
| Same `has_main` value | +0.1 |
| Same `module_dir` | +0.15 |
| Both have a `module_dir`, but different | +0.05 |
| The project uses cgo and the example has the tag `cgo` | +0.2 |
| Same sandbox | +0.25 |

The scout context holds `build_system`, `has_main`, `main_path` and `module_dir`. The fixer context holds `build_system` and `error_message`. No caller sets `has_cgo`, so the cgo rule adds no score.

If no example matches the sandbox, the prompt gets no examples. An `error_pattern` that is not a valid regular expression adds no score.

## How do runs add examples?

`finish_node()` calls `_save_learning_data()` after a successful build. Only a verified port adds examples: the build must succeed, and the artifact scan must prove riscv64 output. An unverified or wrong-architecture build adds nothing.

| Agent | What a verified port adds |
| --- | --- |
| Scout | One example: name `Auto: <repo> (<build system>)`, tags `[<build system>, <repo>]`, the `trigger` and the `plan` phases |
| Fixer | One example for each fix that worked: the first 80 characters of the error message as an escaped regular expression, the strategy, and each executed command as an action |
| Builder | One example with the phases. `timeout_recommendation` is `600s` for more than 2 phases, else `120s`. |

The same step writes the recipe cache entry. See [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/). Performance mode (`--optimize`) adds no few-shot example. After a native measurement, it can add its result to the recipe cache entry.

`save_learned_example()` writes each example with these rules:

- It needs `name` and `build_system`. Without them it saves nothing.
- It sets `sandbox` from the active platform when the field is empty.
- It skips a duplicate. In the same sandbox, an example is a duplicate when one of these conditions is true:
  - It has the same `repo_name` and `build_system`.
  - It has the same set of commands (scout and builder only).
  - It has the same `error_pattern` and `build_system` (fixer only).
- It sets `id` to `<agent>-auto-NNN`, one above the highest existing auto number, `source` to `auto` and `timestamp` to the date.
- It holds a file lock, `<file>.lock` next to the JSON file, and replaces the file in one atomic step.

## What is the cap?

`MAX_EXAMPLES_PER_AGENT` in `src/memory.py` is 100. When a file holds more than 100 examples after a save, Atesor keeps all manual examples and removes the oldest auto-learned examples first, by `timestamp`.

:::caution
When a file goes above 100, Atesor keeps only the entries with `source` set to `manual` or `auto`. It removes an entry with another `source` value. It never removes a manual entry, so a file with more than 100 manual entries stays above the cap.
:::

## How do CI runs merge new examples?

The `batch-port` workflow collects the `data/` changes of all shards. `.github/scripts/merge_data_artifacts.py` merges the example files by `id`. A `manual` entry wins over an entry that is not manual. Between two entries of the same kind, the newer `timestamp` wins. The workflow then opens a draft pull request with the merged `data/` files.

## How do you add an example by hand?

1. Choose the file for the agent: `scout_examples.json` or `fixer_examples.json`. No prompt uses builder examples, and no code reads `supervisor_examples.json`.
2. Give the example a unique `id` that does not have the `<agent>-auto-` form. The manual scout examples use `scout-000` to `scout-007`, and the manual fixer examples use `fixer-000` to `fixer-011`.
3. Set `source` to `manual`, or leave the field out. Atesor never removes a manual example at the cap.
4. Set `sandbox` to `alpine-riscv64` or `debian-riscv64`. Without the field, the example counts as Alpine and never appears in Debian or Ubuntu prompts.
5. Use the package manager of that sandbox in each command: `apk` for Alpine, `apt-get` for Debian and Ubuntu.
6. For a fixer example, write one command in each action. The fixer validators reject a chained fix command, so a chained example teaches the model a form that fails.
7. Keep the file valid JSON. If `json.load()` fails, Atesor logs an error and loads no examples for that agent.
8. Run the tests:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_memory.py tests/test_data_files.py
```

`tests/test_data_files.py` fails when a JSON object under `data/` holds the same key twice.

For how the prompts use the examples, see [LLM layer](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/llm-layer/).

---

# Change the docs

Section: Contributing
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/docs/

The Eclipse Atesor™ documentation is a set of Markdown pages in the repository of the project website. This page tells you where the pages are, how to view a change on your computer, and which writing rules apply to each page.

## Where are the pages?

The website repository is [eclipse-atesor/project-website](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/project-website). The documentation pages are in `site/src/content/docs/docs/`. Each folder is one section of the sidebar, and each file is one page:

| File | URL |
| --- | --- |
| `site/src/content/docs/docs/guides/sandboxes.md` | `/atesor/docs/guides/sandboxes/` |
| `site/src/content/docs/docs/contributing/docs.md` | `/atesor/docs/contributing/docs/` |

The sections are `introduction`, `getting-started`, `guides`, `architecture`, `reference`, `contributing` and `project`. Each page also has an edit link that opens its source file on GitHub.

## How do you view a change on your computer?

1. Clone the repository:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/project-website
   cd project-website/site
   ```

2. Install the packages and start the local server:

   ```bash
   npm install
   npm run dev
   ```

3. Open http://localhost:4321/atesor/docs/ in a browser. The server shows each saved change.
4. Run `npm run build` to check that the full site builds.
5. Open a pull request on GitHub.

Maintainers publish the site with `npm run deploy`.

## What is in the page header?

Each page starts with frontmatter with exactly these keys:

```yaml
---
title: Install Atesor
description: One sentence, 160 characters or fewer, that says what the page is about.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---
```

- `title` is the page title. Do not repeat it as a `#` heading.
- `description` is one sentence of 160 characters or fewer.
- `sidebar.order` sets the position of the page in its folder.

## How is a page built?

- Use plain Markdown in a `.md` file. Do not use MDX, imports or components.
- Start the body with a short answer paragraph of 1 to 3 sentences. It says what the topic is and why a reader needs it. Search engines quote this paragraph, so it must make sense alone.
- Use `##` headings and lower levels. Phrase a heading as the question that a user asks, where it is natural.
- Give each code block a language tag: `bash`, `text`, `python`, `toml`, `json`, `markdown`, `dockerfile` or `yaml`.
- Use tables for reference data such as flags, environment variables and exit codes. Keep the cells short.
- Use the Starlight asides `:::note`, `:::tip`, `:::caution` and `:::danger`.
- Write internal links as absolute paths with the base and a trailing slash, for example `/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/`.
- Write external links as full `https` URLs. The source repository is `https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor`. Never use `github.com/akifejaz/atesor-ai`, because that address returns 404.
- Write as much as the topic needs and no more. Reference pages can be long. A concept page has about 300 to 900 words.

## Which writing rules apply?

The pages use ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. The rules are:

- Use the active voice and name the actor: "Atesor clones the repository".
- Use simple tenses only: present, simple past and simple future.
- Write one instruction in each sentence. An instruction has 20 words or fewer. A description has 25 words or fewer.
- Do not stack more than 3 nouns. Use one word for one meaning, and do not change between synonyms.
- Keep the articles and the verbs. Do not drop words to save space.
- Use a numbered list for steps. Use a bulleted list for 3 or more conditions or items.
- Keep each paragraph on one topic, with 6 sentences or fewer.
- Define a technical term the first time that you use it, if it is not common English.
- Keep code, commands, flags, file paths, identifiers, log lines and error text exactly as they are in the code. Put them in backticks or code blocks.
- Use the plain voice of an engineer. Do not use marketing words, slogans, rhetorical questions in body text, exclamation marks or emojis.
- Do not use em dashes or en dashes. Use a colon, a comma, parentheses or a new sentence.

## How do you name the project?

- The first mention of the project in the body of a page is `Eclipse Atesor™`. After that, write `Atesor`.
- Do not write "ATESOR" or "Atesor AI" as the project name.
- The command and the package are `atesor-ai`, in code font.
- Write `RISC-V` for the architecture family. The architecture name in code and in tool output is `riscv64`.

## How do you keep a page correct?

1. Check each fact against the code on the `main` branch. Read the CLI flags in `main.py`, the environment variables with `grep -rn "getenv\|environ" src main.py`, the graph nodes and routing in `src/graph.py`, and the exit codes in `main.py`.
2. When the README and the code disagree, the code is correct. The architecture section of the README is out of date.
3. Do not add numbers that the code does not give. Do not write success rates, counts of ported packages or average times. You can use a count that you make from the code yourself, such as the number of graph nodes.
4. Do not write a fact that you cannot check.
5. Describe future behaviour only on the [Roadmap](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/roadmap/) page.

---

# Releases

Section: Project
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/releases/

Eclipse Atesor™ publishes two kinds of release on [GitHub](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/releases). An application release holds the `atesor-ai` Debian package. A monthly build release holds the packages that the CI workflows ported to riscv64, each zip with its recipe.

## Which releases exist?

On 2026-10-15, the release list holds these entries:

| Kind | Tag | Title | Published |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Application | `v0.2.0` | atesor-ai 0.2.0 | 2026-10-01 |
| Monthly builds | `builds-2026-10`, `builds-2026-10-01` to `builds-2026-10-03` | October 2026 builds, builds 01 to 03 | from 2026-10-01 |
| Monthly builds | `builds-2026-09` | September 2026 builds | 2026-09-08 |
| Monthly builds | `builds-2026-08` | August 2026 builds | 2026-08-04 |
| Monthly builds | `builds-2026-07`, `builds-2026-07-01` | July 2026 builds, builds 01 | from 2026-07-02 |
| Monthly builds | `builds-2026-06`, `builds-2026-06-01`, `builds-2026-06-02` | June 2026 builds, builds 01 and 02 | from 2026-06-04 |
| Earlier | `beta` | atesor-v1.2.0 | 2026-06-17 |
| Earlier | `v1.0-beta` | atesor-v1.0.0 | 2026-04-23 |

The two earlier releases have no assets. Their notes describe a setup from the source tree.

## Which features are on main but not in v0.2.0?

`v0.2.0` is the latest application release. On 2026-10-15, two features came to `main` after it:

- Performance mode (`--optimize`). See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/).
- The Anthropic LLM provider (`LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic`). See [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/).

The `v0.2.0` package does not include them. To use them, run Atesor from a source checkout. See [Development setup](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/development-setup/).

## What is an application release?

An application release holds the Debian package of the `atesor-ai` command. The `v0.2.0` release has two assets:

- `atesor-ai_0.2.0_amd64.deb`
- `atesor-ai_0.2.0_amd64.deb.sha256`

The release notes say that the workflow built the package from commit `38d85b4da4c751626e54e73efac157f430ef9360` on `ubuntu:22.04`. `packaging/deb/README.md` says that the package targets Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian-based systems with `python3.10`. The build container sets the architecture, so the `v0.2.0` package is for `amd64`.

The `Package .deb` workflow (`.github/workflows/package-deb.yml`) makes an application release when a maintainer pushes a tag of the form `vX.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z-<suffix>`. The workflow does these steps:

1. It takes the version from the tag (`v0.2.0` gives `0.2.0`) and writes it into `src/__init__.py`.
2. It runs the test suite with `PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m pytest -q`.
3. It runs `python3 -m flake8 main.py src/ tests/ .github/scripts/`.
4. It builds the package with `packaging/deb/build_deb.sh`.
5. It checks the package with `packaging/deb/validate_deb.sh`, which runs 9 checks in a clean container.
6. It writes the SHA-256 file and the release notes, and publishes the release.

To install the package, see [Install](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/install/).

## How do you check the application package?

1. Download the `.deb` file from the [v0.2.0 release](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/releases/tag/v0.2.0).
2. Calculate the SHA-256 value:

   ```bash
   sha256sum atesor-ai_0.2.0_amd64.deb
   ```

3. Compare the value with the `SHA256` line in the release notes. The `.sha256` asset holds the same value. The workflow wrote that file in the `dist/` directory, so the file name in it starts with `dist/`. For this reason, `sha256sum -c` looks for the package in `dist/`.
4. After the install, check the version:

   ```bash
   atesor-ai --version
   ```

   The command prints `atesor-ai 0.2.0`.

5. Check the installed files against the checksums in the package:

   ```bash
   dpkg -V atesor-ai
   ```

   `packaging/deb/README.md` says that the build writes `DEBIAN/md5sums`, so that `dpkg -V` can check each installed file.

## What is a monthly build release?

A monthly build release holds zip files of packages that the batch workflows ported to riscv64. The `release-zips` action (`.github/actions/release-zips/action.yml`) publishes them with these rules:

- The tag is `builds-YYYY-MM`, and the title is `<Month YYYY> builds`.
- GitHub limits a release to 1000 assets. When the release for the month is full, the action continues in an overflow release `builds-YYYY-MM-NN`, with the title `<Month YYYY> builds NN`. `NN` starts at `01`.
- Each new month starts again with the base tag.
- Each repository has one zip for each platform in a month. Before an upload, the action deletes older zips of the same repository and platform from all releases of that month.
- The file name is `<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip`. The platform is `alpine` or `debian`.

The `ATESOR AI Batch Porting Tests` workflow (`batch-port.yml`) and the `batch-port-retry` workflow upload the zips. The batch workflow runs a full sweep on both platforms each Saturday at 01:17 UTC. It also runs one on the first day of each month at 01:07 UTC. Maintainers can also start it by hand. A full run skips the packages that a release of the current month already holds for that platform, unless the run sets the `force_all` input. The retry workflow runs after each batch run and builds the packages that the batch run did not produce.

The [package index](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/downloads/) on this site lists the packages of the monthly build releases.

## What is in a package zip?

`src/packager.py` writes each zip with this layout:

```text
<owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip
├── build_recipe.md     the porting recipe
├── manifest.json       the verification verdict and the riscv64 outputs
├── <repo>.log          the batch log of the package, if there is one
├── agent_<repo>.log    the debug log of the run, if there is one
├── optimized/          the files of the accepted tune (--optimize only)
└── <repo>/             the source tree, without .git/ and symbolic links
```

For a run without `--optimize`, `src/packager.py` writes `"schema_version": 2` in `manifest.json`, with these main fields:

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `repo_url`, `platform`, `created_at` | Where the source came from, the sandbox and the time of the zip |
| `verification.status` | The verdict of the artifact scan |
| `verification.verified` | `true` only when the scan proved riscv64 output |
| `verification.source_commit` | The commit of the source that the build used |
| `artifacts` | One entry for each riscv64 output: `path`, `type`, `arch`, `abi`, `size`, `in_zip`, and for a file in the zip, `path_in_zip` and `sha256` |
| `package_tests` | The result of the package tests. These tests never decide the port. |

A run with `--optimize` writes `"schema_version": 3`. It adds a `machine` section and an `optimization` section. When Atesor accepts a tune, the zip also holds the `optimized/` folder. The batch workflows do not pass `--optimize`, so the zips of the monthly build releases use schema 2.

For the verdicts, see [Verification](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/architecture/verification/). For the output files of a local run, see [Output files](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/output-files/).

## How do you check a package zip?

The release notes of the monthly builds give no check procedure. The manifest gives you the data for one:

1. Download the zip from the release, or find it in the [package index](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/downloads/).
2. Extract the zip:

   ```bash
   unzip <owner>-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>-<platform>.zip -d port
   ```

3. Read `port/manifest.json`. Make sure that `verification.verified` is `true`. A zip can come from a build whose commands passed but that proved no riscv64 output. For that build, `verified` is `false`.
4. For each entry in `artifacts` with `"in_zip": true`, calculate the SHA-256 value of the file and compare it with `sha256`:

   ```bash
   sha256sum port/<repo>/<path_in_zip>
   ```

An output that the build installed outside the source tree, for example in `/usr/local/bin`, has `"in_zip": false` and no `sha256` value.

# Roadmap

Section: Project
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/roadmap/

This page lists the work that the Eclipse Atesor™ sources on `main` describe as planned. Nothing on this page is in a release, and the sources give no dates for it. For what Atesor can do today, see [Limitations](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/introduction/limitations/).

## Where does the roadmap come from?

The [source repository](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor) has no roadmap file. On `main`, only `README.md` states a plan.

## Which items are planned?

| Item | State on `main` | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| More build systems | The README lists Make, CMake, Meson, autotools, Cargo and Go modules, and says that more build systems will follow. | `README.md` |

For the build systems that Atesor supports, see [Build systems](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/reference/build-systems/).

Performance mode and the Anthropic provider are finished features, not plans. See [Performance mode](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/optimize/) and [Configure the LLM](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/getting-started/configure-llm/). [Releases](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/releases/) lists the features that are on `main` but not in `v0.2.0`.

## How do you follow the roadmap?

- Read the commits on `main` in the [source repository](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor).
- Watch the [releases](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/releases). See [Releases](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/releases/) for the release types.
- Ask on the [developer mailing list](https://accounts.eclipse.org/mailing-list/atesor-dev) or in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/issues).

# Governance

Section: Project
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/governance/

Eclipse Atesor™ is an Eclipse Foundation project in incubation, under the OpenHW Group. The code is under the MIT licence. This page tells you who makes decisions, how you can contribute or become a committer, and where the project communicates.

## What is the status of the project?

- **Foundation**: Atesor is a project of the Eclipse Foundation. The project ID is `openhw.atesor`.
- **Parent**: the project is under the OpenHW Group.
- **Phase**: incubation. The [Eclipse Foundation Project Handbook](https://www.eclipse.org/projects/handbook/) describes the phases of a project.
- **Licence**: MIT. The `LICENSE` file is in the root of the [source repository](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor), and each module in `src/` carries the header `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT`.

The official project data is on the project pages of the Eclipse Foundation:

- [Project page](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/openhw.atesor)
- [Who is involved](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/openhw.atesor/who)

## Who makes decisions?

Atesor follows the Eclipse Foundation Development Process, like each Eclipse project. The handbook describes the process and the roles:

- **Committers** have write access to the project repositories. They review contributions and merge them.
- **Project leads** lead the project and represent it in the Eclipse Foundation processes.

The [Who is involved](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/openhw.atesor/who) page lists the current project leads and committers.

## How do you contribute?

Any person can contribute through a pull request. `CONTRIBUTING.md` lists these ways to help:

- Port a package and submit the recipe.
- Add a new platform profile. See [Add a platform](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/add-a-platform/).
- Improve the error classification in `classify_error()` in `src/state.py`.
- File a bug report for a package that fails in a repeatable way.
- Improve prompts, tests or documentation. See [Change the docs](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/docs/).

To prepare a checkout and submit a change, see [Development setup](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/contributing/development-setup/). The handbook describes what the Eclipse Foundation asks of each contributor.

## How do you become a committer?

The existing committers of an Eclipse project elect new committers. The [Eclipse Foundation Project Handbook](https://www.eclipse.org/projects/handbook/) describes the election and what a nominee needs.

## Where does the project communicate?

| Channel | Use |
| --- | --- |
| [atesor-dev mailing list](https://accounts.eclipse.org/mailing-list/atesor-dev) | Development discussion |
| [GitHub issues](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/issues) | Bug reports and other problems |
| [Pull requests](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/atesor/pulls) | Code and data changes |
| [project-website](https://github.com/eclipse-atesor/project-website) | Changes to the website and these docs |

## What does a bug report contain?

`CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for these items when a package fails to build:

- The exact `main.py` command.
- The URL of the package.
- The sandbox profile: `alpine` or `debian`.
- The related part of `workspace/logs/agent_{repo}.log`.
- The related part of `workspace/logs/agent-call_{repo}.log`, the LLM transcript.
- The `AgentState` snapshot from `workspace/output/{repo}_state_*.json`, if there is one.

For other problems, open an issue with the steps that show the problem again.

For the origin of the name, see [About the name](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/name/).

# About the name

Section: Project
URL: https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/project/name/

The name Eclipse Atesor™ comes from Rosetta, read from right to left. Rosetta is the binary translator that Apple uses to run programs built for one processor architecture on another. Atesor has the same goal, a working program on a new architecture, but it takes the other route: it builds the program from source as native riscv64 code.

## Where does the name come from?

1. Start with `ROSETTA`.
2. Read it from right to left: `ATTESOR`.
3. Drop one `T`: `ATESOR`.

The project team chose to drop the second `t`. The result is a short name that is easy to say and to search for.

## Why right to left?

Rosetta is named after the Rosetta Stone. The stone carries one decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. In 1822 it helped Jean-François Champollion read Egyptian hieroglyphs.

The Egyptians usually wrote hieroglyphs from right to left. Signs of people and animals face the start of the line, so the reader knows the direction. When you read Rosetta in the same direction, you get Atesor.

## How is Atesor different from Rosetta?

| | Rosetta | Atesor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | A compiled binary for another architecture | The source code of a package |
| Method | Translates machine code before or while the program runs | Builds the package natively on riscv64 and repairs build failures |
| Output | The same binary, translated on each machine | A native riscv64 binary and a recipe that anyone can replay |
| Lifetime | A transition aid: Apple limits Rosetta from macOS 28 | The native build stays valid |

Apple advises users to replace translated apps with native versions. Atesor does that work for RISC-V: it produces the native version.

## Is there a second meaning?

Yes. With one `t`, the name is close to the Spanish verb *atesorar*. The Real Academia Española defines it as "to gather and keep money or things of value". *Atesoro* means "I treasure".

Atesor keeps what it learns. Each verified port goes into the recipe cache, and each successful fix can become a few-shot example for later runs. See [Recipe cache](https://eclipse.dev/atesor/docs/guides/recipe-cache/).

## What does the logo show?

The logo has three parts:

- **A stone with one cut corner.** It recalls the broken top of the Rosetta Stone. On a chip package, a cut corner also marks pin 1.
- **One line in three rows.** The line starts on the right and reverses direction on each row, like boustrophedon, an old way of writing where each line turns back. The three rows recall the three scripts on the stone. The 45-degree bends are the bends of a trace on a circuit board.
- **An open ring and a solid pad.** The line starts at an open ring, the source, and ends at a solid pad, the native riscv64 binary.

## Sources

- [Rosetta (software)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_(software)), Wikipedia
- [Using Intel-based apps on a Mac with Apple silicon](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102527), Apple Support
- [Rosetta Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone) and [Egyptian hieroglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_hieroglyphs), Wikipedia
- [Boustrophedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boustrophedon), Wikipedia
- [atesorar](https://dle.rae.es/atesorar), Diccionario de la lengua española (RAE)

:::note
Rosetta is a product name of Apple Inc. Atesor is not related to Apple or to the Rosetta Stone language-learning products.
:::

---

## Colours

| Name | Hex | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Granodiorite | `#1B1E22` | The mark on light backgrounds; dark surfaces |
| Granodiorite deep | `#111316` | Dark page background |
| Chalk | `#ECEEEF` | Text and the mark on dark backgrounds |
| Paper | `#F2F2EF` | Light page background |
| Egyptian blue | `#2142B0` | The pad of the mark, buttons and links on light backgrounds |
| Egyptian blue, light | `#8CA3FF` | The pad, accents and links on dark backgrounds |
| Malachite | `#2E9B6F` light, `#3FBF88` dark | "Verified riscv64" only |

## How do I use the logo?

- Keep clear space on all sides, at least the size of the cut corner.
- Use the full mark at 24 pixels or larger. Below 24 pixels, use the favicon.
- Use the dark-background files on dark backgrounds.
- Do not rotate, stretch, outline or shade the mark.
- Do not change its colours, other than to the one-colour file.
- Do not put the mark on photos or busy patterns.
- Do not set "atesor" in a font as a logo. Use the wordmark file.

## How do I write the name?

- The first time on a page, write **Eclipse Atesor™**. After that, write **Atesor**.
- Do not write "ATESOR" or "Atesor AI".
- The command and package name is `atesor-ai`, in code font.
- The tagline is "From source to verified riscv64."

## Other trademarks

- Eclipse, the Eclipse logo, Eclipse Atesor and Atesor are trademarks of Eclipse Foundation AISBL. For the Eclipse logo, see [Logo and artwork](https://www.eclipse.org/org/artwork/).
- RISC-V and the RISC-V logo are registered trademarks of RISC-V International. This site shows the RISC-V symbol from the official logo file, unchanged. For the RISC-V logo, see the [RISC-V branding guidelines](https://riscv.org/about/risc-v-branding-guidelines/).
